states.summary: Alabama is a governance-first state. Its ALSDE template is one of the most operationally detailed model AI policies in the set, organized around eight pillars (Strategy, Governance, Data Privacy and Security, Procurement, Implementation, Competency Development, Risk Management, and Utility and Effectiveness) and built on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. It reads like a compliance and procurement instrument for district administrators rather than a classroom-pedagogy guide. Its most distinctive provision is a required process for students to contest AI-generated grades (same, Use of AI Systems).

documents.title: AI Policy Template for Local Education Agencies, Version 1.0
documents.issuer: Alabama State Department of Education (ALSDE), Dr. Eric G. Mackey, State Superintendent
documents.type: Model policy (template LEAs adopt and customize; voluntary)

documents.title: HB 329 Enrolled, "An Act Relating to public K-12 schools... to expand the definition of computer science; to require all Alabama public school students to complete an approved computer science course as a requirement for graduation"
documents.issuer: Alabama Legislature (Reps. Faulkner, Collins, Baker, Hulsey, Colvin)

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Responsible integration that maximizes benefit while mitigating risk** is the template's stated primary goal (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, Executive Summary and Purpose).
- **AI supplements, not replaces, human instruction.** "AI systems will be used to supplement, not replace, human instruction" (same, Purpose). The eight pillars "place students and educators at the core... ensuring that AI systems supplement, rather than replace, human instruction" (Executive Summary). *[Recommendation / stated principle]*
- **A create-not-just-consume stance in statute.** HB 329 amends the computer-science definition so that "Content should focus on teaching students how to create new technologies, not simply how to use technology" (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.1, §16-46B-1(2)). *[Requirement — definitional]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- The template addresses LEA leadership and defines "Users" broadly as "parents/guardians, students, educators, administrators, and management" (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, Terminology). *[Scope]*
- HB 329 applies to all Alabama public K-12 schools (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.2, §16-46B-1(10)). *[Scope, Requirement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- The template sets **permissive default use with conditions**: "All users are allowed to use AI systems" (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, Use of AI Systems). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- Conditions on use (model rules a district would adopt): users "need to indicate that the work is the result of AI"; must "cite in their works the AI systems used"; must "verify and validate the content before it is submitted"; teachers must tell students "when AI system(s) will be in their classrooms and how the AI system(s) work" (same). *[Recommendation / model rules]*
- **Restriction on AI surveillance/profiling:** where law does not authorize it, "LEAs shall ensure the AI systems do not track student's behaviors and are not used for profiling students" (same). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- **Vendor data-training prohibition (Appendix A):** a Data Usage Restriction Clause states the contractor "is expressly prohibited from using any data provided to it... for the purpose of training a new AI System to be used in a new product" (same, Appendix A). *[Recommendation / model contract language]*
- **This is a template, so none of these are statewide mandates on content.** They become binding only where a district adopts them.

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Data privacy and security is one of the eight pillars**, tied to federal, state, and local compliance, plus compliance audits and Corrective Action Plans from contractors (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, Data Privacy and Security).
- **Academic integrity** is handled through the disclosure-and-citation model rules above rather than a detection regime.
- **Accessibility/equity:** the template commits that "everyone gets access to the AI System" under the Utility and Effectiveness pillar (same). A deeper equity or accessibility framework (for example specific assistive-tech requirements) is **Not found in the provided documents**. *[Recommendation, limited]*
- **Ethics/bias:** procurement requires a contractor statement that they "have taken steps to minimize bias" and used "human-in-the-loop during model development" (same, AI Procurement). *[Recommendation / model rule]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Competency Development pillar:** LEAs "will develop an education and training program to ensure all users understand how AI works" across "computer science, mathematics, social studies, sciences" and safe/effective/responsible use (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, AI Competency Development).
- **Assessment/grading:** teachers using AI for grading "need to verify and validate the accuracy and completeness of the grading," and "LEAs shall develop a process for students to contest the grades generated by AI systems" (same, Use of AI Systems). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- **Curriculum (statute):** HB 329 requires the department to identify approved CS courses and to "develop and publish a set of minimum standards that must be taught in every course with embedded computer science skills and experiences" (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.4, §16-46B-7(c)(1)). *[Requirement on the agency]* The AI-specific content of those minimum standards is **Not found in the provided documents** (not yet published). *[Unresolved]*
- **Implementation/governance:** the template requires (as a model) an AI Governance Committee or expansion of a Data Governance Committee, plus a risk register with Low/Medium/High risk levels under the NIST AI RMF (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, AI Governance; Risk Management). *[Recommendation / model structure]*
sections.offloading:
- The template's core anti-offloading commitment is the repeated "supplement, not replace, human instruction" principle and the human-in-the-loop requirement: LEAs are "committed to using human judgment during the implementation and use of AI systems and will develop a process as to why and when a human will be involved" (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, Utility and Effectiveness).
- The verify-and-validate rule (users must check AI content before submission or use) is a light guard against uncritical acceptance of AI output (same, Use of AI Systems). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- HB 329's definitional emphasis on creating rather than merely using technology (p.1) is the closest statutory signal toward preserving higher-order skill. *[Requirement — definitional]*
- **A developed cognitive-science treatment (metacognition, independent reasoning, creativity, over-reliance) comparable to some other states is Not found in the provided documents.** Alabama's documents are governance and compliance instruments, not pedagogy guides. *[Evidence gap]*
sections.graduate:
- **Near-term graduates (before class of 2032):** No guaranteed statewide AI or CS exposure. Experience depends entirely on which LEA policies were adopted from the voluntary template and on existing CS offerings. *Basis: template is voluntary; HB 329's graduation requirement starts class of 2032 (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.4).*
- **Graduates from the class of 2032 onward:** Will have earned at least one department-approved CS credit (or a course with embedded CS skills), where "computer science" is statutorily defined to include artificial intelligence and to emphasize creating technology (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.1, p.4). *Basis: §16-46B-1(2), §16-46B-7(c)(1).*
- **Where a district adopted the template:** students may have experienced explicit AI-disclosure and citation expectations, teacher notice when AI is used in class, and a formal route to contest an AI-generated grade (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, Use of AI Systems).
- **Higher-education implication:** For the next several admission cycles, assume no common Alabama AI baseline and high inter-district variance. Do not assume incoming Alabama students have had formal AI instruction. The guaranteed baseline is a 2032-and-later phenomenon.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Alabama students from adopting districts may arrive expecting a *right to contest an algorithmic grade* (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, Use of AI Systems). Most university grade-appeal policies say nothing about AI-assisted assessment, so these students may expect a due-process step their institution has not defined.
- **Higher-education implication:** Alabama's vendor Data Usage Restriction Clause (Appendix A) is a ready-made procurement model. An institution negotiating enterprise AI contracts could adopt the same "your data will not train a new product" attestation language.
- **Higher-education implication:** HB 329 already reaches into higher education in two concrete ways that in-state universities should note. A completed CS course can satisfy a math or science freshman-admission requirement at a public in-state institution (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.4, §16-46B-7(b)), and higher-education institutions are eligible "High Quality Professional Learning Providers" for K-12 CS teacher training (p.2, §16-46B-1(7)). In-state institutions may already be admissions-linked to, or PD partners of, the K-12 system.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because the statutory baseline is dated to 2032, institutions should plan for a transition cohort problem. Students arriving in the late 2020s and early 2030s will straddle the "no guaranteed baseline" and "guaranteed CS-with-AI credit" regimes within a single incoming class.
sections.response:
- **AI tool availability:** Adopt Alabama's vendor data-protection attestation (Appendix A) into institutional AI procurement so student and faculty data are contractually barred from training vendor products.
- **Onboarding:** Because near-term Alabama cohorts have no common AI baseline, run an entry AI-literacy check rather than assuming prior instruction. Revisit this assumption for 2032-and-later cohorts.
- **Assessment design and academic integrity:** Mirror the template's disclosure-and-citation expectation (students disclose and cite AI use) so the college expectation is continuous with what adopting Alabama districts taught. Consider defining an explicit appeals path for AI-assisted or AI-generated grades, which Alabama students from adopting districts may expect.
- **Governance:** Alabama's eight-pillar, NIST-based structure is a usable scaffold for an institutional AI governance committee, risk register, and audit cycle.
- **Faculty development:** Position institutional CS/AI PD offerings for the K-12 pipeline, since HB 329 makes higher-education institutions eligible PD providers (p.2).
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Build on the statute's "create, not just use" framing (p.1) and the template's human-in-the-loop and verify-and-validate rules to keep AI positioned as a tool under human judgment.
sections.unique:
- **A required student process to contest AI-generated grades** (ALSDE-AI-Policy-Template.docx, Use of AI Systems). This algorithmic-grade due-process idea is rare in the set.
- **Appendix A vendor Data Usage Restriction Clause** — detailed model contract language prohibiting use of LEA data to train a new AI product, with a Request-for-Approval process for district-specific customization (same, Appendix A).
- **Eight-pillar, NIST-AI-RMF governance architecture** with a formal risk register and Corrective Action Plans from vendors (same, Risk Management; AI Governance).
- **Statutory higher-education linkage:** CS course counts toward public in-state university math/science admission requirements, and universities are named PD providers (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.4 and p.2).
- **Statutory AI-in-CS definition** effective October 1, 2026, with the graduation requirement dated to the class of 2032 (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.1, p.4, p.5).
sections.gaps:
- **Template adoption is unknown.** The document is a voluntary model, so how many of Alabama's LEAs adopted it, and with what customizations, is **Not found in the provided documents**. Student experience cannot be assumed statewide.
- **The AI content of the class-of-2032 CS standards is not yet defined.** HB 329 directs the department to publish minimum standards for embedded-CS courses, but those standards are **Not found in the provided documents**. *[Unresolved]*
- **Provenance of the template host.** The only retrievable copy is on a third-party site (aiforeducation.io), not an ALSDE domain. Content was verified by extraction, but an agency-hosted original was not located. Treat the text as authentic per extraction while noting the host caveat.
- **No classroom-level student-use scale, prohibition list of specific tasks, or grade-band literacy progression** appears in either document. Those instruments are **Not found in the provided documents**.
- **Signing date and gubernatorial action on HB 329** were not the subject of the enrolled text beyond the October 1, 2026 effective date (HB329-enrolled.pdf, p.5); a signing date is **Not found in the provided documents**.

states.summary: Alaska's framework is a values-and-governance document organized around seven guiding principles: Human-Centered, Fair Access, Transparency, Oversight, Security, Ethical Use, and Cultural Responsiveness. Its governing stance is a deliberate middle path: "an outright ban impedes skill and career development, while unrestricted access falls short of needed protections" (p.3). Its most distinctive feature is that Cultural Responsiveness is a first-class principle, requiring that AI tools "affirm, rather than diminish, the diverse cultures of Alaska" and aligning with the Alaska Standards for Culturally Responsive Schools (p.11).

documents.title: Alaska's Strategic Framework: Artificial Intelligence for K-12 — Recommendations and Considerations for Districts
documents.issuer: Alaska Department of Education & Early Development (DEED), with the Alaska AI K12 Advisory Group
documents.date: October 2025 (presented to the State Board of Education)
documents.type: State education-agency framework (explicitly recommendations, not mandates)

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human augmentation over replacement.** "AI must augment human capabilities, critical thinking, and creativity, never replacing human judgment or decision-making... All AI use should begin with human inquiry and culminate in human reflection and insight" (Alaska-K12-AI-Framework.pdf, p.4, Human-Centered principle). *[Recommendation / stated principle]*
- **A balanced anti-ban, anti-free-for-all stance** (p.3).
- **Equity across a vast, rural, connectivity-challenged state** is a stated first-order objective (p.6, Fair Access).
- **Vision:** "To empower every Alaskan student and educator to ethically and effectively engage with Artificial Intelligence, fostering critical thinking, creativity, and responsible digital citizenship" (p.1). *[Stated vision]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- "Designed to serve as a flexible resource for school boards, administrators, educators, and students" (p.3). The How-to-Use section assigns each audience a use: boards use the Guiding Principles for policy, administrators use the key areas of focus for implementation and PD, educators use it for classroom practice (p.3). *[Scope]*
- Applies to "all students, teachers, staff, administrators, and third parties who develop, implement, or interact with AI technologies... where permitted by local and state policy," covering generative AI, intelligent tutoring systems, conversational agents, automation, and analytics tools (p.3). *[Scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **Permissive-with-oversight default.** Districts "should move beyond outright bans and instead develop a balanced approach" (p.5).
- **Restriction on high-stakes automation:** "Robust human oversight is mandatory for any decisions that directly impact students, such as grading or disciplinary actions" (p.8, Oversight principle). *[Recommendation, phrased as imperative within a voluntary document]*
- **Prohibition guidance on data:** "Explicit prohibitions against entering sensitive student data, PII, or confidential information into publicly accessible AI tools are essential" (p.9, Security). The "Do's and Don'ts" suggest using anonymized data in prompts and "never uploading documents containing confidential school or district information" (p.9). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- A printed student-use permission scale is **referenced but not reproduced**: "Districts can utilize an AI Acceptable Use Scale to build clear expectations for AI use on specific assignments" (p.10). The scale's levels are **Not found in the provided documents**. *[Unresolved]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Security** is a dedicated principle: cybersecurity, PII protection, and compliance with "the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), and the Children's Internet Protection Act (CIPA)" (p.9).
- **Fair Access / equity:** addresses "the digital divide, particularly concerning equitable broadband access and device availability in Alaska's diverse and often remote regions," referencing a 2023 DEED survey of device access and connectivity (p.6).
- **Ethics / academic integrity:** "Submitting AI-generated work as original without proper citation is considered plagiarism"; policies should require disclosure and citation (p.7 Transparency; p.10 Ethical Use).
- **Accessibility** as an explicit assistive-tech requirement comparable to some states is **Not found in the provided documents** beyond general equity framing. *[Limited]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Educator autonomy is emphasized:** "Educators must have the autonomy to make professional decisions regarding AI use in their classrooms. Districts should support educators in updating syllabi and classroom policies to include AI integrity guidelines" (p.5).
- **AI literacy for all** staff and students: "basic AI principles and applications," "recognize when AI is employed and an awareness of its limits," and "ethical and responsible AI use, including topics of safety, bias, and disinformation" (p.6).
- **Curriculum:** AI aligns with existing Alaska Digital Literacy Standards (p.5).
- **Effective prompting frameworks** named: EVERY ("Evaluated, Verify, Edit, Revise, You are responsible") and PREP ("Prompt, Role, Explicit Information, Parameters") (p.10). *[Instructional guidance / examples]*
- **Implementation supports:** the framework points to a companion resource website with policy roadmaps, classroom strategies, and student guides (p.5), and provides ready templates (sample district board policy, school handbook language, family/community AI FAQ) (p.7). *[Recommendation / examples]*
sections.offloading:
- The Human-Centered principle is the core anti-offloading commitment: AI "never replacing human judgment," with "all AI use" beginning "with human inquiry" and culminating "in human reflection and insight" (Alaska-K12-AI-Framework.pdf, p.4).
- The EVERY prompting framework builds user accountability directly into practice, ending in "You are responsible" (p.10). *[Instructional guidance]*
- The Research and Evidence Base section directs districts to assess AI's impact on "student engagement, motivation, cognition, and deep learning" and notes "robust, large-scale independent evidence on AI's effectiveness in education is still limited" (p.5).
- "Rethinking Education" frames AI as a lever for "problem-solving, innovative design, and creative expression" rather than task completion (p.5).
- **A named, developed treatment of cognitive offloading, metacognition, or over-reliance comparable to New Mexico's is Not found in the provided documents.** Alaska's guard is the human-in-the-loop principle plus the accountability-oriented prompting frameworks, rather than an explicit cognitive-science section. *[Evidence gap]*
sections.graduate:
- **Uneven by district.** Because the framework is recommendation-level and the document itself lists divergent district policies (Fairbanks, Mat-Su, Wrangell, Anchorage, p.8), a single incoming Alaska cohort will vary widely in AI exposure. *Basis: p.3 (recommendations not mandates); p.8 (district examples).*
- **Where districts adopted the framework's posture:** students may have experienced disclosure-and-citation expectations for AI use (p.7, p.10), teacher-set per-assignment expectations (possibly via an AI Acceptable Use Scale, p.10), and AI-literacy instruction covering AI's limits, bias, and disinformation (p.6).
- **Exposure to prompting frameworks** (EVERY, PREP) where educators taught them (p.10).
- **Higher-education implication:** Assume high variance and rural/connectivity effects. Some Alaska students, especially from remote regions, may have had limited device or broadband access to AI tools despite the framework's equity aims (p.6), so prior hands-on AI experience cannot be assumed uniform.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Alaska students from adopting districts may arrive expecting AI use to be governed per assignment with disclosure and citation, rather than banned outright (p.5, p.10). A silent or blanket-ban syllabus will contrast with that experience.
- **Higher-education implication:** The Cultural Responsiveness principle (p.11) means some Alaska students, particularly Alaska Native students, may have been taught to interrogate AI tools for cultural bias, misappropriation, and exclusion of local context. Institutions serving these students should expect and support that critical stance rather than treat AI as culturally neutral.
- **Higher-education implication:** Alaska's framework was co-authored with higher-education partners (UAA College of Engineering, ANSEP, p.1). In-state institutions may already be connected to the K-12 AI-readiness effort and could formalize that pipeline.
- **Higher-education implication:** The equity/connectivity emphasis (p.6) signals that "bring your own AI access" assumptions will disadvantage rural Alaska students. Institutions should provide sanctioned, no-cost AI access rather than assume students arrive with paid tools and reliable bandwidth.
sections.response:
- **AI tool availability and equity:** Provide institution-sanctioned, no-cost AI access with reliable infrastructure, since Alaska's own framework treats access as an equity precondition (p.6).
- **Onboarding:** Run an entry AI-literacy check keyed to the framework's own literacy definition (principles, recognizing AI and its limits, ethical use, p.6), given high inter-district variance.
- **Assessment design:** Adopt an explicit per-assignment AI-permission approach continuous with the "AI Acceptable Use Scale" idea Alaska districts were pointed to (p.10). Pair assignments with disclosure-and-citation expectations (p.7).
- **Academic integrity:** Mirror the disclosure-and-attribution model rather than a detection regime, matching what adopting Alaska districts taught (p.7, p.10).
- **Accessibility and cultural responsiveness:** Extend the Cultural Responsiveness principle (p.11) into course and tool selection, especially for Alaska Native students, and involve community/cultural expertise in AI-integrated course design.
- **Governance:** Use the seven principles and the "level of human oversight the tool requires and allows" evaluation criterion (p.8) as a ready scaffold for institutional AI tool vetting.
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Adopt the human-inquiry-to-human-reflection framing (p.4) and the accountability-ending EVERY prompting framework (p.10) for continuity from high school to college.
sections.unique:
- **Cultural Responsiveness as a named guiding principle** (p.4, p.11), requiring AI to "affirm, rather than diminish, the diverse cultures of Alaska," aligning with the Alaska Standards for Culturally Responsive Schools, and engaging elders and community members. Distinctive in naming a specific cultural community rather than gesturing at diversity abstractly.
- **Explicit balanced stance** rejecting both outright bans and unrestricted access (p.3).
- **Named prompting frameworks** EVERY and PREP with user accountability built in (p.10).
- **AI Use Disclaimer** (p.12): the framework discloses it was itself drafted with Gemini and ChatGPT, modeling the transparency it asks of others.
- **Higher-education co-authorship** via the advisory group (UAA College of Engineering, ANSEP) (p.1).
sections.gaps:
- **Recommendation-level status limits every student claim.** District adoption data is **Not found in the provided documents**, and the framework itself shows divergent district policies (p.8).
- **The referenced "AI Acceptable Use Scale" is not reproduced** in the framework (p.10); its levels are **Not found in the provided documents**.
- **Companion subpages** were not part of the provided file and were not analyzed. *[Scope limit]*
- **No enacted Alaska statute** on AI in K-12 appears in the provided files. sources records "No enacted statute identified." *[Absence]*
- **Definitions, references, and the advisory roster** (pp.1, 12-15) are supporting material and were read but not exhaustively transcribed; they do not add policy requirements.

states.summary: Arizona's guidance is the most pedagogically and ethically developed document reviewed so far, and it is aimed squarely at the questions a higher-education faculty member cares about. It supplies eight ethical considerations (pp.10-20), a five-goal AI-literacy framework aligned to state standards and the State 48 Graduate Profile (p.23), teacher and student use cases (pp.24-25), and — unusually — an explicit, research-cited treatment of cognitive offloading (pp.26-27).

documents.title: HB 4005 (Senate engrossed) — AI instruction in grades 3, 6, 8, 10, 12
documents.issuer: Arizona Legislature, 57th Legislature 2nd Regular Session
documents.date: Senate-engrossed June 11, 2026; vetoed by Gov. Hobbs June 19, 2026

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human agency and oversight at every stage.** "This guidance was built around a core value of human agency and oversight at every stage of GenAI use and implementation" (p.7). *[Recommendation / stated value]*
- **AI literacy as the central imperative** ("A Call for AI Literacy," cover; p.22): AI literacy "includes technical understanding, ethical reasoning, and human judgment needed to engage thoughtfully with AI systems" (p.22).
- **A balanced posture:** "AI presents extraordinary opportunities... It also raises important questions related to bias, misinformation, privacy, security, mental well-being, and access. Both realities deserve our thoughtful attention" (p.4). *[Stated stance]*
- **Alignment to Arizona's own frameworks:** the State 48 Graduate Profile (4 Futures, 8 Essential Skills) and Arizona Academic Standards anchor instructional decisions (pp.6, 21, 23).

### Intended audiences and scope
- Designed "to support Arizona education leaders as they lead GenAI implementation" (p.7), with role-based use: boards for policy, administrators for implementation and PD, educators for classroom practice (p.7 organization table). *[Scope]*
- Covers instruction, operations, and administration; addresses generative AI, multimodal, reasoning, and agentic AI (pp.8-9). *[Scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **No statewide permission or prohibition rules** exist; the document models district-level approaches rather than issuing rules. *[Not a mandate]*
- It endorses **per-assignment AI-use expectations set locally**, citing Chandler Unified's AI Integration Model (adapted from an AI Scale) (p.28), Brophy College Preparatory's AI Usage Guide (GenAI use for research, brainstorming, minor revisions as default permission), and Maricopa Unified's student-use system (p.34). *[Examples]*
- **Data-privacy prohibition guidance:** board policy should "mandate that no personally identifiable information (PII) be entered into non-vetted or public AI platforms" (p.35); "never uploading documents containing confidential school or district information" (implied throughout the security discussion, pp.14, 19). *[Recommendation / model rule]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
The eight ethical considerations (pp.10-20) are the document's spine:
- **Bias** (p.11): data, model (including sycophancy), and human bias; "GenAI will never be bias-free." *[Instructional guidance]*
- **False and misleading content** (p.12): "stochastic parrot," hallucination, synthetic media/deepfakes. *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Intellectual property** (p.13): authorship/ownership, training-data fair use, and **Indigenous/tribal cultural knowledge** governed by community-specific protocols. *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Data and information privacy** (p.14): FERPA; explicit reference to honoring "the data authority of the state's 22 sovereign tribal nations."
- **Equitable access** (p.16): the digital use gap, digital design gap, and digital access gap (from the 2024 NETP); IDEA and Section 504; accessibility to "WCAG 2.1 Level AA."
- **Mental well-being** (p.17): anthropomorphism, parasocial attachment, sycophancy; note that "72% of teens have used AI companions." *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Environmental impact** (p.18): data-center energy/water, with Arizona-specific data-center context. *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Cybersecurity** (p.19): AI-enhanced phishing, agentic AI as attack surface, prompt injection, "narrow access" principle. *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Academic integrity** is handled under Transparency and Ethical Use plus the Responsible Classroom Use section: disclose and cite AI use, build a framework rather than a "gotcha" regime (pp.28, 34).
- **Ten recommendations** close the ethics chapter (p.20), including "Establish a culture of human oversight" and treating "human in the loop" as "more than a catch phrase."

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Five AI-literacy goals** (p.23), each mapped to Arizona Academic Standards and State 48 Essential Skills: Foundational Understanding of AI Systems; Intentional and Strategic Use of AI; Ethical, Responsible, and Human-Centered Use; Critical Evaluation of AI Outputs and Information; Human Agency and the Human Advantage. *[Instructional guidance / framework]*
- **Teacher use cases** (p.24): instructional thinking and design, designing for learner variability, professional workflow support. **Student use cases** (p.25): sense-making and exploration, creation and iteration, access and agency. *[Examples]*
- **Assessment and grading** (p.27): LLMs are "unreliable for grading" (Xue et al., 2026); teacher judgment is primary (MLA, 2026); Arizona students "tend to prefer teachers, as opposed to AI, to provide guidance, feedback, and grades." *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Implementation** (pp.32-36) uses a "boat" analogy and a "3ssential" early-moves framework: determine and communicate approved tools; train staff on top-line guardrails; clarify expectations for GenAI use. Plus PD (build then deepen AI literacy) and adaptation/refinement cycles.
sections.offloading:
Arizona's treatment here is the most explicit and research-grounded in the corpus so far.
- The **"Cognitive Offloading"** subsection (pp.26-27) argues "not all cognitive offloading is harmful" and reframes the question as "not whether students offload thinking, but which thinking they offload and why" (p.26). *[Instructional guidance]*
- It cites research on both sides: overreliance where students "complete entire tasks from beginning to end... may retain less understanding" (Kosmyna et al., 2025), and "purposefully-designed AI tutors may help students manage cognitive load... resulting in higher achievement" (Kestin et al., 2025) (p.27). *[Instructional guidance, cited]*
- Its mitigation is a **microtask / productive-friction** model (Furze, 2026a): teachers decide "which cognitive muscles to focus on and which ones rest," design "AI-infused tasks in which students explain their reasoning, defend their choices, or apply ideas in performance-based tasks," and use "checkpoints and reflection to make thinking visible." The goal is "productive resistance that support[s] learning," not eliminating all offload (p.27). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Over-reliance** is named as a distinct risk: "Offloading mental tasks can... remove productive struggle that helps learners develop persistence and strengthen problem-solving skills" (p.26). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **The Redesign: AI Inspiration** (p.29) proposes preserving higher-order learning by redesigning around "authentic creation and problem-solving," project-based and interdisciplinary learning, portfolios, exhibitions, and performance-based assessment, with teachers as "Designers of Learning, Coaches of Growth, and Expert Guides."
- The five AI-literacy goals explicitly protect "Human Agency and the Human Advantage" and "Critical Evaluation of AI Outputs" as learning targets (p.23). *[Framework]*
sections.graduate:
- **Uneven by district; no guaranteed statewide baseline.** The guidance is voluntary and university-authored, HB 4005 (AI-instruction requirement) was vetoed, and the document itself cites divergent district models (pp.28, 34). *Basis: p.7; sources.*
- **Where districts adopted the guidance's approach**, students may bring: familiarity with per-assignment AI-use expectations (Chandler AI Integration Model, Brophy, Maricopa examples, pp.28, 34); a disclosure-and-citation habit (p.28); exposure to the five AI-literacy goals including critical evaluation of AI outputs and bias awareness (p.23); and the idea that they are accountable for AI-assisted work.
- **A learned skepticism toward AI detectors**, which the guidance calls unreliable and biased against non-native English speakers and neurodivergent students (p.28).
- **Exposure to cognitive-offloading language** ("tool not a crutch," "productive struggle") where teachers taught it; student quotes in the document itself reflect this framing (pp.26-27).
- **Higher-education implication:** Assume wide variance within any Arizona cohort. The students most shaped by this guidance will arrive fluent in the exact vocabulary (human-in-the-loop, per-assignment AI levels, critical evaluation) that a well-designed college syllabus uses; others will have had little formal exposure.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Arizona's guidance mirrors mature higher-education thinking on integrity. Students from adopting districts may arrive expecting disclosure-based integrity, per-assignment AI permissions, and *no reliance on AI detectors* (p.28). Institutions still using detectors as primary evidence may face students taught that those tools are unreliable and discriminatory.
- **Higher-education implication:** The cognitive-offloading framing (pp.26-27) means some Arizona students were taught to distinguish productive from unproductive AI use. Faculty can build on this rather than introduce it cold, using the same microtask/productive-friction language.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because the guidance is authored by a university institute (NAU) and reviewed by ASU-affiliated and ADE staff (p.5), Arizona higher education is already a producer of K-12 AI guidance. In-state institutions can formalize that role and align entry expectations to the five AI-literacy goals (p.23).
- **Higher-education implication:** The equity and accessibility emphasis (digital use/design/access gaps, WCAG 2.1 AA, IDEA/504, p.16) signals that Arizona students may expect accessible, sanctioned AI access. Rural and tribal students may have had constrained access despite the guidance's aims.
- **Higher-education implication:** Tribal data-sovereignty content (pp.13-14) means some Arizona students, particularly from the state's 22 sovereign tribal nations, may have been taught that cultural knowledge carries community-specific use protocols. Institutions handling Indigenous materials should expect and respect that stance.
sections.response:
- **Academic integrity:** Move away from AI-detector-based enforcement toward disclosure-and-process approaches, matching what adopting Arizona districts taught (p.28). Adopt an explicit per-assignment AI-permission structure continuous with the district models students saw (p.28, p.34).
- **Assessment design:** Apply the microtask / productive-friction model (p.27) — specify which cognitive work students must do unaided and where AI may assist — and favor performance-based tasks, portfolios, and reasoning-defense (p.29).
- **AI tool availability and accessibility:** Provide sanctioned, accessible (WCAG 2.1 AA) AI access so access does not depend on ability to pay, echoing the equity framing (p.16).
- **Onboarding and faculty development:** Use the five AI-literacy goals (p.23) as an entry rubric and a faculty-development scaffold, since incoming students may already have met them.
- **Governance:** Adopt the "human agency and oversight imperative" (p.7) and the eight-consideration ethics map (pp.10-20) as a ready institutional AI-governance scaffold, including tribal data sovereignty where relevant.
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Import the document's central reframing — the question is which thinking students offload and why (p.26) — into course design so AI supports targeted skills while core reasoning stays with the student.
sections.unique:
- **An explicit, research-cited cognitive-offloading section** (pp.26-27) with the microtask / productive-friction model and citations to Kosmyna et al. (2025), Kestin et al. (2025), and Furze (2026a). Rare depth for a state-level document.
- **Five AI-literacy goals mapped cell-by-cell to state academic standards and the State 48 Essential Skills** (p.23).
- **Eight-consideration ethics chapter** including tribal data sovereignty (22 sovereign nations), environmental impact with Arizona data-center specifics, and mental well-being (anthropomorphism, sycophancy) (pp.13-19).
- **University authorship** (NAU's Arizona Institute for Education and the Economy) rather than a state agency — a higher-education-produced state guidance, comparable to Florida's UF-coordinated effort.
- **Direct anti-AI-detector stance** with equity rationale (p.28) and an explicit statement that LLMs are unreliable graders (p.27).
sections.gaps:
- **Not a state-agency document and not a mandate.** Actual district adoption is **Not found in the provided documents**; the guidance is university-authored and voluntary (p.7).
- **No enacted statute.** HB 4005 was vetoed and HB 4040 died; the HB 4005 bill text is in the folder but its veto is secondary-sourced. The HB 4040 higher-ed provision (Board of Regents universities adopting AI policies) is **unconfirmed at primary source** and did not become law. *[Unresolved]*
- **Referenced district instruments** (Chandler AI Integration Model / AI Scale, Brophy AI Usage Guide, Maricopa student-use system) are cited but their full contents are **Not found in the provided documents** (external links). *[Unresolved]*
- **Pages 38-41** (Additional Resources, References, Long Alt Descriptions) are supporting material, read but not transcribed; they add no policy requirements.
- **HB 4005's exact grade-level instruction requirements** were summarized from sources (grades 3, 6, 8, 10, 12) and not independently read from the bill text in this pass. *[Partial]*

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **No ADE guidance exists**. *[Absence — confirmed]*
- The Virtual Arkansas guide's objective is to help districts plan AI integration via a maturity model — but it is a **third-party** resource, not state policy (VirtualArkansas-AI-Planning-Guide.pdf, p.1). *[Recommendation — third-party]*
- The AI CoE's objectives are government-wide: "Protect Arkansans and Their Data," "Improve Government Services," and "Prepare Arkansas for the AI Economy" (AI-CoE-Initial-Report.pdf, Executive Summary). *[Other — state strategy, not K-12]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- Virtual Arkansas guide: district leaders adopting/planning AI (third-party, voluntary) (VirtualArkansas-AI-Planning-Guide.pdf). *[Scope]*
- AI CoE report: state government, a Data and Transparency Panel, a proposed Chief AI Officer, and the state workforce (AI-CoE-Initial-Report.pdf, Recommendations). *[Scope — not schools]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **Not found in the provided documents** at the state level. The Virtual Arkansas guide includes appendices on "Policy Considerations," "Recommended Language for Existing AUP," and an "AI Risk Assessment for School Districts" (VirtualArkansas-AI-Planning-Guide.pdf, Table of Contents), but these are third-party templates, not state rules. *[Absence at state level]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- The Virtual Arkansas guide's "Policy, Ethical, & Legal Considerations" domain mirrors Michigan's rubric (VirtualArkansas-AI-Planning-Guide.pdf, p.12). *[Third-party rubric]*
- The AI CoE report recommends state data classification, risk management, and safeguards against misuse (AI-CoE-Initial-Report.pdf, Recommendations 1-2) — government data governance, not student privacy guidance. *[Other]*
- State-agency guidance on these dimensions is **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Absence]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- The Virtual Arkansas guide contains Professional Learning, Instructional Framework, and Measuring Student Learning & Assessments domains (mirroring Michigan) (VirtualArkansas-AI-Planning-Guide.pdf, Table of Contents) — third-party, not state. *[Third-party rubric]*
- The AI CoE recommends "Develop an AI-Ready State Government Workforce" and "Build Employer-Aligned AI Talent Pipelines" (AI-CoE-Initial-Report.pdf, Recommendations 5-6) — workforce, not K-12 instruction. *[Other]*
sections.offloading: - **Not found in the provided documents** at the state level. The Virtual Arkansas guide, as a Michigan-lineage maturity rubric, describes maturity outcomes (see the Michigan analysis) rather than cognitive-offloading pedagogy; and it is third-party. *[Absence at state level]*
sections.graduate:
- **No common baseline; extreme variance.** With no ADE guidance, incoming Arkansas students' AI exposure depends entirely on their district. *Basis: sources.*
- Districts that used the Virtual Arkansas planning guide would have followed the Michigan-lineage maturity model, so their students' experience resembles the Michigan "stage-dependent" profile.
- **Higher-education implication:** Do not assume any shared Arkansas AI baseline. Plan for large district-to-district variation and confirm rather than infer.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** The absence of a state baseline means Arkansas cohorts will be heterogeneous in AI literacy and governance experience; institutions should establish a common entry baseline rather than assume prior instruction.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because the state's substantive K-12 planning resource is a Michigan-Virtual adaptation, Arkansas and Michigan graduates from planning-guide-using districts may share the same maturity-model framing — useful if an institution enrolls from both.
- **Higher-education implication:** Arkansas's state AI strategy is workforce- and government-services-oriented (the AI CoE), with "employer-aligned AI talent pipelines" (AI-CoE-Initial-Report.pdf, Rec. 6). Higher education's tie-in here is workforce development, not K-12 classroom preparation.
sections.response:
- **Onboarding:** Given no state baseline, run an explicit AI-literacy orientation and assume high variance among Arkansas students.
- **Academic integrity and assessment design:** Provide clear per-assignment AI-permission structures, since Arkansas students are unlikely to arrive with a shared AI-use framework.
- **Governance:** If a maturity self-assessment is useful, the Michigan-lineage rubric that Arkansas districts may have used is a ready model.
- **Workforce alignment:** Engage the Arkansas AI CoE's talent-pipeline agenda (AI-CoE-Initial-Report.pdf, Rec. 6) as the state's actual higher-ed-adjacent AI hook.
sections.unique:
- **A third-party (Virtual Arkansas / Michigan Virtual) planning guide stands in for state guidance** — the same Michigan-lineage maturity rubric, adapted for Arkansas (VirtualArkansas-AI-Planning-Guide.pdf, p.1). A notable "borrowed framework" pattern.

- **Both provided documents are non-agency or non-K-12:** the Virtual Arkansas guide is third-party (Michigan Virtual lineage) and the AI CoE report is government-wide. Neither should be cited as Arkansas Department of Education guidance. *[Provenance caution]*

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence in California: Learning with AI, Learning about AI
documents.issuer: California Department of Education (CDE)

documents.title: Model Policy: Artificial Intelligence in Education
documents.issuer: California Department of Education, developed with the California AI in Education Working Group under SB 1288 (Becker, 2024)
documents.type: Model policy (voluntary template for LEAs/charters; explicitly non-binding)

documents.title: AI Resource Kit
documents.issuer: California Department of Education
documents.type: Supplementary resource (present in folder; see Evidence Gaps)

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human relationships are central; AI supplements, never replaces.** "AI must be used to support human-centered learning environments, not replace them" (CDE-AI-Model-Policy-2026.docx, framing); "AI or any other technology cannot replace the value of a student's relationship with a caring educator" (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf, Introduction).
- **Learning with AI and learning about AI** as twin goals (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf, throughout).
- **Equity and the digital divide** are throughlines, tied to the state's "Closing the Digital Divide" and "Antibias Education" initiatives (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf, "Pros and Cons," "Social Impacts").
- **AI literacy as a core academic competency** for all students and educators, per Education Code §33548 (CDE-AI-Model-Policy-2026.docx, "AI Literacy as a Core Academic Competency"). *[Recommendation, tied to statute]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- The 2023 guidance addresses educators, administrators, and educational leaders (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf). *[Scope]*
- The Model Policy is written for a Governing Board to adopt at the LEA/charter level, covering students, educators, and staff (CDE-AI-Model-Policy-2026.docx). *[Scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses (Model Policy)
- **Acceptable use:** AI "should be used to support learning, instruction, and operations in ways that enhance human decision-making and should not substitute for critical thinking or required academic work"; all AI "must be [District or Charter School] authorized" (CDE-AI-Model-Policy-2026.docx, "Acceptable Use"). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- **Instructional discretion (per-assignment):** "Educators should have the discretion to determine when and how AI may be used in individual assignments... Permitted AI use may vary from one assignment to another" (Model Policy, "Instructional Discretion"). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- **Plagiarism:** "submitting AI-generated content without clear disclosure constitutes plagiarism and academic dishonesty" (Model Policy, "Plagiarism, Disclosure, & Citation"). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- **Safety prohibitions:** AI "should not be used to harm individuals, encourage self-harm, or cause harm to the school community" (Model Policy, "Safe & Responsible AI Use"). *[Recommendation / model rule]*
- **Data-entry restrictions:** students and educators "should not enter education records or other confidential information into AI tools unless expressly authorized"; personal AI accounts must not be used for student data or work (Model Policy, "Data Entry Restrictions," "Institutional AI Access"). *[Recommendation / model rule]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **AI detection software** "should not be used as the sole basis for disciplinary action or grade penalty," with reliance instead on "educator evaluation of student engagement, alternative assessment, and documented evidence of authorship," and "clear criteria for rebutting claims" made available to students and parents (CDE-AI-Model-Policy-2026.docx, "AI Detection Software").
- **Privacy by design:** AI tools should "protect student data, prohibit its use for training public AI models or advertising, and maintain strong security safeguards"; compliance with FERPA and California Education Code §49073.1 (Model Policy, "Privacy by Design," "Legal Compliance").
- **Parent/guardian review rights:** guardians "should have the right to request timely human review of any AI-generated outputs that inform decisions about their child"; annual informed consent required before autonomous AI-powered student-interaction tools (Model Policy, "Parent/Guardian Review Rights," "Transparency & Informed Consent").
- **Vendor safeguards:** pre-deployment evaluation for educational value, bias, and equity; enforceable contract provisions (breach notification, audit rights, data deletion on termination) (Model Policy, "Pre-Deployment Evaluation," "Vendor Contractual Safeguards").
- **Accessibility:** the 2023 guidance ties AI to Universal Design for Learning and assistive uses (text-to-speech, translation, screen readers) (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf, "Accessibility & personalization").
- **Ethics/bias:** algorithmic bias and social impacts are a dedicated theme (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf, "Social Impacts"); ethical risk assessment including "environmental costs, effects on mental health, embedded bias" (Model Policy, "Ethical Risk Assessment").

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Grading:** students "should be informed when their work will be submitted to AI to support grading or feedback," and "the educator of record retains sole authority to determine final grades" (CDE-AI-Model-Policy-2026.docx, "Grading and Assessment").
- **Curriculum and assessment redesign:** emphasize "human thinking, process, equity, and insight... over easily AI-generated products," with "cross-disciplinary grade-band progressions across all grade levels (TK-12) incorporating the foundational concepts of AI: Perception, Representation and Reasoning, Learning, Natural Interaction, and Societal Impact" (Model Policy, "Curriculum & Assessment Redesign").
- **AI literacy skills** named concretely: "claim extraction, confidence calibration, source triangulation, and mismatch detection," and analysis of "misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation" (Model Policy, "AI Literacy as a Core Academic Competency").
- **Curriculum integration** in the 2023 guidance builds on the California Computer Science Standards and the 5 Big Ideas of AI (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf, "Integrate 5 big ideas of AI").
- **PD:** the 2023 guidance ties to the State Superintendent's professional-learning initiative; the Model Policy requires "ongoing professional development and user training addressing AI literacy, data fluency, and learning science" (Model Policy, "Professional Development & User Training").
sections.offloading:
- **Critical thinking as the explicit design goal:** "Educators and students are urged to leverage AI to foster and not inhibit critical thinking" (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf, "Demystify").
- **Substitution guardrail:** AI "should not substitute for critical thinking or required academic work" (CDE-AI-Model-Policy-2026.docx, "Acceptable Use").
- **Redesign against easy AI outputs:** curriculum and assessment redesign should emphasize "human thinking, process, equity, and insight... over easily AI-generated products" (Model Policy, "Curriculum & Assessment Redesign").
- **Modeling the efficiency-vs-learning distinction:** educators "should model the difference between using AI for efficiency and using AI to support learning, giving students opportunities to practice and demonstrate both" (Model Policy, "Modeling, Practice, & Ongoing Discussion").
- **Students as creators, not just consumers:** the 2023 "Developing AI in Schools" section frames students "becoming creators and innovators," which positions AI as an object of study rather than a shortcut (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf, "Developing AI in Schools").
- A single named cognitive-offloading section (as in Arizona) is not present, but the substitution guardrail plus the redesign and modeling principles function as California's learning-preservation strategy.
sections.graduate:
- **Uneven and time-dependent.** Both documents are voluntary; the Model Policy is brand-new (June 25, 2026), so most near-term incoming cohorts predate it and were governed, if at all, by the 2023 guidance as adopted locally. *Basis: Educ. Code §33308.5 disclaimers; Model Policy posting date.*
- **Where adopted**, California students may bring: familiarity with the 5 Big Ideas of AI and the learning-with/about distinction (2023 guidance); per-assignment AI-permission expectations and disclosure habits (Model Policy); a taught skepticism of AI detectors (Model Policy); exposure to AI-creation and computer-science-standards-based AI concepts (2023 guidance); and a human-connection framing.
- **Higher-education implication:** The most California-shaped students may arrive already fluent in the exact critical-evaluation vocabulary (claim extraction, source triangulation, confidence calibration) the Model Policy names — an unusually strong foundation to build on. But assume wide variance given voluntariness and the Model Policy's recency.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** California's Model Policy anticipates key higher-education debates. Students from adopting LEAs may arrive expecting that AI detectors are not used as sole evidence and that authorship concerns rely on process and engagement (Model Policy, "AI Detection Software"). Institutions relying on detectors as primary evidence will be out of step with these students' K-12 experience.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students may expect per-assignment AI-permission clarity and disclosure norms (Model Policy, "Instructional Discretion," "Plagiarism, Disclosure, & Citation"). A silent syllabus will contrast with that.
- **Higher-education implication:** The 2023 guidance explicitly connected K-12 to postsecondary via its webinar "featuring educators from K12 and postsecondary spaces" and a college/career-readiness section (CDE-Learning-with-AI-2023.pdf). California higher education is already positioned as a partner in this pipeline.
- **Higher-education implication:** California students may expect privacy-by-design guarantees — that their data will not train public models (Model Policy, "Privacy by Design"). Institutions should confirm their sanctioned tools meet that expectation.
- **Higher-education implication:** Note AB 2148 is a "natural person" law, not a ban on instructional AI; do not overstate it as restricting classroom AI. Its exact scope should be confirmed from bill text not in the provided files.
sections.response:
- **Academic integrity:** Align with California's stance — do not treat AI detectors as sole evidence; use process, engagement, and authorship evidence, with rebuttal criteria available to students (mirrors Model Policy, "AI Detection Software").
- **Assessment design:** Adopt per-assignment AI permissioning and redesign assessments to emphasize human process over easily AI-generated products (Model Policy, "Instructional Discretion," "Curriculum & Assessment Redesign").
- **AI literacy onboarding:** Use California's named literacy skills (claim extraction, confidence calibration, source triangulation, mismatch detection) as an entry rubric, since some students will already have them (Model Policy, "AI Literacy as a Core Academic Competency").
- **AI tool availability and privacy:** Provide sanctioned tools that bar student data from training public models, matching the privacy-by-design expectation (Model Policy, "Privacy by Design").
- **Governance:** The Model Policy's ~two dozen principles are a ready scaffold for an institutional AI policy, including vendor contractual safeguards and pre-deployment evaluation.
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Adopt the efficiency-vs-learning modeling distinction (Model Policy, "Modeling, Practice, & Ongoing Discussion") and the students-as-creators framing (2023 guidance) to keep AI a subject of study, not a shortcut.
sections.unique:
- **A two-instrument approach:** an early (2023) conceptual guidance plus a detailed (2026) model policy under SB 1288 — few states have both.
- **Explicit anti-sole-evidence stance on AI detectors** with parent/student rebuttal criteria (Model Policy, "AI Detection Software").
- **Parent/guardian right to human review** of AI-generated outputs and annual informed consent for autonomous AI tools (Model Policy).
- **AI literacy as a core academic competency tied to statute** with concrete misinformation-analysis skills.
- **Students-as-AI-creators** framing and the 5 Big Ideas of AI foundation (2023 guidance).
- **Curriculum/assessment redesign** guidance emphasizing human process over AI-generated products, with TK-12 grade-band AI-concept progressions.
sections.gaps:

documents.title: Colorado Roadmap for AI in K-12 Education: Guidance for Integrating AI into Teaching and Learning
documents.issuer: Colorado Education Initiative (CEI), a nonprofit, in collaboration with the Colorado Department of Education (CDE); funded by the Gill Foundation

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **AI to make learning more human and deepen critical thinking**, not to stop at "the easily accessible answer" (Colorado-Roadmap-AI-K12-Aug2024.pdf, p.7).
- **The four Cs of digital literacy** — critical thinking, creativity, communication, and collaboration — are "core to a student navigating an AI-infused future" (p.9).
- **Equity across a largely rural state**, framed around three digital divides (p.15).
- **Principles over policy** given the pace of change (p.18).

### Intended audiences and scope
- Designed for K-12 public education, addressed to "educators, stakeholders, and community members," with role-based recommendations for districts and statewide organizations (pp.3, 20-21). *[Scope]*
- Higher education is present in the governance: the steering committee includes University of Colorado Denver and the CU Boulder Institute of Cognitive Science (p.24). *[Scope / higher-ed involvement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **A deliberately positive framing:** "focus on a list of 'yes's' and 'do's' rather than 'no's' and 'don'ts'" (Colorado-Roadmap-AI-K12-Aug2024.pdf, p.18, "Promote a Positive Approach").
- **Acceptable-use modeling:** districts should "define specific use cases for both students and staff" to "delineate permissible, cautious, and prohibited uses of AI," and disclose when AI is used in critical decisions (p.18, "Acceptable Use"). *[Recommendation / model]*
- **Limit blocking tools:** "Limit the use of blocking tools, as students will likely use AI at home, which could inadvertently deepen the access divide" (p.15).
- **No standalone prohibition list**; prohibitions are to be defined locally within acceptable-use frameworks and conduct policies (pp.18-19).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **AI detection tools discouraged:** "Current AI detection tools are already failing to be helpful to districts as AI 'learns' and improves. A more effective approach is to establish guidelines for the ethical use of AI and integrate these into existing conduct policies" (p.15).
- **Student data privacy:** Colorado's "current Student Data Privacy rules are among the most protective in the nation"; regular policy and vendor-contract review recommended (p.17-18).
- **Three digital divides** defined: the digital access divide (connectivity/devices/content), the digital design divide (educator capacity to design tech-rich learning), and the digital use divide (students as passive consumers versus creators) (p.15). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Accessibility:** UDL alignment and AI assistive technologies (screen readers, text-to-speech) for diverse learners (p.9).
- **Academic integrity:** "Be open to rethinking academic integrity; include clear definitions of plagiarism and academic dishonesty while emphasizing how students can responsibly use AI as a tool, eliminating the need for a separate AI plagiarism policy" (p.19, "Student Use of AI").
- **Discrimination and harassment:** integrate AI into safe-school policies with disciplinary actions for inappropriate AI use and parent notification (p.18).
- **Procurement:** "avoid long-term vendor contracts and instead opt for pilot windows," with student-driven feedback to guard against bias (p.18, "Procurement").

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **AI literacy** defined via TeachAI and illustrated with the AI4K12 Five Big Ideas and Gwinnett County's AI Learning Framework (p.8). *[Instructional guidance / examples]*
- **Graduation requirements:** the roadmap recommends updating "local graduation requirements to include AI literacy, data literacy, and ethical AI use," building on Colorado's Computer Science Standards (p.9).
- **Balanced capability map:** eight ways "AI can support students," seven ways it "can support teachers," and five areas "where AI falls short" (emotional/cultural nuance, complex decisions, personalized interaction, contextual adaptation, and the need for human oversight) (pp.10-12). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Two named reusable instruments** (p.13): the **If and How Checklist** ("a guide to 'if and how' for AI usage in the classroom") and an **AI Resource Evaluation Tool** ("based on ISTE's Teacher Ready Evaluation Tool"). *[Instruments / recommendations]*
- **PD:** dedicated time and coaching so teachers can "experiment with AI in low-risk ways"; ongoing professional development as tools evolve (p.16).
- **Implementation:** semi-annual review of AI plans (p.18); district and statewide next-step recommendations including device-access audits and student-inclusive task forces (pp.20-21).
sections.offloading:
- Colorado's central anti-offloading commitment is explicit in the Reshaping-Teaching sidebar: AI should "support students to build deeper critical thinking skills, not just stop at the easily accessible answer" (Colorado-Roadmap-AI-K12-Aug2024.pdf, p.7).
- The **four Cs** (critical thinking, creativity, communication, collaboration) are positioned as the durable human skills AI must reinforce (p.9).
- **Reflection on skill development:** "Teach students to leverage AI productively and ethically, including through reflection on their own academic skill development," and "teach students and educators to critically evaluate AI outputs" (p.15-16).
- **"First Draft Thinking":** a guiding tenet encouraging safe experimentation while protecting PII and guarding against bias (p.18).
- **The digital use divide** frames offloading structurally: students should use technology "to analyze, build, produce, and create," not "solely as passive consumers" (p.15). *[Instructional guidance]*
- A single named cognitive-offloading section is not present, but the critical-thinking-preservation framing, the "where AI falls short" list (pp.11-12), and the reflection recommendation together constitute Colorado's learning-preservation approach.
sections.graduate:
- **Uneven by district (local control).** The roadmap is voluntary and Colorado emphasizes local control, so a Colorado graduate's AI experience reflects district choices. *Basis: pp.3, 17.*
- **Where districts adopted the roadmap's approach**, students may bring: the four Cs framing and AI-literacy grounding (p.9); experience with responsible-use expectations rather than blanket bans (p.18); a taught habit of verifying AI outputs and reflecting on their own skill development (pp.15-16); and possibly the expectation of an appeal process for AI-related grading or accusations (p.19).
- **Rural/connectivity variance:** given the state's rural profile and a documented access gap (64,878 households without reliable internet, p.15), some Colorado students may have had limited hands-on AI access despite the roadmap's equity aims.
- **Higher-education implication:** Assume variance. The most roadmap-shaped students may arrive expecting a "yes's and do's" culture, disclosure-based integrity, and due-process protections around AI accusations — expectations a college should be ready to meet or explicitly reset.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Colorado students from adopting districts may arrive expecting that AI detectors are not trusted and that AI-misuse concerns are handled through engagement and process, not detection software (p.15). Institutions relying on detectors will diverge from that experience.
- **Higher-education implication:** The recommended student **appeal process for AI grading and for accusations of AI use** (p.19) is more protective than most university integrity processes. Colorado students may expect a right to contest an AI-use accusation; institutions should define how they handle such contests.
- **Higher-education implication:** Colorado explicitly involved higher education (CU Denver, CU Boulder) in producing the roadmap (p.24) and recommends embedding AI literacy in graduation requirements (p.9). In-state institutions are positioned to align entry expectations with that pipeline.
- **Higher-education implication:** The "positive approach" (yes's and do's, p.18) means some Colorado students experienced AI as encouraged-with-guardrails. A restrictive or silent college posture will feel like a step backward to them.
sections.response:
- **Academic integrity:** Follow Colorado's lead — do not rely on AI detectors; define AI expectations within existing integrity policy rather than a separate AI plagiarism rule (mirrors p.15, p.19). Establish an explicit process for students to contest AI-use accusations, which Colorado students may expect (p.19).
- **Assessment design:** Adopt per-context acceptable-use definitions (permissible, cautious, prohibited) and design assessments that reward analysis, building, and creation over passive completion (pp.15, 18).
- **AI tool availability and equity:** Provide sanctioned, no-cost access and avoid over-blocking, addressing the rural access gap the roadmap documents (p.15).
- **Onboarding:** Use the four Cs and AI-literacy framing (p.9) plus the If and How Checklist and AI Resource Evaluation Tool (p.13) as ready scaffolds for student orientation and institutional tool vetting.
- **Governance:** Borrow Colorado's guiding tenets (transparency, positive approach, regular review, principles over policy, pp.18) and its procurement caution (pilot windows over long contracts, p.18).
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Adopt the "deeper critical thinking, not the easily accessible answer" framing (p.7) and the reflection-on-skill-development practice (p.15) for continuity from high school to college.
sections.unique:
- **A student appeal process for AI grading and for accusations of AI use** (Colorado-Roadmap-AI-K12-Aug2024.pdf, p.19) — a notably student-protective due-process recommendation.
- **Two ready-to-use instruments:** the If and How Checklist and an ISTE-based AI Resource Evaluation Tool (p.13).
- **A "positive approach"** framing ("yes's and do's rather than no's and don'ts," p.18) and "principles over policy" stance (p.18).
- **Three-divide equity model** (access, design, use) with an explicit push against over-blocking (p.15).
- **Embedded student voice** (a student advisory panel and student quotes throughout) and **higher-education co-governance** (CU Denver, CU Boulder on the steering committee, p.24).
- **Clear anti-AI-detector position** (p.15).
sections.gaps:
- **Voluntary and local-control.** District adoption and student exposure are **Not found in the provided documents**; the roadmap is guidance, not a mandate (pp.3, 17).
- **The two instruments are named but not reproduced** in the roadmap body; the actual If and How Checklist and AI Resource Evaluation Tool live on the CEI website and are **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Unresolved]*
- **Colorado's "Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence law"** is referenced (p.18), but sources notes Colorado repealed/replaced its AI Act in May 2026 with a narrower disclosure framework that carves out FERPA-covered institutions; that statutory change is **Not found in the provided documents** and should be confirmed before citing the law's current form. *[Unresolved]*
- **Issuer nuance:** the roadmap is a CEI (nonprofit) product in collaboration with CDE, funded by the Gill Foundation — not a unilateral CDE issuance (pp.3, 24). Weight accordingly.
- **No enacted Colorado K-12 AI statute** appears in the provided files. *[Absence in provided files]*

sections.graduate:
- **Minimal common baseline.** Because Connecticut's state guidance is a light advisory overview that delegates specifics to districts and linked policies, a Connecticut graduate's AI experience will reflect local district choices rather than a state model. *Basis: content is advisory, instrument-light, and points outward to linked policies.*

sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Connecticut's explicit naming of "Social and Emotional" as a distinct AI risk category suggests some students were taught to consider AI's wellbeing effects, not only its academic-integrity effects. Institutions can connect AI onboarding to student wellbeing and counseling supports rather than framing AI purely as an integrity issue.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because Connecticut's state guidance is advisory and instrument-light, incoming Connecticut students are less likely than students from instrument-heavy states to arrive with a shared per-assignment AI-use vocabulary. sections.response:
- **Onboarding:** Given the light state baseline, run an explicit AI-literacy orientation and do not assume prior instrument exposure.
- **Assessment design and academic integrity:** Introduce a clear, explicit per-assignment AI-permission structure, since Connecticut students are unlikely to arrive with one.
- **Support services:** Build on Connecticut's social-emotional risk framing by linking AI guidance to student wellbeing resources.
- **Governance:** Reference the Connecticut Responsible AI Policy Framework and CABE sample policy for continuity with what Connecticut districts were pointed to.
