### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses (DCPS)
- **Permitted with conditions:** responsible, ethical, supplement-not-substitute use (p.7). *[Requirement — within DCPS]*
- **Specifically prohibited:**
 - "Bullying and Harassment: Students are prohibited from using AI in a way that could harm themselves or others. Using AI tools to manipulate media to impersonate others is prohibited" (p.7). *[Requirement]*
 - "Plagiarism and Cheating: Students are prohibited from submitting AI-generated work as their original work or using AI to answer test, exam, or other assignment questions (unless directed to do so by their teacher)" (p.8). *[Requirement]*
- **Enforcement:** disciplinary responses follow the Safe and Positive Schools Policy, "beginning with the least severe appropriate response," ranging "from providing an opportunity to re-submit the work, to grade reduction" (p.8). *[Requirement]*
- **Staff AI use:** DCPS "maintains a list of approved AI-enhanced tools for student learning" with PD; off-list tools require an AI Tool Approval Form meeting EdTech Team criteria; staff "must verify the truthfulness of any AI-produced content" and "review and critically reflect on all AI-generated content before use" (p.8). *[Requirement — for DCPS staff]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Procurement security review:** "any applications or websites procured by schools must undergo a full security review and receive approval by DCPS' Office of Data and Technology," especially systems containing student information (p.5). *[Requirement]*
- **Privacy law:** the AUP is grounded in CIPA, COPPA, and DC's Protecting Students Digital Privacy Act (pp.1-2, Authority and Applicable Law); staff data-sharing without approval "violates the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)" (p.6). *[Requirement]*
- **Monitoring:** DCPS uses "a safety management system to analyze and review content found in online file storage, inbound and outbound DCPS email... and links to websites," and reserves broad monitoring rights (p.4). *[Requirement]*
- **Accessibility:** students with disabilities receive IEP-based accommodations to complete required Digital Citizenship courses, and assistive technology may go home per IEP teams (pp.6, 12). *[Requirement]*
- **Academic integrity:** handled via the plagiarism/cheating prohibition and disclosure-by-teacher-direction model (p.8). A position on AI-detection tools is **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Limited]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **AI literacy delivery:** "DCPS will provide students with lessons on the benefits and risks of AI through Digital Citizenship and AI-specific courses" (p.7). Students complete Digital Citizenship & Literacy courses, sometimes required before device issuance (p.3). *[Requirement — within DCPS]*
- **PD:** DCPS "will provide professional development to support the appropriate deployment of these [approved AI] tools" (p.8). *[Requirement — within DCPS]*
- A detailed curriculum-integration framework (SAMR, grade-band literacy progression, assessment redesign) is **Not found in the provided documents.** The AUP is a conduct policy, not a curriculum framework. *[Limited]*
sections.offloading:
- The only relevant provision is the DCPS principle that "AI tools should be used... as a supplement, not a substitute, for learning" (DCPS-AcceptableUse-SY25-26.pdf, p.7), reinforced by the prohibition on using AI to answer test/assignment questions unless teacher-directed (p.8). These guard against wholesale offloading but do not constitute a developed cognitive-science strategy. *[Requirement / limited]*
- A treatment of metacognition, productive struggle, or preserving independent reasoning is **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Evidence gap]*
sections.graduate:
- **DCPS graduates:** likely experienced AI framed as a compliance-and-conduct matter — responsible-use expectations, Digital Citizenship and "AI-specific courses" (p.7), and clear prohibitions on AI impersonation and on using AI for test answers without teacher permission (pp.7-8). Their AI use was governed, but the policy describes little about AI-creation skills or literacy depth. *Basis: DCPS AUP pp.7-8.*
- **Non-DCPS (charter) graduates:** governed by their own LEA policies, which are **Not found in the provided documents**; their experience cannot be characterized here. *[Evidence gap]*
- **Higher-education implication:** For DC-origin students, assume no uniform baseline. DCPS graduates may arrive with a conduct-oriented understanding of AI ("cite it, do not impersonate, do not use it on tests unless allowed") rather than a literacy-oriented or instrument-based one, and charter-origin students may vary entirely.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** DCPS students may arrive expecting a teacher-permission model for AI on assessments (AI on tests is barred "unless directed... by their teacher," p.8). A college syllabus that specifies AI permission per assignment will feel continuous; a silent syllabus will not.
- **Higher-education implication:** DCPS frames AI within an acceptable-use and disciplinary structure, so some DC students may associate AI misuse primarily with conduct consequences (grade reduction, discipline) rather than with academic-integrity adjudication. Institutions should make their own AI-integrity process explicit.
- **Higher-education implication:** DC's fragmentation (a district policy plus many independent charter LEAs, and no citywide strategy per SR24-12) means DC-origin cohorts will be especially heterogeneous. Do not treat "from DC" as a single policy background.
- **Higher-education implication:** SR24-12's call to "establish a common student use policy" (p.2) signals DC intends to move toward a citywide standard. Institutions enrolling many DC students should watch for that policy, since it would create the shared baseline that does not yet exist.
sections.response:
- **Onboarding:** Given DC's fragmentation and the absence of a citywide framework, run an explicit AI-literacy orientation and do not assume prior instrument exposure.
- **Assessment design:** Adopt clear per-assignment AI-permission language continuous with the DCPS teacher-permission model (p.8).
- **Academic integrity:** Define an explicit AI-integrity process; DCPS students may have experienced AI issues as conduct/discipline rather than integrity adjudication.
- **Procurement and governance:** DCPS's Office of Data and Technology security-review requirement (p.5) is a usable model for institutional AI-tool vetting, especially for tools touching student data.
- **AI tool availability and accessibility:** Provide sanctioned tools with IEP-style accessibility support, echoing the DCPS accommodations model (pp.6, 12).
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Build on DCPS's "supplement, not substitute" principle (p.7) with an explicit learning-preservation model the district policy itself does not supply.
sections.unique:
- **A state-board resolution that documents its own jurisdiction's absence of strategy** (SR24-12-draft.pdf, p.1) and calls for a common citywide student-use policy (p.2) — an unusually candid "we don't have this yet" state-level artifact.
- **A district AUP that names AI explicitly** — including a definition (p.2), a supplement-not-substitute principle, AI-impersonation and AI-on-tests prohibitions, and a staff AI-tool approval process (pp.7-8) — inside a broader conduct policy effective January 2026.
- **A strong procurement security-review gate** through the DCPS Office of Data and Technology (p.5).
sections.gaps:
- **No OSSE / citywide framework exists** (confirmed by SR24-12-draft.pdf, p.1). DC is not an absence state in the sense of "nothing," but it lacks a state-agency instructional framework.
- **SR24-12 is a draft copy** on a third-party host; although the date-adopted line reads 5/15/2024, its final-adopted status and text should be confirmed against an official DC State Board source. A newer resolution (SR26-10) is referenced in sources but **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Unresolved]*
- **Charter LEA policies are Not found in the provided documents**, so a large portion of DC K-12 AI governance is uncharacterized here. *[Scope gap]*
- **No pedagogy/AI-literacy framework, student-use scale, or detection-tool position** appears; the DCPS document is a conduct/acceptable-use policy. *[Limited]*
- Pages 13-20 of the DCPS AUP (appendices, responsible-use agreements) were not transcribed in this pass; they are agreement forms rather than additional AI policy. *[Scope limit]*

documents.title: Leveraging AI in the K-12 Setting: Ensuring the ethical, effective, and secure use of AI tools and systems in Georgia's schools
documents.issuer: Georgia Department of Education (GaDOE); Richard Woods, State School Superintendent

documents.title: Ethical Considerations in the Appropriate Use of AI for Educators
documents.issuer: Georgia Professional Standards Commission (GaPSC)

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **AI as tool, not replacement.** "AI is a tool to increase efficiencies and effectiveness, not a replacement for human interaction during the teaching and learning process" (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.1). GaPSC: "AI is not a primary source" and "should not take the place of the teacher" (GaPSC..., Important Understandings #1).
- **Supportive, not high-stakes, use.** The four ethical musts: use AI "in a supportive, not high-stakes manner"; "enhance, not replace, human judgment"; "promote transparency"; "respect privacy" (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.3).
- **Academic integrity via attribution.** Proper attribution of AI-generated content is "crucial" (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.14).

### Intended audiences and scope
- GaDOE guidance addresses district and school leaders and educators across Georgia K-12 public schools (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.1). *[Scope]*
- GaPSC guidance addresses "pre-service and in-service administrators, educators, and staff," explicitly including **educator preparation providers (EPPs)** (GaPSC..., Audience; Purpose). *[Scope — includes teacher-prep]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- The GaDOE **high-stakes vs non-high-stakes table** (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.4) is the closest thing to a prohibition list, framed as uses to "refrain from":
 - **High-stakes uses to avoid:** "Write IEP goals for individual students"; "Evaluate lesson plans"; "Evaluate educators"; "Evaluate the resumes and applications of job candidates to narrow a group of finalists"; "Grade student assignments or projects that are subjective"; "Analyze student data to predict future success, recommend class placements, or flag potential disciplinary issues." *[Recommendation — confirms the previously tracker-flagged IEP/evaluation/subjective-grading list at primary source]*
 - **Non-high-stakes uses permitted:** create learning targets; assist in lessons/lesson plans; develop job descriptions; develop a rubric; feedback on non-graded work; "Grade multiple choice exams"; modify reading level of grade-level text (p.4).
- The **redlight system** (p.12): "educators may use a 'redlight system' to communicate to students when AI use is allowable and to what extent," adapted from Phil Hintz's THINK guide. Per sources's image-based read, RED = not allowed / academic dishonesty; YELLOW = content-creation assistance; GREEN = encouraged with citation. *[Instrument / recommendation; color definitions confirmed via graphic, not plain text]*
- **PII prohibition:** "Never input PII, such as social security numbers, home addresses, health information, academic information... into AI systems" (p.5). *[Recommendation, strong]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Privacy:** dedicated PII-safeguarding section; use anonymized/aggregated data; annual PII professional learning; federal statutes listed (COPPA, FERPA, Privacy Act, PPRA) plus Section 504 and IDEA accessibility requirements (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, pp.5-6).
- **Vendor governance:** formal vendor agreements, TrustEd Apps catalog reference, and a formal vetting process with a review committee (pp.9-10).
- **Bias:** GaPSC Principle #6 — evaluate AI output for bias, choose vendors documenting bias-mitigation, ensure tools "do not exacerbate disparities" (GaPSC..., Principle #6).
- **Academic integrity:** attribution/citation of AI content; integrate AI into existing academic-integrity, acceptable-use, grading, and code-of-conduct policies (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, pp.8, 14; GaPSC Principle #2).
- **AI detection tools:** a position on detection software is **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Limited]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Tool-vetting instrument — the Evaluation Process Rubric** (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.10): seven criteria — Educational Value, Data Privacy, Usability, Cost, Scalability, Vendor Reputation, and Age restrictions. *[Instrument / recommendation]*
- **District policy-adoption process** (p.7): engage stakeholders, needs assessment, draft, pilot, finalize/implement, regular review.
- **Professional learning** is emphasized as ongoing, not one-off; GaPSC repeatedly stresses that "effective professional development regarding AI cannot be accomplished in single, standalone sessions" (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.11; GaPSC..., Important Understandings #4).
- **Assessment:** GaPSC Principle #1 — "Humans should always review and take responsibility for the output of AI tools when they are used to make decisions about student performance, placement, and/or discipline"; transparency when AI is used for assessment/feedback (GaPSC..., Principle #1).
sections.offloading:
- The GaDOE classroom section ties clear AI boundaries to preserving thinking: "Clear guidelines help maintain academic integrity and ensure that students develop their own critical thinking and problem-solving skills," and educators should "Encourage critical thinking about AI limitations" (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.12).
- The redlight system's Level RED ("must rely on their own knowledge... during exams or assessments," p.12) preserves unaided demonstration of understanding.
- GaPSC Principle #2: "Aid students in understanding AI should be used as a tool and not a replacement for learning" (GaPSC..., Principle #2).
- A developed cognitive-science treatment (metacognition, productive struggle, over-reliance research) comparable to Arizona's is **Not found in the provided documents.** Georgia's guard is the redlight boundaries plus the high-stakes/non-high-stakes framing. *[Limited]*
sections.graduate:
- **Uneven by district (voluntary guidance).** Both documents are voluntary, so exposure depends on district adoption. *Basis: p.1; GaPSC Purpose.*
- **Where adopted**, Georgia students may bring: familiarity with a per-assignment traffic-light signal for AI permission (redlight system, p.12); a disclosure-and-attribution habit for AI-assisted work (p.14); awareness that AI should not be used on assessments meant to show individual understanding (p.12); and general AI-literacy including AI's limitations and bias (GaDOE p.12; GaPSC Principle #6).
- **Higher-education implication:** The most Georgia-shaped students may arrive already understanding a three-signal AI-permission convention and an attribution expectation — a strong, transferable foundation. But assume variance given voluntariness.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Georgia's redlight system (p.12) is the closest K-12 analogue to a syllabus AI-permission statement. Faculty can adopt the same three-signal convention (with attribution credit to Phil Hintz's THINK guide) and expect partial prior familiarity from Georgia students.
- **Higher-education implication:** The high-stakes/non-high-stakes table (p.4) transfers directly to higher-education practice — it is a ready decision rule for what faculty and administrators should never delegate to AI (subjective grading, evaluations, individualized high-stakes decisions like accommodations).
- **Higher-education implication:** GaPSC explicitly involves educator preparation providers (university teacher-prep programs) and urges districts to "work closely with their EPP partners" (GaPSC..., Important Understandings #7). Georgia colleges of education are already positioned in this pipeline.
- **Higher-education implication:** Georgia students may expect AI use to be signaled per assignment and attributed, not silently banned. A syllabus that adopts the redlight convention will feel continuous; a silent one will not.
sections.response:
- **Assessment design:** Adopt a per-assignment AI-permission signal modeled on the redlight system (p.12), and preserve unaided "own knowledge" assessments where the goal is individual understanding.
- **Academic integrity:** Require AI attribution/citation as the GaDOE and GaPSC documents do (p.14; Principle #2), and fold AI into existing integrity policy rather than a separate rule.
- **Governance and procurement:** Reuse the seven-criterion Evaluation Process Rubric (p.10) and the high-stakes/non-high-stakes distinction (p.4) as institutional tool-vetting and decision-boundary instruments.
- **Faculty development:** Treat AI PD as ongoing, not one-off, per GaPSC's explicit point (Important Understandings #4).
- **Teacher-prep alignment:** Georgia colleges of education should align with GaPSC's seven principles, since EPPs are named participants (GaPSC..., Purpose).
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Build on the "develop their own critical thinking and problem-solving skills" framing (p.12) and the "AI is not a primary source" stance (GaPSC..., Important Understandings #1).
sections.unique:
- **The redlight (traffic-light) system** for per-assignment AI permission (Leveraging-AI-in-K12-Setting.pdf, p.12) — the project's flagship portable artifact, confirmed in primary text and adapted from Phil Hintz's THINK guide.
- **A high-stakes vs non-high-stakes use table** (p.4) that names specific uses to avoid (IEP goals, educator evaluations, subjective grading, predictive data uses) and specific permitted uses.
- **A seven-criterion Evaluation Process Rubric** for AI-tool vetting (p.10).
- **Two complementary state documents** — GaDOE operational guidance plus GaPSC educator-ethics guidance grounded in the Georgia Code of Ethics, with seven principles, standards, and guiding questions.
- **Explicit inclusion of educator preparation providers (EPPs)** — a higher-education teacher-prep hook (GaPSC..., Purpose, Important Understandings #7).
sections.gaps:
- **Voluntariness.** District adoption and student exposure are **Not found in the provided documents.**
- **The "SB 179" statute and any graduation mandate are Not found in either document.** Neither the GaDOE nor GaPSC document references SB 179 or a CS-with-AI graduation requirement. Consistent with sources's flag that the "SB 179" citation is likely erroneous, this analysis does not assert any Georgia AI graduation statute. *[Unresolved — likely citation error]*
- **The redlight color definitions (RED/YELLOW/GREEN)** are in an embedded graphic not captured by text extraction; they were confirmed via an image-based read recorded in sources. The plain text confirms only the existence and Phil-Hintz attribution of the "redlight system" (p.12). *[Partial]*
- **No AI-detection-tool position and no developed cognitive-offloading section** appear. *[Limited]*
- **GaPSC's "AI Ethical Guidance Position Statement"** and forthcoming resources are referenced but **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Scope]*

documents.title: Senate Bill 1227 — an act adding Chapter 70, Title 33, Idaho Code, "Generative Artificial Intelligence in Education" (§§33-7001 to 33-7008)
documents.issuer: Idaho Legislature (Senate Education Committee); signed by Gov. Little
documents.date: Enacted 2026 Regular Session; effective July 1, 2026 (emergency clause)

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Legislative intent:** "safeguard student privacy, protect the role of the educator, promote human-centered learning, increase transparency, and prepare Idaho students for success in an economy increasingly influenced by generative artificial intelligence," ensuring "responsible, ethical, safe, and effective use." *[Requirement — statutory intent]*
- **Human authority as final:** "generative artificial intelligence in education" is defined as responsible use "while ensuring that human judgment remains the final authority" (§33-7002(2)). *[Requirement — definitional]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- Applies to K-12 Idaho public schools and public charter schools; governs "students and employees in school buildings, on school grounds, during school activities, and on school-issued devices". *[Scope, Requirement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- The statute does not itself list permitted/prohibited uses; it **requires each district/charter policy to "Define appropriate and prohibited uses of generative AI for instructional, administrative, and communication purposes"** (§33-7004(2)). *[Requirement — delegated to local policy]*
- The specific appropriate/prohibited-use definitions are therefore **Not found in the provided documents** (they will live in local policies aligned to the forthcoming framework). *[Unresolved]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Privacy/security:** district policies must include "safeguards for student privacy, data security, accessibility, and academic integrity" and comply with Idaho student data privacy law, FERPA, CIPA, and COPPA (§33-7004(3)-(4)). Procurement requires vendor disclosure of ML/predictive/generative features and "assurances regarding data protection, algorithmic transparency, and responsible use". *[Requirement]*
- **Accessibility:** the framework must "Address accessibility, accommodations, and access to generative AI tools" (§33-7003(1)(c)). *[Requirement — framework content pending]*
- **Academic integrity and digital citizenship:** the framework must "Provide guidance on instructional integration, academic integrity, digital citizenship, and responsible student use" (§33-7003(1)(b)). *[Requirement — content pending]*
- A specific position on AI detection tools is **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Limited]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Literacy standards + assessments (notable):** SDE must develop "Generative AI literacy standards for K-12 students" covering "what generative AI is, how it works, its appropriate and age-appropriate uses, and how to use it ethically, securely, and transparently," plus "Assessment guidelines to evaluate student understanding of generative AI concepts, ethics, and responsible use" (§33-7005(1)-(2)). *[Requirement — content pending]*
- **Professional development plan** to build educator capacity (§33-7005(3)). *[Requirement — content pending]*
- **Parental engagement:** SDE must develop a GenAI guidance document for parents/guardians. *[Requirement — content pending]*
- **Framework as foundation:** the framework serves as "the foundation for local school district and public charter school policies, professional development, procurement practices, and statewide standards" (§33-7003(1)(d)). *[Requirement]*
sections.offloading:
- The statute's learning-preservation posture is expressed through **human-centered authority**: "human judgment remains the final authority" (S1227-enacted.pdf, §33-7002(2)), and legislative intent to "protect the role of the educator" and "promote human-centered learning". *[Requirement — intent]*
- The framework must address "academic integrity... and responsible student use" (§33-7003(1)(b)), and literacy standards must cover "appropriate and age-appropriate uses" (§33-7005(1)) — but the detailed cognitive-offloading strategy is delegated to the not-yet-published framework and is **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Unresolved]*
sections.graduate:
- **Near-term graduates predate any baseline.** The framework, standards, and assessments are not yet published; district policies must align to a framework that does not yet exist. Per sources, classroom implementation "could begin as early as 2027-28." *Basis: §§33-7003 to 33-7005; sources.*
- **Future graduates (post-implementation)** should, by statute, have: been governed by a district policy defining appropriate and prohibited AI uses; been taught to GenAI literacy standards (§33-7005(1)); and potentially been **assessed on their understanding of GenAI concepts, ethics, and responsible use** (§33-7005(2)). *Basis: statute; content pending.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Idaho is a "watch this space" state. In a few years its graduates may arrive with statutorily standardized, and even assessed, AI literacy — a stronger and more uniform baseline than voluntary-guidance states. For now, assume no guaranteed baseline.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Idaho drew a distinction higher education has largely avoided — a policy on file is not the same as a governance function that runs. The statute requires operational governance (district policies, standards, assessments, PD, procurement rules), not just aspirational guidance. Institutions can borrow that "governance that runs" framing.
- **Higher-education implication:** If Idaho implements assessment of student AI understanding (§33-7005(2)), future Idaho applicants may have documented AI-literacy outcomes. Admissions and placement could eventually treat AI literacy as a measured competency rather than an assumption.
- **Higher-education implication:** The statute contains **no explicit higher-education hook** (no naming of universities or teacher-prep programs) in the provided text. Idaho's relevance to higher education is via the future graduate profile, not a direct binding of institutions.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because the substantive framework is pending, institutions should not yet assume any specific Idaho student AI competency; the guaranteed baseline is a future-tense phenomenon.
sections.response:
- **Governance:** Adopt Idaho's "governance that runs" model — pair any institutional AI policy with defined roles, standards, PD, and procurement rules rather than a standalone statement.
- **Onboarding:** Treat current Idaho cohorts as pre-baseline; run an AI-literacy entry check. Revisit this once Idaho's standards and assessments are implemented.
- **Assessment design and academic integrity:** Provide explicit appropriate/prohibited-use definitions per assignment, mirroring what Idaho districts will be required to define (§33-7004(2)).
- **Procurement:** Reuse Idaho's vendor-disclosure requirements as institutional AI-procurement criteria.
- **Monitoring:** Track publication of Idaho's SDE framework, literacy standards, and assessment guidelines; when released, align entry expectations to them.
sections.unique:
- **A statutory duty, not guidance:** SB 1227 makes AI policy a legal requirement for every district and charter, one of the first states to do so.
- **Mandated assessment of student AI understanding** (§33-7005(2)) — an unusually strong provision requiring the state to develop guidelines to *evaluate* student GenAI literacy, not just teach it.
- **A statutory definition centering human authority** — "human judgment remains the final authority" (§33-7002(2)).
- **Emergency-clause enactment** effective July 1, 2026, signaling urgency.
- **A required parent-guidance document** as a distinct deliverable.
sections.gaps:
- **The substantive framework, literacy standards, assessment guidelines, PD plan, and parent-guidance document are not yet published.** Their contents are **Not found in the provided documents.** This analysis characterizes the statutory requirements, not the (pending) instructional substance. *[Unresolved]*
- **District policy contents** (appropriate/prohibited uses) are delegated to local adoption aligned to the forthcoming framework and are **Not found in the provided documents.**
- **No explicit higher-education hook** appears in the statute text; sources notes "None specific in the K-12 statute."
- **Implementation timing** ("as early as 2027-28") is from sources, not the statute, which sets only a July 1, 2026 effective date. *[Partial]*
- **A public-private training partnership (Microsoft, Micron)** was announced at signing per sources but is **Not found in the provided documents.**

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Guidance
documents.issuer: Illinois State Board of Education (ISBE), with a "Blue Ribbon Panel" of experts
documents.type: State guidance (recommendations; ~409 pages) developed under Public Act 104-0399

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **The teacher-student interaction is the centerpiece.** "It is organized around the enduring educational premise that the teacher-student interaction is the centerpiece of teaching and learning" (ISBE-AI-Guidance.pdf, p.2).
- **AI as means, not end** (Tenet 3, p.4): AI "must remain a means to inform teaching and learning rather than a substitute for educator judgment, student relationships, or the developmental and civic purposes of public schooling" (p.2).
- **Schools serve academic, developmental, and civic purposes concurrently** (Tenet 2, p.4).
- **Locally determined use** (Tenet 4, p.4): informed use is "deliberate, context-sensitive, and locally determined."

### Intended audiences and scope
- Explicitly multi-audience: FAQ answers are tagged by audience — "Superintendent; principal; teacher; parent/caregiver; advocate/stakeholder group; community" (ISBE-AI-Guidance.pdf, p.4). *[Scope]*
- Covers prekindergarten through Grade 12, at "district, school, and classroom levels" (p.4). *[Scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **No single statewide permission scale**; the document models informed, locally determined use rather than issuing rules. *[Not a mandate]*
- **High-stakes cautions:** AI should not be the basis for "student discipline outcomes, teacher evaluations, hiring decisions, or other high-stakes" decisions (line ~8371).
- **Detection tools:** "Schools use AI-detection tools as one data point, not as definitive proof of cheating" and should "Be cautious with AI-detection tools; some district guidance advises against relying on them" (lines ~2004, ~3635).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Academic integrity** is handled through informed-use and disclosure rather than a detection regime; it warns that "early reliance on detection or 'gotcha' approaches can produce false [positives]" (line ~3642).
- **Equity/accessibility:** the guidance foregrounds "equity, accessibility, privacy, safety, accountability, and civic responsibility" (p.3), and includes IEP/504-specific safeguards, e.g., "cognitive load safeguards" and misinformation-review triggers for high-incidence IEP/504 (line ~13987).
- **Safety/privacy:** panel expertise explicitly includes AI safety and youth protection (Common Sense Media), and the guidance addresses hallucinations that are "difficult to detect without verification" (line ~1845).
- **Bias/transparency:** the guidance addresses disparate impact and monitoring for harm (error patterns, uneven quality, misuse) (lines ~4644, ~9291).

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Prompt development** for teachers is treated as a thread of professional learning and a component of student digital citizenship (ISBE-AI-Guidance.pdf, p.5, Q2).
- **Bloom's Taxonomy as a lens** for instructional planning is a named framework ("Taxonomy as a Lens for Instructional Planning," p.5, Q3; Bloom reference in the bibliography, line ~14603). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship** is a major section, including "Development as an Individual and Citizen – An Ecological Framework" (p.5, Q4).
- **Assessment:** the guidance treats participation, persistence, and cognitive engagement "beyond grades or scores alone" (line ~8016) and emphasizes "metacognitive challenge while preserving originality and student voice" (line ~8245).
- **Case studies:** the document includes numbered classroom case scenarios (e.g., "Case 14 – Grade 9-12 Teacher" on AI detection, line ~6936) as practical implementation aids. *[Examples]*
sections.offloading:
- Illinois engages over-reliance directly. It prompts districts to consider what "might decrease (over-reliance, reduced struggle)" when adopting AI (line ~4113) and to weigh "overreliance" as a risk (line ~4638).
- It frames good assessment design around "metacognitive challenge while preserving originality and student voice" (line ~8245) and treats engagement as including "persistence, and cognitive engagement," not grades alone (line ~8016).
- It cautions that "instructional design should not separate cognitive demand from context" and links AI use to "cognitive development, social and emotional development" (lines ~7656-7657). *[Instructional guidance]*
- It cites the over-reliance research base (e.g., "over-reliance (Roscoe et al. 2017)," line ~11915; the GPT-4 System Card on hallucinations and overreliance, lines ~14626-14630). *[Instructional guidance, cited]*
- Its structural guard against offloading is Tenet 3 (AI as means, not end) plus its caution against detection-driven "gotcha" enforcement in favor of learning-centered expectations (lines ~3642, ~3990).
sections.graduate:
- **Uneven and recent.** The guidance is voluntary and locally determined (Tenet 4), and it posted June 2026, so near-term incoming cohorts largely predate district implementation. *Basis: p.4; June 2026 date.*
- **Where adopted**, Illinois students may bring: a human-relationship-centered framing of AI; exposure to AI literacy and digital citizenship as an ecological/developmental competency (p.5); a disclosure-based rather than detection-based integrity experience (lines ~2004, ~3635); and prompt-development skills (p.5).
- **Higher-education implication:** The most Illinois-shaped students may arrive having been taught that AI detectors are unreliable and that AI is a means, not an end. Assume variance given voluntariness and recency.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Illinois students from adopting districts may arrive having been taught that AI detectors are "one data point, not... definitive proof of cheating" (line ~2004). Institutions relying on detectors as decisive evidence will diverge from that experience and may face pushback grounded in the students' K-12 guidance.
- **Higher-education implication:** The high-stakes cautions (no AI as the basis for discipline, teacher evaluations, hiring, line ~8371) transfer directly to institutional practice — a ready list of decisions faculty and administrators should not delegate to AI.
- **Higher-education implication:** Illinois' emphasis on over-reliance and "reduced struggle" (line ~4113) means some students were taught to notice when AI use erodes their own learning. Faculty can build on that self-monitoring stance.
- **Higher-education implication:** The document's own disclosure that AI assisted its drafting models the transparency it asks for — an institution can adopt the same "disclose your AI use" norm for faculty and students.
sections.response:
- **Academic integrity:** Adopt Illinois' stance — detectors as at most one data point, not proof; favor disclosure and learning-centered expectations over "gotcha" enforcement (lines ~2004, ~3642).
- **Assessment design:** Design for "metacognitive challenge while preserving originality and student voice" (line ~8245); assess persistence and engagement, not just products (line ~8016).
- **Decision boundaries:** Reuse the high-stakes list (line ~8371) to define what AI must not decide (discipline, evaluations, hiring).
- **Onboarding and faculty development:** Use Illinois' AI-literacy/digital-citizenship framing and prompt-development thread (p.5) as ready scaffolds; run an entry AI-literacy check given uneven adoption.
- **Governance:** Borrow the four tenets (p.4) as an institutional AI-policy backbone, keeping AI a means to teaching and learning.
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Center the human relationship and treat AI as a means (Tenets 1, 3), mirroring the guidance students may have experienced.
sections.unique:
- **Scale and depth:** a ~409-page statewide guidance built by a Blue Ribbon Panel (Brookings, Khan Academy, EdSAFE AI Alliance, Common Sense Media, and others), organized around four tenets (ISBE-AI-Guidance.pdf, pp.2-4).
- **Explicit caution against AI-detection tools** and "gotcha" enforcement (lines ~2004, ~3635, ~3642).
- **Bloom's Taxonomy as an instructional-planning lens** and an "ecological framework" for development as an individual and citizen (p.5).
- **Disclosed AI-assisted authorship** — the document was drafted with AI assistance and says so, modeling transparency.
- **Audience-tagged FAQ** and numbered classroom case studies as practical navigation aids (pp.4-5; line ~6936).
sections.gaps:
- **Voluntariness and recency.** Adoption and student exposure are **Not found in the provided documents**; the guidance is recommendations, posted June 2026 (p.4).
- **Method limitation:** given the ~409-page length, this analysis relied on framing pages plus systematic keyword search; some claims are cited by descriptive location rather than exact page, and sections not surfaced by those searches were not exhaustively reviewed. *[Partial]*
- **The "support but not score a teacher evaluation" distinction** the dataset flagged is substantially **confirmed in substance** — AI may "support aspects of evaluation (development of rubrics)" (line ~2085) while "teacher evaluations" are listed among high-stakes uses AI should not decide (line ~8371) — but the exact phrasing was not isolated to a single passage; treat as confirmed-in-substance. *[Partial]*
- **Enabling statute:** Public Act 104-0399 (the enacted SB 1920) is referenced within the guidance (p.2); its full text is **Not found in the provided documents.** Pending bills (e.g., HB 4411, full-year CS+AI) are noted in sources, not in the provided files. *[Partial]*
- **No explicit higher-education hook** (naming of universities/teacher-prep) surfaced in the searched sections; treat as Not found in the provided documents pending a fuller read. *[Limited]*

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **AI literacy as civic and workforce empowerment:** literacy "transforms students into versatile problem-solvers and promotes critical thinking," quoting Code.org's definition of AI literacy (Indiana-AI-Guidance.pdf, "AI Literacy").
- **AI supports, not replaces, human judgment:** the "human-in-the-loop" approach is named explicitly ("Impact," Educator Experience).
- **Integrate into existing policy** rather than build anew ("Policy Prerequisites," "Examine Existing Policies").

### Intended audiences and scope
- Addresses educators, students, administrators, and parents/caregivers, with side-by-side educator/student framing throughout ("Instruction and Learning," "Impact," "Security"). *[Scope]*
- Policy guidance directs districts to "Provide clarity about who your policy applies to, including students, administrators, teachers" ("Process Guidance"). *[Scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **No statewide permission scale**; the document guides local policy. It advises districts to "Define acceptable and unacceptable uses of AI, but avoid restricting innovative educational uses or instituting overly broad restrictions" ("Process Guidance").
- **Avoid naming specific platforms** because "AI tools evolve quickly" ("Process Guidance").
- **Detection tools:** "Reconsider the use of AI detection tools as the sole source of intervention related to academic dishonesty" ("Process Guidance"), reinforced by a linked resource, "AI Detection Software Doesn't Work. Do This Instead."

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Security/privacy:** "Ensure inputs into public-facing AI tools are free from personal identifiable information (PII)," "Ensure compliance with FERPA/COPPA before using AI with students," and use age-appropriate approved tools ("Security").
- **Bias/ethics:** AI/CS integration competency includes "Ethically evaluate AI systems to minimize bias," and students should "understand how data is used to train AI and how that can lead to biased results" ("AI Literacy"; "Impact").
- **Academic integrity:** handled via citation of AI usage ("Properly cite AI usage," "AI Literacy") and the detection-tool caution ("Process Guidance").
- A dedicated accessibility section is **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Limited]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **AI + Computer Science integration** is a named pairing, with competencies like "Break down complex problems," "Analyze data critically," "Identify patterns and trends" ("AI Literacy").
- **Educator sandbox:** "Develop a 'sandbox' where educators can practice making decisions about security issues related to AI" ("Security").
- **Feedback and time:** AI can make feedback "more immediate and actionable" and open time for "building relationships, developing content, and providing feedback" ("Instruction and Learning").
- **Policy process:** prerequisites include AI-literacy capacity before policy work, defining goals first ("Simply using AI should not be the goal"), stakeholder input, and flexibility ("Policy Prerequisites").
- **Resources:** TeachAI, ISTE, the CGCS/CoSN/AWS Gen AI Readiness Checklist, and an Indiana Learning Lab collection ("Resources"). *[Examples]*
sections.offloading:
- Indiana's central anti-offloading commitment is explicit: students "use AI to boost thinking and creativity, using tools to support, rather than replace, their own critical thought and original expression" (Indiana-AI-Guidance.pdf, "Impact").
- Educators "design learning experiences that leverage AI to enhance content understanding while intentionally preserving academic rigor, promoting student independence, and cultivating transferable skills" ("Impact").
- AI-as-scaffold framing: "Students using AI tools as a scaffold can open up time for higher level thinking and problem solving" ("Instruction and Learning").
- The "human-in-the-loop" model and educator modeling of output-monitoring ("Impact") reinforce human judgment.
- A developed cognitive-science treatment (metacognition research, over-reliance studies) comparable to Arizona's is **Not found in the provided documents**; Indiana's guard is the supplement-not-replace and preserve-rigor framing. *[Limited]*
sections.graduate:
- **Uneven by district (voluntary).** Exposure depends on district adoption. *Basis: voluntary guidance; no statute.*
- **Where adopted**, Indiana students may bring: an "empowered learner/citizen" framing of AI literacy; the "I CAN" competencies including properly citing AI use and evaluating AI systems for bias ("AI Literacy"); a supplement-not-replace stance toward their own thinking ("Impact"); and awareness of PII/data-privacy cautions ("Security").
- **Higher-education implication:** Indiana-shaped students may arrive expecting AI to be framed as a scaffold that preserves rigor and independence, and expecting to cite AI use. Assume variance given voluntariness.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Indiana students from adopting districts may have been taught that AI detectors don't work as sole evidence ("Process Guidance"). Institutions relying on detectors will diverge from that experience.
- **Higher-education implication:** Indiana's citation expectation ("Properly cite AI usage when writing or creating," "AI Literacy") aligns with a disclosure-based integrity model; a college can build on that habit.
- **Higher-education implication:** The "Impact" section frames K-12 AI explicitly toward students who "will enroll in higher education, enlist in the military, or seek employment" ("Impact") — a college/career-readiness framing, though not a binding higher-education hook.
- **Higher-education implication:** Indiana's "human-in-the-loop" and preserve-rigor language ("Impact") gives a shared vocabulary a college can adopt for continuity.
sections.response:
- **Academic integrity:** Do not rely on AI detectors as sole evidence, matching Indiana's caution ("Process Guidance"); require AI-use citation as Indiana teaches ("AI Literacy").
- **Assessment design:** Design assessments that preserve rigor and student independence while allowing AI as a scaffold ("Impact," "Instruction and Learning").
- **Onboarding and faculty development:** Use Indiana's "I CAN" AI-literacy competencies as an entry rubric; consider an educator/faculty "sandbox" for safe practice, mirroring Indiana's recommendation ("Security").
- **Governance:** Fold AI into existing policies (acceptable-use, integrity) rather than creating a standalone AI policy, per Indiana's "Examine Existing Policies" ("Policy Prerequisites").
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Adopt the supplement-not-replace and human-in-the-loop framing ("Impact") for continuity from high school to college.

states.summary: Iowa is a no-current-guidance state with active legislation. The Iowa DOE has issued no K-12 AI classroom guidance. The substantive activity is a pair of introduced bills — HF 2540 (successor to HSB 610) and SF 2094 — that would, beginning with the 2030-31 graduating class, require one semester of computer science and artificial intelligence for graduation. sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **No current state guidance.** The honest finding is that Iowa has issued no statewide K-12 AI classroom guidance. *[Absence — confirmed]*
- **Proposed objective (pending bills):** establish CS+AI education "setting a foundation for personal and professional success in a high-technology, knowledge-based Iowa economy" (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 2). *[Unresolved — introduced bill]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- The bills would apply to "all students in school districts and accredited nonpublic schools" at the high-school graduation level, with CS+AI instruction offered at additional grade levels (HF2540.pdf, Secs. 1, 5-6). *[Scope — proposed]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **Not found in the provided documents.** Iowa has no guidance defining permitted/prohibited classroom AI *use*; the bills concern AI *as a subject of instruction* (a CS+AI course), not student AI-use permissions. *[Absence / distinction]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Ethics as curriculum content:** proposed standards require instruction on "the societal and ethical impacts of artificial intelligence" (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 2). *[Unresolved — proposed]*
- **Equity via small-school support:** the department's proposed teacher-capacity plan must "specifically address targeted support for schools with a total enrollment of less than five hundred students in grades nine through twelve" (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 4). *[Unresolved — proposed]*
- A privacy/academic-integrity framework for student AI *use* is **Not found in the provided documents** (no guidance exists). *[Absence]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Proposed department duties (HF 2540):** publish a list of qualifying CS+AI courses by June 30, 2027 (Sec. 4); create and publish a teacher-capacity expansion plan by June 30, 2027, with input from students, PD providers, industry, and higher-education CS-teacher-prep programs (Sec. 4); maintain a statewide K-12 CS+AI instruction plan (Sec. 3). *[Unresolved — proposed]*
- **Course structure:** one semester of CS+AI would satisfy both the CS+AI requirement and one semester of the math or science requirement (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 1). *[Unresolved — proposed]*
- **Deployed AI tool:** Iowa DOE launched a $3M AI reading tutor (voice-recognition EPS Reading Assistant) free to elementary schools. *[Other — deployed program, not guidance]*
sections.offloading: - **Not found in the provided documents.** Iowa has no guidance addressing cognitive offloading, over-reliance, or learning-preservation. The pending bills treat AI as a curricular subject (understanding what AI is and how it works) rather than governing student AI use, so they contain no cognitive-offloading strategy. *[Absence]*
sections.graduate:
- **Near-term (current and next several cohorts): no guaranteed baseline.** With no state guidance and the graduation requirement not effective until the class of 2030-31 (if enacted), incoming Iowa students' AI exposure is entirely district-dependent. *Basis: sources; HF2540.pdf, Sec. 1.*
- **Youngest students:** may have used the state-funded AI reading tutor in elementary school, an early exposure to AI as a learning tool.
- **Future (class of 2030-31 onward, if enacted):** would have completed a semester of CS+AI covering what AI is, how it works, and its societal/ethical impacts (HF2540.pdf, Secs. 1-2).
- **Higher-education implication:** For all current admissions cycles, assume no common Iowa AI baseline and high inter-district variance. Do not assume incoming Iowa students have had formal AI instruction; the guaranteed CS+AI credit is a 2030-31-and-later phenomenon and contingent on enactment.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Because Iowa has no state guidance and no enacted requirement yet, Iowa cohorts will be especially heterogeneous in AI literacy. Plan for a common entry baseline rather than assuming prior instruction.
- **Higher-education implication:** If enacted, the bills reach higher education directly: the department must consult "higher education institutions that offer computer science teacher preparation pathways" (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 4), and SF 2094 reportedly includes college-admissions provisions. Iowa teacher-prep programs could be formally embedded in implementation.
- **Higher-education implication:** The proposed course would double-count as a math or science credit (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 1). Admissions offices evaluating Iowa transcripts should understand that a CS+AI course may occupy a math/science slot.
- **Higher-education implication:** Iowa's youngest students already use a state-funded AI reading tutor, so early AI-as-tool familiarity may precede any formal AI literacy instruction.
sections.response:
- **Onboarding:** Treat Iowa cohorts as pre-baseline; run an explicit AI-literacy entry check. Revisit once/if the CS+AI requirement is enacted and implemented.
- **Academic integrity and assessment design:** Provide explicit per-assignment AI-permission structures, since Iowa students are unlikely to arrive with a shared AI-use framework.
- **Teacher-prep alignment:** Iowa CS-teacher-preparation programs should monitor HF 2540 / SF 2094, which would name them as consulted parties (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 4).
- **Admissions:** Track SF 2094's college-admissions provisions and the math/science double-counting (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 1) when evaluating Iowa transcripts.
- **Monitoring:** Watch for enactment; the bills are introduced, not law.
sections.unique:
- **A CS+AI graduation requirement structured to double-count** as a math or science credit (HF2540.pdf, Sec. 1) — an unusual scheduling design.
- **AI content standards written into statute (proposed)** — "what artificial intelligence is, how artificial intelligence works, and the societal and ethical impacts of artificial intelligence" (Sec. 2).
- **Explicit small-school equity provision** in the proposed teacher-capacity plan (Sec. 4).
- **A deployed statewide AI reading tutor** for elementary students — AI adoption preceding AI guidance.

sections.gaps:
- **No enacted law and no guidance.** HF 2540 and SF 2094 are *introduced* bills; none of their provisions is current law. Iowa has no statewide AI guidance. All legislative provisions are Unresolved/pending.
- **SF 2094 was not read in full** in this pass; its CS+AI graduation scheme, practitioner-prep, and college-admissions provisions are characterized from sources and its similarity to HF 2540. *[Partial]*

states.summary: Kansas has no state education-agency AI guidance. The KSDE statement of no guidance is now nearly three years old (October 2023), and while Kansas is "no longer inactive," the substantive activity is not agency guidance. In February 2026 the State Board heard a University-of-Kansas-authored "Framework for Responsible AI Integration in Pre-K-20 Education" (Basham, Vasquez, Fulchini Scruggs) — a KU product spanning K-12 through higher education, not a KSDE-issued framework. Separately, Kansas is home to the marquee K-12 AI-surveillance case: the Lawrence USD 497 Gaggle lawsuit, filed August 2025, raising First and Fourth Amendment and Kansas Student Publications Act claims over AI monitoring of student communications.

states.summary: Kentucky's brief is distinctive for two moves. First, it deliberately normalizes AI as one emerging technology among many — framed through "Consistency, Balance, Normalization" — arguing that "treating it differently than other emerging technologies can hinder its effective integration and create unnecessary anxieties". These paradigms are its signature instrument and map cleanly onto course design.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence Guidance Brief 2025
documents.issuer: Kentucky Department of Education (KDE), Office of Education Technology (OET)
documents.type: State guidance brief (voluntary; "an example... for districts")

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Normalize AI as an emerging technology** to defuse fear: Consistency, Balance, Normalization (KDE-AI-Guidance-Brief.pdf, p.2).
- **KETS Master Plan goal:** "Encourage, engage and empower the safe and responsible uses of Artificial Intelligence... ensuring humans remain in the loop with strong AI implementations" (p.4, p.7).
- **AI complements, not replaces, educators:** "AI is not a means to replace educators but could complement their strengths, automate routine tasks, and enhance their ability to differentiate" (p.5).

### Intended audiences and scope
- Addresses KDE, districts, and school communities, with distinct "Policy-in-Action Spotlights" for CIOs, Digital Learning Coaches, STLP, Library Media Specialists, and Online/Virtual programs (KDE-AI-Guidance-Brief.pdf, pp.4-13). *[Scope]*
- Explicitly "not a one-size-fits-all approach"; districts retain autonomy (pp.5, 10). *[Scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **No statewide permission scale**; the brief models principles for local policy. *[Not a mandate]*
- **Seven guiding questions for AI integration** function as a use screen — e.g., PII exposure, whether the tool is in the KETS/KDE ecosystem or an unfamiliar third party, over-broad permissions, "freemium" data-as-payment models, ethics of the output, need for review against hallucinations/bias, and consulting a supervisor about unseen risks (p.3). *[Recommendation / screen]*
- **Disclosure rule:** "It is best practice to disclose the use of generative AI tools in all formal publications, presentations, outputs... However, the informal use of generative AI does not require citation" (p.9).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Privacy:** adhere to FERPA, COPPA, and Kentucky HB 5 (2015); treat student/educator data with confidentiality (KDE-AI-Guidance-Brief.pdf, p.10).
- **Equity/bias:** "AI systems should not perpetuate or exacerbate disparities"; check GenAI content for bias and inaccuracy (p.9).
- **Ethics:** references UNESCO's AI Ethics framework and the Partnership on AI for evaluating tools (p.10).
- **Transparency/accountability:** people "should be able to understand how AI systems make decisions" and there should be "ways to hold them accountable" (p.9).
- **Academic integrity:** students and teachers "should give credit to sources and tools and honestly present work that is genuinely their own" (Ethical AI Use, p.10). A specific AI-detection-tool position is **Not found in the provided documents.** *[Recommendation / limited]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **TeachAI three-stage framework:** develop policies; help educators learn about AI; use AI to improve outcomes — pursued "simultaneously" (KDE-AI-Guidance-Brief.pdf, p.4).
- **Digital Citizenship + Computer Science:** AI literacy connected to STLP (Student Technology Leadership Program), digital citizenship, and CS access in all KY schools (p.10).
- **Post-Adoption Monitoring and Evaluation:** uses the "Emerging Technology Adoption Framework: For PK-12 Education" centered on "investigation, fidelity, and effectiveness" (p.13).
- **Professional learning** via partnerships with "universities, research institutions, and AI vendors" and communities of practice (p.7).
sections.offloading:
- The **three paradigms** (AI-directed/supported/empowered, p.12) are Kentucky's central lens on how much cognitive agency stays with the learner — recipient, collaborator, or leader — which directly frames offloading as a design choice. *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Human-in-the-loop (HITL)** is a named tenet: AI "should not operate autonomously without human oversight and control, especially in applications where AI decisions could have significant consequences" (p.8).
- A caution against uncritical AI instruction: "GenAI-directed instruction could turn out to be 'just plain bad instruction,' or instruction centered around information hallucinations if left on its own and not guided by expert teachers" (p.6). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Empower** framing: technology should "amplify human capacity for collaboration, creativity, and communication," not "support outdated education strategies" (p.8).
- The STLP spotlight notes challenges "that require student original work still encourage AI use for inspiration" (p.6).
- A developed cognitive-science treatment (metacognition, over-reliance research) is **Not found in the provided documents**; Kentucky's guard is the paradigm model plus HITL. *[Limited]*
sections.graduate:
- **Uneven by district (voluntary).** Exposure depends on district adoption. *Basis: pp.4, 10.*
- **Where adopted**, Kentucky students may bring: a "treat AI like other tech" normalized stance (p.2); a disclosure habit for formal AI use (p.9); AI-literacy grounding via STLP/digital citizenship (p.10); and familiarity with AI framed along the directed/supported/empowered spectrum (p.12).
- **Higher-education implication:** Kentucky-shaped students may arrive with a calm, normalized view of AI (neither hype nor panic) and a sense that their role can range from recipient to leader depending on the task. Assume variance given voluntariness.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Kentucky's three paradigms (p.12) map directly onto course design — "who is directing the learning, and does AI change that answer?" Faculty can adopt AI-directed/supported/empowered as a shared vocabulary for setting per-activity expectations.
- **Higher-education implication:** Kentucky explicitly names universities as partners in AI professional learning (p.7) and references the University of Kentucky's CELT (p.11). Kentucky institutions are already positioned in the state's AI-education network.
- **Higher-education implication:** The disclosure rule distinguishing formal (cite) from informal (no citation) AI use (p.9) is a nuanced model a college could adopt to avoid over-broad citation mandates.
- **Higher-education implication:** The "normalize AI as one tool among many" stance (p.2) suggests Kentucky students may resist both AI-panic and AI-hype framings; institutions can meet them with a measured, integration-focused posture.
sections.response:
- **Assessment design:** Use the directed/supported/empowered paradigm (p.12) to specify, per assignment, how much cognitive leadership stays with the student.
- **Academic integrity:** Adopt Kentucky's formal-vs-informal disclosure distinction (p.9) and the "genuinely their own work" standard (p.10); pair with the seven guiding questions (p.3) as a tool-vetting screen.
- **Governance and procurement:** Reuse the seven guiding questions (p.3) and the Emerging Technology Adoption Framework (investigation/fidelity/effectiveness, p.13) for institutional AI-tool evaluation.
- **Faculty development:** Partner with in-state universities' teaching centers (e.g., UK CELT, p.11), extending Kentucky's "Engage" model (p.7) into higher education.
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Center HITL (p.8) and the caution that unguided AI instruction can be "just plain bad instruction" (p.6).
sections.unique:
- **Three application-and-research paradigms** — AI-directed, AI-supported, AI-empowered (learner as recipient/collaborator/leader), grounded in Ouyang & Jiao (2021) and framed alongside SAMR/TCoP (KDE-AI-Guidance-Brief.pdf, p.12).
- **A deliberate "normalize AI as an emerging technology" stance** (Consistency, Balance, Normalization, p.2) intended to defuse fear.
- **Seven guiding questions for AI integration** as a practical vetting screen (p.3).
- **KETS-Master-Plan framing** (Encourage/Engage/Empower/Safe and Responsible/School Efficiency/Humans in the Loop, pp.7-8).
- **A formal-vs-informal disclosure distinction** (p.9) and a research-based post-adoption evaluation framework (p.13).
sections.gaps:
- **Voluntariness.** District adoption and student exposure are **Not found in the provided documents.**
- **No enacted statute**.
- **No AI-detection-tool position, student-use permission scale, or grade-band progression** appears; Kentucky's model is paradigm- and principle-based rather than a leveled scale. *[Limited]*
- **The three paradigms describe learner roles, not permission levels** — they are an instructional lens, not a per-assignment AI-use scale like Oklahoma's or New Mexico's. Do not conflate. *[Clarification]*
- **Higher-education references** (universities as partners, UK CELT) are soft hooks, not binding provisions (pp.7, 11). *[Note]*

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **AI as a supportive tool, not a replacement:** "AI is most effective as a supportive tool that empowers educators rather than serving as a replacement for their expertise" (LDOE-AI-Guidance.pdf, p.3).
- **Five Guiding Principles** (p.2): Data Privacy and Security; Ethical Considerations; Student-Centered Learning ("promote agency and ownership over learning"); Transparency and Explainability; Professional Development.
- **Shared responsibility** for safe use among educators, leaders, families, students, and external stakeholders (p.3).

### Intended audiences and scope
- Addresses "school system leaders, school leaders, teachers and staff members, educational technology innovators, policymakers, and researchers," plus families (LDOE-AI-Guidance.pdf, pp.2-3). *[Scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses — the AI Integration Tiered Approach (p.7)
A four-tier, assignment-level student-use scale, each tier mapped to SAMR:
- **AI-Prohibited (Substitution):** "AI tools are not permitted for assignments or tasks specifically designed to evaluate students' core knowledge and skills." Example: deliver a slideshow without AI. *[Recommendation / instrument level]*
- **AI-Assisted (Augmentation):** "Students may use AI as a feedback tool, but they should create all of the assignment's content themselves." Example: AI as a brainstorming thought partner. *[Instrument level]*
- **AI-Enhanced (Modification):** "Students may use AI as a tool to transform the learning process, but sources should be cited, and all generated content should be reviewed for accuracy." Example: AI to analyze data for a science report. *[Instrument level]*
- **AI-Empowered (Redefinition):** "Students are encouraged to fully engage with AI under human supervision, citing sources and carefully reviewing all generated content for accuracy." Example: AI-powered design software to create 3D models. *[Instrument level]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human judgment central; AI enhances, not replaces:** "Artificial intelligence should enhance, not replace, the educators, counselors, and school leaders who remain Maryland's primary decision makers" (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.2). *[Recommendation / framework expectation]*
- **AI literacy as a core skill** enabling learners to "assess reliability, identify bias, understand underlying assumptions" (p.2). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Statutory objective:** an "Artificial Intelligence Ready Schools Act" establishing guidelines, professional development, and a collaborative (SB0720-enrolled.pdf, title). *[Requirement]*
- **Alignment** with the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and statewide CS/digital-literacy efforts (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.2). *[Framework]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- The framework is "intended for state leaders, LEA and school administrators, educators, students and families, and vendors" and "applies to all AI tools that interact with Maryland students, staff, or data" (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, pp.2-3). *[Scope]*
- SB 720 binds MSDE, county boards, local school systems, and a designated higher-education institution (SB0720-enrolled.pdf). *[Scope, Requirement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- The framework "does not approve or prohibit specific tools" (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.3); districts define permitted/prohibited uses locally. *[Framework — delegated]*
- **Data prohibitions:** "Collection of biometric, behavioral, or location data is prohibited unless legally required and educationally justified"; avoid entering PII into generative tools unless explicitly approved (p.5). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Vendor gate:** "Tools that fail to meet these standards must not be used" (p.4). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Statutory tool certification:** AI tools must be certified "consistent with certain State guidelines," supported by a designated 4-year higher-education institution (SB0720-enrolled.pdf, higher-education provision). *[Requirement]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Privacy/civil rights:** compliance with FERPA, COPPA, PPRA, and Maryland regulations; "Algorithm-assisted decisions remain subject to nondiscrimination requirements"; data minimization (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.5). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Equity and Access** is a dedicated section (p.6). *[Framework]*
- **Academic integrity — detectors not endorsed:** "Maryland does not endorse AI-detection tools as a primary means of enforcing academic integrity, as research shows they are unreliable and inequitable (Liang et al., 2023)"; integrity supported "through instructional design, transparency, and human judgment," and concerns addressed "through instruction rather than punishment" (p.7). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Vendors** must meet transparency, privacy, accessibility, equity, and security standards, including fairness testing and audit participation (p.4). *[Framework expectation]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Assessment redesign:** "Assessment practices must evolve to emphasize reasoning, analysis, reflection, and process over recall. Tasks should require visible evidence of student thinking and reduce opportunities for AI substitution" (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.7). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Professional learning** is role-specific (teachers, administrators, district leaders, specialists), delivered via the MSDE AI Hub, with core educator AI competencies aligned to UNESCO (2023) (p.8). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Student AI literacy and curriculum integration** is a dedicated section (p.10); SB 720 requires AI literacy standards and ties AI literacy to workforce preparation (SB0720-enrolled.pdf, literacy provisions). *[Requirement + framework]*
- **Statutory structures:** a district AI policy by the statutory date; a central-office AI coordinator per district; the Maryland AI Education Collaborative; PD for educators and school leaders including "basic artificial intelligence vocabulary" and applying AI to instruction (SB0720-enrolled.pdf). *[Requirement]*
- Per sources: AI literacy in state standards by June 1, 2027; coordinator designation required now. *[Requirement — dates from sources]*
sections.offloading:
- **Over-reliance named as a first-order risk** in the executive summary: AI introduces risks including "over-reliance on automated systems" (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.2). *[Framework]*
- **AI-resilient assessment:** emphasize "reasoning, analysis, reflection, and process over recall," require "visible evidence of student thinking," and "reduce opportunities for AI substitution"; any use that "replaces essential skill development violates academic integrity" (p.7). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Educator over-trust caution:** professional learning must counter "the documented tendency to over-trust automated recommendations (Goddard et al., 2012)" and emphasize "critical evaluation, verification, and reflective practice" (p.8). *[Framework expectation]*
- **Student critical evaluation:** students "must learn to critically evaluate AI outputs, verify information, and understand AI limitations" (p.7). *[Framework expectation]*
- This is a substantive, research-cited learning-preservation posture, though not a single named cognitive-offloading section. *[Framework]*
sections.graduate:
- **Becoming a mandated baseline, but phasing in.** SB 720 is enacted, but AI literacy in state standards is due June 1, 2027, so near-term Maryland graduates predate a fully standardized baseline; district policies and coordinators are being stood up now.
- **Where implemented**, Maryland students may bring: AI-literacy skills (assess reliability, identify bias, understand assumptions, p.2); experience with disclosure-and-documentation of AI use and AI-resilient assessments (p.7); and a district AI policy governing permitted/prohibited use.
- **Higher-education implication:** Maryland is trending toward a genuinely standardized, statute-backed AI-literacy baseline. In a few years Maryland graduates may arrive with more uniform AI literacy than voluntary-guidance states; for now assume variance and phase-in.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Maryland statutorily assigns a **named 4-year university (Morgan State or another in-state institution) to support certification and evaluation of the AI tools K-12 uses** (SB0720-enrolled.pdf). This is a direct, ongoing higher-education role in K-12 AI governance — Maryland institutions are not just downstream recipients but statutory participants.
- **Higher-education implication:** Maryland students may arrive taught that AI detectors are "unreliable and inequitable" (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.7). Institutions relying on detectors as primary evidence will diverge from that experience.
- **Higher-education implication:** Maryland's AI-resilient assessment standard (reasoning/process over recall, visible thinking, p.7) previews what incoming students will expect assessment to look like; it is also a ready model for university course redesign.
- **Higher-education implication:** Maryland created a named, funded, non-teaching AI coordinator in every district. An institution can ask whether it has an equivalent dedicated AI role or whether the work is spread across people who already have other jobs.
sections.response:
- **Governance and partnership:** Maryland institutions (especially Morgan State) should operationalize the statutory tool-certification role (SB0720-enrolled.pdf) and coordinate entry expectations with the K-12 pipeline; other institutions can adopt the named-coordinator model.
- **Academic integrity:** Follow Maryland's stance — do not use AI detectors as primary evidence; support integrity through instructional design, transparency, and human judgment, addressing concerns "through instruction rather than punishment" (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.7).
- **Assessment design:** Adopt AI-resilient assessment emphasizing reasoning, reflection, and visible thinking (p.7).
- **AI tool availability and privacy:** Apply Maryland's vendor standards and data-minimization/biometric-prohibition expectations to institutional procurement (pp.4-5).
- **Faculty development:** Mirror Maryland's role-specific PD and core AI competencies (p.8) for faculty and staff.
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** Center the enhance-not-replace vision and over-reliance cautions (pp.2, 8).
sections.unique:
- **A named higher-education institution (Morgan State University or another 4-year institution) statutorily tasked with certifying/evaluating K-12 AI tools** (SB0720-enrolled.pdf) — among the most concrete higher-ed-binding provisions in the set.
- **A mandated central-office, non-instructional AI coordinator in every local school system** (SB0720-enrolled.pdf).
- **A statewide Maryland AI Education Collaborative** established by statute.
- **An explicit non-endorsement of AI-detection tools** and an AI-resilient assessment standard (MSDE-AI-Guidance-A.pdf, p.7).
- **A comprehensive June 2026 framework** spanning roles, privacy, equity, integrity, PD, literacy, operations, and procurement, aligned to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future.

- **Phase-in.** AI literacy in state standards is due June 1, 2027; near-term student exposure is uneven, and coordinator/policy implementation is in progress. Adoption specifics are **Not found in the provided documents.**
- **The "$150,000 FY2027 higher-education partnership"** figure was **not located in the enrolled-text grep** here; the statute's named-institution certification role IS confirmed. Confirm the fiscal figure against the fiscal note. *[Partial]*

- **The exact district-policy deadline** (a reported fall-2026, 120-day clock) relies on secondary coverage per sources and was not pinned to statutory text here. *[Unresolved]*
