sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** A4352 is the dataset's most direct obligation on higher education itself. As introduced, "Each public institution of higher education shall offer certificate and degree programs in artificial intelligence" (sec.2.a). If enacted, every New Jersey public four-year institution and county college would have to stand up AI certificate and degree programs, supported by state model curricula (sec.2.b). This is a pending requirement, not current law, and its force depends entirely on passage.
- **Higher-education implication:** The bill corrects a common tracker error in both directions. It is not merely a "model curricula" bill, and it is not merely a K-12 bill. It pairs a K-12 instruction mandate with an affirmative program-offering mandate on public colleges (secs.1-2). Institutions should read the operative text, not the compressed synopsis.
- **Higher-education implication:** The model curricula, if developed, would be built with workforce and county-college input (Labor and Workforce Development, Economic Development Authority, NJ Council of County Colleges, NJ Presidents' Council, sec.2.b) and would have to "account for academic quality and other applicable standards required for accreditation" (sec.2.c). Institutions may face a state-shaped template for AI program design.
- **Higher-education implication:** For students entering before any enactment, there is no state AI baseline to assume, so entry planning should mirror the no-state-guidance states, an explicit orientation and diagnostic at entry.
sections.response:
- **Track the bill.** New Jersey public institutions should monitor A4352/S2862. If it advances, they will need to plan AI certificate and degree programs and engage with the Secretary of Higher Education's model-curriculum process (secs.2.a-b).
- **Engage the consultation channels.** The bill routes model-curriculum development through the NJ Presidents' Council and the NJ Council of County Colleges (sec.2.b). Institutions can shape the template through those bodies rather than receive it passively.
- **Onboarding for current cohorts:** Assume no state AI baseline for students entering now. Give an explicit AI-use orientation and a short literacy diagnostic.
- **Assessment design:** State AI permission explicitly per assignment; New Jersey students do not yet share a standardized state scale or vocabulary.
- **Prepare for a standards-based intake later.** If A4352 is enacted, align entry expectations to its K-12 content (general concepts, user skills, responsible-use best practices, sec.1.c) once those cohorts arrive.

documents.title: New Mexico AI Guidance for K-12 Education 1.0 (v2025.1)
documents.issuer: New Mexico Public Education Department (NMPED), Curriculum & Instruction Division, with the William & Ida Friday Institute for Educational Innovation, NC State University

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human-centric AI is the spine of the document** (Guidance, p.3). "Human-centric AI values the person over the machine throughout the engagement process" and positions AI "as a tool to support rather than replace" human relationships (p.3). *[Recommendation / stated philosophy]*
- **Digital equity is a first-order objective**, tied to the NM Digital Equity in Education Act of 2023 (p. Introduction; p.12). The guidance frames AI as a potential widener of disparity "particularly for students from under-resourced schools or rural areas" (p.11).
- **AI literacy for both educators and students**, "modeled after Digital Promise's Framework (2024)": users should be able to "(1) understand how AI systems function, (2) evaluate its potential and risks, and (3) apply it thoughtfully in real-world contexts" (p.6). *[Recommendation / instructional guidance]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- Explicitly addressed to "educators, administrators and communities" (p. How to Use this Guidance, p. following Introduction). *[Scope statement]*
- Scope is all of K-12, with content broken into Early Grades (K-5), Middle Grades (6-8), and High School (pp.7-9). *[Scope statement]*
- The document is a state-agency resource that defers to local governance. "Local governance allows schools to adapt AI guidelines to their unique needs" (p.20).

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **This is guidance, not a rulebook. It contains no statewide prohibition list.** *[Not a mandate]*
- The AI Assessment Scale (p.19) is the closest thing to a permission structure, but it is offered as an adaptable example, not a rule. Its five levels, verbatim:
 - **Level 1 NO AI** — "The assessment is completed entirely without AI assistance in a controlled environment... You must not use AI at any point."
 - **Level 2 AI PLANNING** — "AI may be used for pre-task activities such as brainstorming, outlining and initial research... final submission should show how you have developed and refined these ideas."
 - **Level 3 AI COLLABORATION** — "AI may be used to help complete the task, including idea generation, drafting, feedback, and refinement. Students should critically evaluate and modify the AI suggested outputs."
 - **Level 4 FULL AI** — "AI may be used to complete any elements of the task, with students directing AI... Focus on directing AI to achieve your goals while demonstrating your critical thinking."
 - **Level 5 AI EXPLORATION** — "AI is used creatively... Students and educators co-design assessments to explore unique AI applications within the field of study."
- Restriction posture on tooling is a **recommended vetting process**, not a banned-tools list: educators "must evaluate tools with a critical lens" before purchase (p.10).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Five ethical protections** drawn from the 2022 Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights (p.10): "Safe and effective systems; Algorithmic discrimination protection; Data privacy; Notice and explanation; Human alternatives, consideration and fallback." Each carries a one-line gloss, e.g. Data privacy requires tools to "respect data sovereignty (where data are stored, who owns the data, and how or when the data is deleted)" (p.10).
- **Accessibility is written into procurement**: "Accessibility features, such as text-to-speech and translation tools powered by AI, must be incorporated into procurement processes" (p.11). *[Recommendation, phrased as an imperative but within a voluntary document]*
- **Academic integrity (pp.18-19)** is handled as a values question, not an enforcement one. The core principle: "all submitted work should reflect a student's own understanding, effort and originality, even when supported by AI tools" (p.18).
- **Position on AI detection tools (p.18):** "AI detectors do not have high reliability in detecting plagiarism (Center for Democracy & Technology, 2023) and are frequently found to be biased against non-native English writers (Liang et al., 2023)." Educators are told to "critically evaluate the validity, accuracy and ethical implications of AI detection tools." *[Recommendation — a caution against detectors]*
- Disclosure and citation of AI use is encouraged as an integrity habit: "Properly citing AI tools or providing disclosure... demonstrates honesty" (p.18).

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Professional development** is framed as prerequisite: PD "should provide the knowledge, skills and confidence educators need" (p.6), with a linked resource list (Digital Promise, MIT, Code.org, TeachAI, Common Sense Media, the Friday Institute's "AI with the FI" course) (p.6). *[Recommendation + examples]*
- **Curriculum integration** favors embedding over standalone units: "it is equally important to embed these skills into existing standards and core curriculum" (p.13, Standards Alignment).
- The **Teaching WITH AI vs. Teaching ABOUT AI** table (p.13) separates using AI as an instructional tool from teaching AI as subject matter, and says both are needed. *[Instructional guidance]*
- **SAMR** (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition) structures the Scaffolded Technology Integration chart (p.16), explicitly labeled "an example to inspire further exploration... not as an endorsement of any tool" (p.16).
- **Implementation/governance:** districts are encouraged to build local AI policies on existing Responsible/Acceptable Use Policies, review them throughout the year, and make "age-appropriate versions" for students (p.20).
sections.offloading:
This document engages cognitive offloading directly and by name, which is unusual.

- The **Critical Thinking & Problem Solving** section (p.17) states the risk explicitly: "concerns persist that over-reliance on AI might erode essential skills by encouraging students to accept AI-generated outputs without questioning them or bypassing the process of independent reasoning." *[Instructional guidance]*
- Its stated mitigation: "AI should be positioned as a tool or assistant, not as a partner or replacement for human thinking. Teachers should guide students in critically evaluating AI outputs, identifying errors and understanding the logic behind AI-generated results" (p.17).
- It supplies concrete interrogation prompts for teachers to model: "'What assumptions does AI make?' and 'How do these results compare to other evidence we've reviewed?'" (p.17). *[Instructional guidance / example]*
- The **4-I framework** (Inquiry, Input, Interpretation, Insight, p.4) is itself an anti-offloading structure. It begins with "human-driven curiosity" and requires humans to "analyze and evaluate the AI-generated output... assess its accuracy, biases and alignment" before integrating findings, so that "AI does not replace human judgment" (p.4). *[Recommendation / framework]*
- The **Human-in-the-Loop / teacher-in-the-loop** construct (p.3) reinforces that "beginning and ending AI use with human inquiry and reflection" is the intended pattern.
- **Preserving subject-matter learning:** the guidance ties AI-literacy skills to core-content standards rather than treating AI as a separate subject (p.13), and its Level 1 NO AI option (p.19) preserves the option of assessing "core skills and knowledge" without AI at all. *[Recommendation / example]*
sections.graduate:
The following describe capabilities and habits a New Mexico graduate *may* bring, each tied to what the document actually recommends. Because the guidance is voluntary and locally adaptable, exposure will be uneven across districts.

- **Familiarity with a leveled AI-permission vocabulary.** A student in a district that adopted the AI Assessment Scale will recognize the idea that each assignment carries an explicit AI level from "No AI" to "AI Exploration" (p.19). *Basis: p.19, offered as adaptable example.*
- **Exposure to AI as subject matter, scaled by grade.** High-school content recommends "neural networks, deep learning and natural language processing," building text classifiers, AI auditing for bias, and "Career Pathways" connecting AI to professions (p.9). Middle grades recommend building simple models in Scratch or Python and analyzing datasets for bias (p.8). *Basis: pp.8-9, recommendations.*
- **A disclosure-and-citation habit around AI use** where districts adopted it (p.18). *Basis: p.18.*
- **An interrogation stance toward AI output**, if their teachers modeled the p.17 prompts. *Basis: p.17.*
- **Higher-education implication:** These are *ceilings of possibility, not guarantees.* Because the document is voluntary, a faculty member should assume a wide range within a single New Mexico cohort, from students who ran district AI tools daily (Gadsden, Santa Fe examples, pp.5, 14) to students whose district adopted little of this.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Incoming New Mexico students may already speak the exact AIAS vocabulary that a university syllabus can adopt. Because the K-12 scale and the peer-reviewed source (Perkins et al. 2024) share level names, a faculty member can align a course to that scale and expect partial prior familiarity rather than starting from zero (basis: p.19 attribution).
- **Higher-education implication:** Students from adopting districts may arrive expecting AI use to be *specified per assignment* rather than globally banned or allowed. A blanket "no AI" or silent syllabus will read as less clear than what they experienced (basis: the per-assignment logic of p.19).
- **Higher-education implication:** Students may have been taught that AI *detectors are unreliable and biased* (p.18). Institutions that rely on AI-detection software for integrity enforcement may face students who were explicitly taught to distrust those tools, which is a defensible position the K-12 document itself takes.
- **Higher-education implication:** New Mexico's guidance names an explicit K-16 pipeline. The New Mexico AI Consortium (NMAIC) unites Los Alamos and Sandia National Laboratories with UNM, NMSU, NM Tech, and Central New Mexico Community College "to establish pathways for AI research and education" and to integrate "AI literacy into school curricula, leveraging the resources of higher education" (p.21). A New Mexico higher-education institution may already be a named partner in the pipeline feeding it.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because exposure is uneven, the safest planning assumption is high variance in AI literacy within any New Mexico cohort, driving a need for a common baseline at entry rather than assumed competence.
sections.response:
- **AI tool availability and equity:** New Mexico's equity framing (pp.11-12) implies incoming students may expect accessibility features (text-to-speech, translation) as standard. Institutions should confirm their sanctioned AI tools carry those features and that access does not depend on a student's ability to pay for a premium tier.
- **Onboarding:** Give a short entry diagnostic of AI literacy rather than assuming it. The state's own AI-literacy definition (understand, evaluate, apply thoughtfully, p.6) is a ready rubric for such a diagnostic.
- **Assessment design:** Adopt an explicit per-assignment AI-permission scale. Because New Mexico students may recognize the AIAS levels, adopting the same Perkins et al. (2024) source gives continuity from high school to college. Preserve "Level 1 NO AI" assessments where the learning goal is core skill demonstration (mirrors p.19).
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Reconsider reliance on AI detectors, which the students' own K-12 guidance calls unreliable and biased against non-native English writers (p.18). Favor process-based and disclosure-based integrity approaches, which is exactly the habit the guidance tried to build (p.18).
- **Faculty development:** Offer faculty the teaching-with vs. teaching-about distinction (p.13) and the anti-offloading interrogation prompts (p.17) as ready-made pedagogy, since incoming students may already have met them.
- **Governance:** Where the institution sits in New Mexico, check whether it is a NMAIC partner (p.21) and coordinate entry expectations with that pipeline.
- **Advancing learning rather than replacing thinking:** The 4-I cycle (p.4) and the p.17 mitigation language give a shared K-16 framework for keeping the human in the loop. Adopting the same language lowers the translation cost for incoming students.
sections.unique:
- **The AI Assessment Scale with explicit academic attribution** to "Perkins, Furze, Roe & MacVaugh (2024). The AI Assessment Scale," printed under the table with a CC BY-NC-SA mark (p.19). This is a primary-source-confirmed lineage to the peer-reviewed AIAS, per the folder's sources.
- **The 4-I framework** (Inquiry → Input → Interpretation → Insight), a named, cyclical human-in-the-loop reasoning model (p.4). Distinctive terminology.
- **M.A.Z.E.** tool-vetting mnemonic — "Monitor data privacy, Assess for accuracy, Zero-in on bias, Evaluate value" — credited to the Friday Institute (p.10).
- **National-laboratory partnership.** The NMAIC brings Los Alamos and Sandia into a K-16 AI-education pipeline (p.21), a hook few other states can claim.
- **Cultural/equity grounding** in the NM Digital Equity in Education Act (2023) and a three-divide model (digital use divide, digital design divide, digital access divide, p.11).
sections.gaps:
- **Voluntariness limits every claim about students.** The document mandates nothing, so actual student exposure to any instrument is unknown and district-dependent. Per-district adoption data is Not found in the provided documents.
- **No statute in the provided files.** sources notes HB 330 (AI ethics as a CS elective) as pending; the bill text is not in this folder, so no enacted requirement can be asserted. *[Unresolved]*
- **M.A.Z.E. wording** was flagged in earlier project passes as tracker-sourced; it is now confirmed on p.10 of the primary document, attributed to the Friday Institute. The prior data.js gloss of the scale endpoints ("No AI to AI Exploration") is correct on endpoints; the full internal level names (AI Planning, AI Collaboration, Full AI) are now verbatim-confirmed (p.19).
- **Glossary, acknowledgements, and references (pp.22-24)** were not required for this analysis and were not transcribed in detail. Not a substantive gap for policy claims.
- **District examples** (Gadsden p.5, Santa Fe p.14) are illustrative spotlights, not evidence of statewide practice. Treat as Examples only.

states.summary: North Carolina's guidance is a recommendation-level, unusually instrument-rich living document. It is organized around the five focus areas of the NC Digital Learning Plan and covers PK-13, meaning it deliberately runs from pre-kindergarten through grade 13 (the community-college and educator level). documents.title: North Carolina Generative AI Implementation Recommendations and Considerations for PK-13 Public Schools
documents.issuer: NC Department of Public Instruction (NCDPI), Office of Digital Teaching and Learning, AI Guidelines Committee, with AI for Education
documents.date: First published Jan 16, 2024; living document, last updated 2/25/2026 (per the document's title page)

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **AI literacy as a graduate necessity.** The document frames AI literacy as "a must-have for every graduate" and a durable skill (p.11), organized around the NC Digital Learning Plan's five focus areas (p.1).
- **Human-centered co-creation.** The goal is "not to adapt education to AI, but to adapt education for the Intelligence Age," leveraging "what AI does best... to unlock what humans do best (innovation, empathy, judgment, collaboration)" (p.33). *[Recommendation / stated philosophy]*
- **Developmental appropriateness is a first-order design rule**, with distinct expectations by grade band (pp.17-19 and the AI-literacy stages).
- **Local control governs adoption.** "Each PSU may determine its own guidelines and policies" (p.17). *[Scope statement]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- Scope is PK-13, explicitly including educators. The AI Fluency stage is titled "Working ALONGSIDE AI (Grades 9-13 and Educators)" (p.~53 of the doc's flow). *[Scope statement]*
- Authored by the NCDPI AI Guidelines Committee (lead contributor Vera Cubero) in collaboration with AI for Education, with a dedicated Office of Exceptional Children appendix (title page; Appendix D). *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **The permission structure is the "0 to Infinity" AI Use Continuum v. 2.0** (Appendix B), offered as an adaptable acceptable-use scale, not a rule. Its five levels, per the educator version:
 - **Level 0 AI Free** — "students rely solely on their own thinking, knowledge, and skills... creates a clear baseline."
 - **Level 1 AI for Planning** — "AI is introduced as a thought partner in the earliest stages... a planning scaffold... without building the final product."
 - **Level 2 AI Collaboration** — "AI and students work together in a collaborative loop... students remain the decision-makers."
 - **Level 3 Full AI Use** — "students use AI as a strategic partner throughout the entire process... while maintaining critical oversight."
 - **Level 4 AI Exploration** — "the transformative zone, where students use AI as a launchpad for innovation."
- The document says the scale "should be referred to clarify what level, if any, is acceptable use of AI on a given task" and be "explicitly taught and posted" (p.31).
- **A developmental restriction on chatbots.** For grades PK-5, "direct chatbot use is not recommended," and "students should not engage directly with the chatbots" (p.17). This is the document's clearest use restriction, framed as developmental protection, not prohibition-by-rule.
- **AI-Resistant, AI-Assisted, and AI-Partnered assignment categories** are provided for assessment design (Update Log p.29). *[Instructional guidance]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Data privacy is a throughline.** Users must "never put PII (Personally Identifiable Information) into an AI tool" (AI Fluency stage), and a dedicated Office of Exceptional Children appendix governs AI use with student records and IEP drafting under human review (Appendix D).
- **Accessibility has a named advisor** on the committee and dedicated AI-for-accessibility guidance for exceptional children (title page; Appendix D).
- **Academic integrity is process- and disclosure-based.** The document teaches "mandatory AI-use disclosure statements," notes the US Copyright Office position that "purely AI-generated material is not copyrightable," and treats suspected over-reliance as "a teachable moment... rather than a 'gotcha'" (pp.29, 32).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** strongly cautionary. "AI detectors have proven not to be dependable, therefore they should never be used as the only factor when determining if a student 'cheated'," citing false positives for non-native English speakers and creative writers and false negatives for skilled AI users (p.32). *[Recommendation — a caution against detectors]*
- **Environmental impact is named**, "every AI prompt carries an environmental" cost (p.~678 of the flow). *[Instructional guidance]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **A developmental AI-literacy progression** structures curriculum integration (pp.~1860-1980 of the flow):
 - **AI Awareness (PK-5):** learn ABOUT AI, literacy-first, no direct chatbot use.
 - **AI Literacy (6-8):** learn ABOUT and WITH AI, heavily scaffolded chatbot use under teacher direction.
 - **AI Fluency (9-13 and Educators):** working ALONGSIDE AI as a "thinking partner," advanced prompting, iterative co-creation, metacognition portfolios.
- **Named support tools:** the EVERY framework (below), the CRAFT 2.0 prompting framework with "Power-Ups" (Appendix C), and multiple custom GPTs and interactive teaching guides (pp.29, Appendix C). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Assessment guidance emphasizes process evidence.** "Collect outlines, drafts, or chat links at Levels 2-4 to assess thinking, not just the final product," and "differentiate gradually," starting the year at Level 0 or 1 (Appendix B). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Implementation support** runs through regional Digital Teaching and Learning Consultants and the DTL Hub (About this Resource).
sections.offloading:
North Carolina engages offloading through both its scale design and its developmental gating.

- **Level 0 AI Free exists precisely to preserve unaided cognition.** It builds "essential cognitive habits, such as personal problem-solving, self-reliance, and academic integrity" and "creates a clear baseline" (Appendix B). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **The PK-5 no-chatbot recommendation is an anti-offloading control for early learners**, grounded in the argument that "young children are not developmentally ready to critically evaluate AI outputs" and that lifelike chatbots can "blur that boundary" between fantasy and fact (p.17).
- **The EVERY framework builds verification into every AI interaction.** Created by AI for Education and Vera Cubero (NCDPI), it is "Evaluate, Verify, Engage, Revise, and remember that You are responsible for the final product" (p.29). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Assessment shifts to process evidence** so that thinking, not output, is graded (Appendix B). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **It reframes over-reliance as teachable, not punitive.** Suspected over-dependence "should be viewed as a teachable moment to reinforce the appropriate partnership with AI tools" (p.32).
- The document also acknowledges the flip side, noting that when routine generation "can now be offloaded to AI, teachers and students can spend more time on deeper learning" (p.~1106 of the flow), so offloading is managed, not uniformly resisted. *[Instructional guidance]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a North Carolina graduate *may* bring. Because the guidance is voluntary and PSU-implemented, exposure varies.

- **Familiarity with a five-level, AIAS-derived permission scale.** A student in an adopting PSU will recognize that assignments carry an explicit level from "AI Free" to "AI Exploration," posted and taught (Appendix B). *Basis: Appendix B, adaptable instrument.*
- **A grade-scaled AI-literacy trajectory.** Under the developmental progression, a graduate likely had no direct chatbot use before upper elementary, scaffolded use in middle school, and "AI Fluency" co-creation in high school (pp.17-19). *Basis: AI-literacy stages.*
- **A disclosure-and-verification habit** via the EVERY framework and mandatory disclosure modeling (p.29). *Basis: p.29.*
- **An expectation that AI detectors are unreliable and not decisive** (p.32). *Basis: p.32.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat these as ceilings of possibility, not guarantees. Because adoption is by PSU, faculty should expect a range, but North Carolina's instruments are specific enough that adopting-PSU students may arrive with genuinely transferable vocabulary.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** North Carolina's student-use scale shares its lineage with the peer-reviewed AI Assessment Scale (Furze, Perkins, Roe, McVaugh; p.31). A university can adopt the same source and expect adopting-PSU students to recognize the level structure, from "AI Free" to "AI Exploration," rather than starting from zero.
- **Higher-education implication:** The framework already extends to "Grades 9-13 and Educators" (AI Fluency stage), so its top band is explicitly postsecondary-facing. Community colleges and early-college programs in North Carolina may find the K-12 and entry-level college vocabulary already aligned.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students were taught that *AI detectors are unreliable and biased against non-native English writers* (p.32). Institutions relying on AI-detection software may face students explicitly trained to distrust it, a position the state document takes.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students from adopting PSUs may arrive expecting AI permission to be *specified per assignment* and *posted*, and expecting to submit process evidence (drafts, chat links) rather than only final products (Appendix B). A silent or blanket syllabus will read as less clear than what they experienced.
- **Higher-education implication:** The developmental gating means younger cohorts had *deliberately limited* early AI exposure. A faculty member should not assume long AI histories; formal fluency work is concentrated in high school and up.
sections.response:
- **Assessment design:** Adopt an explicit per-assignment AI-permission scale and consider using the same Furze/Perkins/Roe/McVaugh AIAS source (p.31) for continuity. Preserve Level 0 AI-Free assessments where core-skill demonstration is the goal (Appendix B).
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Favor process- and disclosure-based integrity, mirroring EVERY and the state's disclosure norm (p.29). Do not rely on AI detectors, which the students' own K-12 guidance calls undependable (p.32).
- **Onboarding:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic at entry. The state's grade-band progression (Awareness → Literacy → Fluency) is a ready rubric for placing students.
- **Prompt-literacy scaffolding:** Build on the CRAFT 2.0 framework and EVERY checklist students may already know (pp.29, Appendix C), extending toward source verification and citation.
- **Community-college alignment:** Because the framework already names grade 13, two-year and early-college programs can align entry AI expectations directly to the state's Fluency band.
sections.unique:
- **The "0 to Infinity" AI Use Continuum v. 2.0**, a five-level (0-4) student scale with both educator and student versions, primary-source-attributed to the Furze/Perkins/Roe/McVaugh AI Assessment Scale (p.31; Appendix B). A clear anchor for the project's Perkins-spine instruments library.
- **A PK-13 scope that names grade 13 and educators**, extending the framework into the community-college and educator space explicitly.
- **A developmental grade-band progression** (AI Awareness PK-5, AI Literacy 6-8, AI Fluency 9-13) with a strong PK-5 no-direct-chatbot recommendation grounded in child development (p.17).
- **The EVERY responsible-use framework** (Evaluate, Verify, Engage, Revise, You) and the **CRAFT 2.0 prompting framework** with Power-Ups (pp.29, Appendix C), both with interactive custom-GPT tools.
- **A firm anti-detector section** with a rationale and a "teachable moment" alternative (p.32).
- **A dedicated Office of Exceptional Children AI acceptable-use appendix** (Appendix D, launched Nov 2025) governing AI in IEP drafting under human review.
- **A genuine living-document practice** with a detailed public Update Log tracking every revision (pp.2-3).
sections.gaps:
- **Voluntariness limits every claim about students.** The document mandates nothing and is PSU-implemented, so actual exposure is unknown and PSU-dependent. Per-PSU adoption data is Not found in the provided documents.
- **This resolves two prior sources flags.** The CRAFT framework, flagged "unverified this pass," is confirmed in the captured living document as CRAFT 2.0 with Power-Ups (Appendix C). The EVERY framework is confirmed, though the captured text expands it as "Evaluate, Verify, Engage, Revise, You" while the press release reportedly rendered the third step as "Edit"; the document's own wording is used here. *[Resolved with a minor wording discrepancy]*
- **The document is a moving target.** It is a living Google Doc updated continuously; the analysis reflects the 2/25/2026 export. Later versions may differ. To fix an "original in hand," a dated PDF export should be archived. *[Unresolved by nature]*
- **The scale's graphics were not captured as images.** The level text is verbatim from Appendix B, but the printable posters (teacher and student versions) are image downloads not rendered in the text extract. The student version's disclosure column is described but not transcribed. *[Unresolved]*
- **No standalone statute is in the folder.** The document references an existing NC computer-science requirement (elective CS in middle school, a CS graduation requirement) but that statute is not provided as a source here, so it is treated as context, not a verified AI mandate. *[Unresolved]*

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **AI is framed as one more instructional tool**, not a rupture. "Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the latest in a long and continuing list of tools that can be used to transform teaching, streamline business operations, and personalize learning". *[Recommendation / framing]*
- **Developmental appropriateness is the organizing principle**, expressed through four grade bands.
- **Equity and inclusion recur as objectives.** The leadership checklist stresses that AI "has the potential to address inequities. Without this focus, it can intensify existing inequities and make school more difficult for already marginalized students" (Checklist-School-Leadership).
- **Local control governs adoption.** The framework is a springboard for district policy, not a rule. *[Scope statement]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- The framework is K-12 and role-segmented. Its five checklists address School Leadership, Educators, Business and IT, Policy/Ethical/Legal, and Public Outreach separately (files). *[Scope statement]*
- Scope is classroom, operational, and community-facing, the Public Outreach checklist targets parents and the public with events and take-home guides (Checklist-Public-Outreach). *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **There is no statewide permission scale and no statewide prohibition list.** Permitted and prohibited uses are delegated to districts. Leadership is told to "help educators determine when, where, and how AI tools can be used on assignments" (Checklist-School-Leadership), and educators to "determine when and how AI tools can be used" (Checklist-Educators). *[Recommendation / not a mandate]*
- **The high-school posture is explicitly anti-policing.** "Rather than police AI use, teach students about how AI works and its limitations, including the effects of bias, stereotypes, and inaccuracies".

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **A dedicated Policy/Ethical/Legal checklist anchors compliance.** It asks whether tools comply with FERPA and HIPAA and local privacy policies, how they protect and communicate breaches of student and staff data, and how copyright, licensing, and plagiarism will be handled (Checklist-Policy-Ethical-Legal). *[Recommendation restating Requirement-level law]*
- **Accessibility is a named section** ("AI for Accessibility"), and educators are prompted to modify lessons "to make them more accessible to all students (special needs, EL, etc.)" (Checklist-Educators; Checklist-School-Leadership).
- **Equity of access to tools** is explicit, including attention to "free and paid versions of tools" and whether "all students have equal access to tools both in and out of school" (Checklist-Educators).
- **Academic integrity is handled by assignment redesign and disclosure.** Educators should "rethink assignments and set clear guidelines on what standards/skills are being addressed" and decide "how you will require students to reference" AI-generated research (Checklist-Educators).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** neutral, not a caution. The educators checklist notes only that "the internet has multiple tools to help educators recognize original or AI generated content" (Checklist-Educators). It neither endorses nor warns against detectors, unlike the anti-detector states. *[Instructional guidance]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Curriculum integration is developmental**, following the grade bands, with critique of AI outputs beginning in middle school.
- **Professional development is a leadership checklist item**, prompting districts to assess PD needs for administrative staff, classroom staff, and "IT staff, media specialists, and librarians" (Checklist-School-Leadership).
- **Implementation favors piloting.** "It may be helpful to start with a single school or grade level/band before a districtwide roll-out," followed by feedback and review of whether learning goals were met (Checklist-School-Leadership).
- **Assessment guidance is process-oriented.** Educators should "support students in sharing their writing processes" and "create opportunities for students to problem solve, analyze, and synthesize results" (Checklist-Educators). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Librarians and media specialists are explicitly named** on the recommended AI-policy team (Checklist-School-Leadership), a distinctive inclusion.
sections.offloading:
North Dakota states the offloading concern directly in its grade-band text, which is unusual for so compact a document.

- **The upper-elementary band names offloading as the core risk.** "Technology, powered by AI, can be good at answering questions, but an overreliance on that kind of technology can short-circuit students' development of problem-solving skills". *[Instructional guidance]*
- **The K-2 band protects against anthropomorphizing.** Young students "need to understand that AI is not a real person," because at that developmental stage they "are more likely to attribute human qualities to artificially intelligent technologies like smart speakers and chatbots". *[Instructional guidance]*
- **The middle-school band builds critique as the mitigation.** Students should "ask a generative AI chatbot to answer a question or write an essay and then critique it, looking for factual errors and the like". *[Instructional guidance / example]*
- **The high-school band substitutes understanding for surveillance.** Teaching "how AI works and its limitations" replaces policing.
- **The educators checklist reinforces synthesis over generation.** It asks teachers to "create opportunities for students to problem solve, analyze, and synthesize results" and to help students "critically analyze results" (Checklist-Educators). *[Instructional guidance]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a North Dakota graduate *may* bring. Because the framework is voluntary and district-implemented, exposure varies.

- **Governed by a district policy, not a state scale.** A North Dakota student's AI rules came from a local policy the framework encouraged. *Basis: content, sources.*
- **A developmental trajectory from "AI is not a real person" to critique to understanding-not-policing**, where teachers followed the grade bands. *Basis: content.*
- **A habit of critiquing AI output for factual errors and bias**, if their middle- and high-school teachers used the recommended exercises. *Basis: content.*
- **Some experience sharing their writing process** as an integrity practice (Checklist-Educators). *Basis: Checklist-Educators.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat these as ceilings of possibility, not guarantees. North Dakota's framework is compact and district-adopted, so faculty should expect uneven exposure and no shared leveled vocabulary.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** North Dakota provides no higher-education hook. No college, university, or postsecondary partnership appears in the framework or its checklists, so a faculty member should not expect an institutional pipeline or shared K-16 vocabulary from the state document.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students were taught to *understand rather than be policed* on AI. Incoming North Dakota students may respond better to AI policies framed as literacy and responsibility than to surveillance-first enforcement.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because the state set no permission scale, incoming students are unlikely to share a leveled AI-use vocabulary. Faculty should specify per-assignment AI expectations explicitly.
- **Higher-education implication:** The state emphasized *critiquing AI output for factual errors and bias* from middle school onward. This verification habit is a foundation universities can build on toward source evaluation and citation.
- **Higher-education implication:** North Dakota did not adopt an anti-detector stance (Checklist-Educators). Unlike students from the anti-detector states, North Dakota graduates were not necessarily taught to distrust detection tools, so their expectations on that point are unknown.
sections.response:
- **Onboarding:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic at entry. District-level variance will be high and there is no state scale to anchor assumptions.
- **Assessment design:** State AI permission explicitly per assignment. Preserve tasks that require independent problem-solving, mirroring the state's grades 3-5 offloading caution.
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Favor process-based integrity (sharing writing processes) that continues the state's approach (Checklist-Educators). Do not assume any particular prior stance on detectors.
- **Literacy framing:** Lean into the "understand, don't police" posture North Dakota students may have absorbed, extending their critique habit toward disciplinary source evaluation.
sections.unique:
- **A web-native framework with no single PDF.** North Dakota publishes its guidance as a page plus five downloadable checklists rather than a bound document.
- **Five role-based implementation checklists**, School Leadership, Educators, Business and IT, Policy/Ethical/Legal, and Public Outreach, an operations-and-community delivery model few states match.
- **Compact but pointed grade-band cognitive cautions**, especially the K-2 "AI is not a real person" and grades 3-5 "short-circuit... problem-solving skills" language.
- **An explicit anti-policing high-school posture**.
- **Librarians and media specialists named on the AI-policy team** (Checklist-School-Leadership).
- **A dedicated public-outreach instrument** with concrete events (AI literacy week, Hour of Code nights, take-home parent guides) (Checklist-Public-Outreach).
sections.gaps:
- **Voluntariness limits every claim about students.** The framework mandates nothing and is district-implemented, so actual exposure is unknown and district-dependent. Per-district adoption data is Not found in the provided documents.
- **The framework is web-native and undated.** No publication date appears on the page, and no separate PDF exists; to fix an original in hand, the page should be printed to a date-stamped PDF. *[Unresolved by nature]*
- **No leveled student-use instrument exists.** North Dakota offers grade-band guidance, not a 0-4 or 1-5 permission scale, and adapts no external scale. This is a genuine absence.
- **The grade-band text is terse.** content captures verbatim guidance for each band, but the framework's fuller narrative (definitions, teacher resources, implementation roadmap, accessibility section) was summarized rather than transcribed in full. The analysis rests on the captured verbatim text plus the five checklists. *[Partial capture]*
- **No statute or bill is recorded** for North Dakota in this folder. No enacted or pending AI-in-education requirement can be asserted. *[Unresolved]*

states.summary: Ohio's approach pairs a statutory adoption mandate with a ready-made model policy. HB 96 required DEW to publish a model policy by Dec 31, 2025 (met, published Dec 30, 2025) and requires all districts, community schools, and STEM schools to adopt some AI-use policy by July 1, 2026 (model policy p.2). The model policy is a fill-in-the-blank board policy, not a narrative framework or a student-use scale. Its ten sections run Purpose, Definitions, AI Literacy, Stakeholder Engagement, Data Privacy and Security, Procurement, Ethical Use, Acceptable Use, Academic Integrity, and Implementation and Review, plus notes on non-consensual intimate imagery (model policy pp.2-5).

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human-centered AI is the stated value.** AI implementation "should be human-centered and should empower students, educators, and communities. It is a tool to support learning and teaching, not a substitute for student effort or the role of the educator" (model policy p.4, Ethical Use). *[Recommendation within the model]*
- **Prepare students for an AI-shaped future** while providing "consistent expectations, standards, and approval processes for safe and responsible implementation" (model policy p.2, Purpose).
- **Statewide consistency through required adoption.** The animating objective of HB 96 is that every covered school have an AI-use policy in force by July 1, 2026 (model policy p.2). *[Requirement — adoption only]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- The model policy is written for adoption by a district or school Board of Education (bracketed "[insert name of district/school]," p.2). *[Scope statement]*
- The statutory mandate reaches traditional public districts, community schools (Ch. 3314), and STEM schools (Ch. 3326) (model policy p.2). *[Requirement scope]*
- Scope covers both educational and operational AI use, including generative AI (model policy p.2). *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **There is no statewide leveled permission scale.** The Acceptable Use section delegates the permission line to educators per assignment: responsible uses "will vary depending on the context, including but not limited to grade level, subject, and/or the nature of the classroom activity," and expectations should be specified "in course syllabi and assignment instructions when relevant" (model policy p.4).
- **The model does contain clear prohibitions where adopted.** "Use of tools that have not been approved is not permitted" (p.4), "Using AI tools for bullying, harassment, and any form of intimidation is strictly prohibited" (p.4), and "No assignment shall require the use of a tool that cannot be provided by the [district/school]" (p.4). *[Recommendation, becomes Requirement if a district adopts the model]*
- **Non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) is flagged**, with a reference to Ohio's Braden's Law classifying sexual extortion as a felony (model policy p.5). *[Recommendation + statutory context]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Data privacy is a full section.** AI tools "must adhere to existing data privacy and security policies that include... PII, FERPA, and any other relevant state of Ohio and federal laws," should practice data minimization, and must be vetted for encryption and access control (model policy p.3). *[Recommendation restating Requirement-level law]*
- **Procurement is governed** by existing procurement policy plus AI-specific checks for data privacy, instructional and operational alignment, accessibility, and cost, with third-party vendors required to meet state and federal data-protection, ethical-use, and accessibility standards (model policy pp.3-4).
- **Ethical use is human-centered**, requiring users to "critically analyze AI output, respect safeguards and rules, and be transparent about its use" (model policy p.4).
- **Academic integrity is explicit and process-oriented.** "AI-enabled tools may be used to support student work (such as brainstorming or feedback), but AI-generated work must not replace student work," with proper citation "according to existing policies and expectations... (such as APA or MLA style formats)" (model policy p.4).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** the model policy does not mention AI detectors at all. It neither endorses nor cautions against them, leaving integrity enforcement to existing academic-integrity procedures (model policy p.4). *[Not addressed]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **AI literacy for all is a policy section.** The Board is to "responsibly integrate AI by building AI literacy for all students and educators, including integration of AI into relevant curriculum, professional learning opportunities, and safe and responsible usage" (model policy p.2).
- **Educator use is bound to professional standards.** "Educator use should be in alignment with the Licensure Code of Conduct for Ohio's Educators" (model policy p.4).
- **Assessment design is a named consideration.** Educators "should consider the impact on learning objectives and assessment of student learning when designing related instruction" (model policy p.4). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Implementation is workgroup-driven and iterative.** An ongoing AI workgroup monitors developments and updates the policy, which "should be reviewed often" (model policy p.5).
sections.offloading:
Ohio's model policy addresses offloading through its Ethical Use and Academic Integrity sections rather than a dedicated framework.

- **AI is defined as no substitute for student effort.** "It is a tool to support learning and teaching, not a substitute for student effort or the role of the educator" (model policy p.4).
- **AI-generated work must not replace student work.** Students "are expected to complete assignments and assessments in a manner that reflects their own understanding and effort, critically analyze AI-generated content and not misrepresent it as original work" (model policy p.4).
- **Critical analysis of AI output is a standing user obligation.** Users "should critically analyze AI output, respect safeguards and rules, and be transparent about its use" (model policy p.4).
- **The document does not develop a grade-band cognitive-offloading progression** (unlike North Carolina or North Dakota). Its offloading controls are integrity- and effort-based statements, not developmental scaffolding. *[Absence noted]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits an Ohio graduate *may* bring. The adoption mandate raises the floor, but policy content still varies by district.

- **Governed by a formally adopted AI-use policy.** From July 1, 2026, every Ohio public district and community/STEM school must have one, so an Ohio graduate's schooling was more likely than in voluntary states to carry an explicit, board-adopted AI policy. *Basis: model policy p.2; ORC 3301.24. [Requirement — adoption only.]*
- **Familiar with per-assignment, per-syllabus AI expectations**, if the district adopted the model, since it directs educators to specify AI use in syllabi and assignment instructions (model policy p.4). *Basis: p.4.*
- **A citation-and-effort integrity habit**, where the district adopted the model's academic-integrity language (APA/MLA citation of AI-assisted work; no misrepresentation) (model policy p.4). *Basis: p.4.*
- **An "approved tools only" expectation**, where the model was adopted (model policy p.4). *Basis: p.4.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat the *existence* of a policy as a reasonable assumption for recent Ohio graduates, but treat the *content* as unknown and district-specific. The mandate guarantees a policy, not a common vocabulary or scale.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Ohio names higher education in the primary text. The model policy recommends an AI workgroup with "external representatives such as local businesses and postsecondary institutions" (model policy p.3). An Ohio college or university may be invited onto a district AI workgroup, a direct, if recommendation-level, K-16 hook.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because of the July 1, 2026 mandate, incoming Ohio students (from that point forward) came from schools that were *required to have an AI-use policy*. Faculty can reasonably assume a policy existed, which is a firmer starting point than the voluntary states, while still not assuming any particular content.
- **Higher-education implication:** Where districts adopted the model, students met an integrity norm that *AI may assist but not replace student work* and that AI-assisted work must be cited in APA or MLA (model policy p.4). This maps cleanly onto typical university integrity expectations.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students from model-adopting districts may expect AI permission to be *specified per syllabus and per assignment* and to use only *approved tools* (model policy p.4). A university syllabus that states AI expectations explicitly will feel continuous with that experience.
- **Higher-education implication:** Ohio's model is silent on AI detectors (model policy p.4), so Ohio students were neither trained to expect nor to distrust detection tools. Their expectations on that point are unknown and should not be assumed.
sections.response:
- **Governance and partnership:** Ohio institutions should expect, and can seek, seats on district AI workgroups, which the model policy explicitly invites (model policy p.3). This is a channel to align entry expectations with feeder districts.
- **Assessment design:** State AI permission explicitly per assignment and per syllabus, mirroring the model's Acceptable Use language (model policy p.4). Ohio students from adopting districts will recognize this pattern.
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Build on the model's assist-not-replace and cite-your-AI norms (model policy p.4). These translate directly to university integrity policy.
- **Onboarding:** Assume a policy existed but not a shared scale. Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic; content varied across the many districts that wrote their own policies rather than adopting the model.
- **Do not assume a detector stance.** Because the model is silent on detectors, set your own integrity-tooling expectations explicitly.
sections.unique:
- **A genuine statewide adoption mandate.** ORC 3301.24 (HB 96) requires every district, community school, and STEM school to adopt an AI-use policy by July 1, 2026, one of the dataset's few true statewide requirements.
- **A fill-in-the-blank model policy**, a board-policy template with bracketed placeholders rather than a narrative guidance document (model policy pp.2-5).
- **A primary-confirmed higher-education hook**, postsecondary institutions named as recommended AI-workgroup members (model policy p.3).
- **Explicit non-consensual intimate imagery language**, tied to Ohio's Braden's Law on sexual extortion (model policy p.5), a specific harm few state documents name.
- **Tight integration with existing board policies** (bullying, academic integrity, procurement, special education) rather than a standalone regime (model policy p.5).
- **Educator use bound to the Licensure Code of Conduct for Ohio's Educators** (model policy p.4), linking AI use to professional licensure standards.
sections.gaps:
- **The mandate is adoption, not content.** ORC 3301.24 requires each school to adopt *a* policy; it does not require the DEW model or any specific provision. Districts "may adopt the department's model policy... or write their own," so the actual student experience varies by district. The only Requirement-level claim is the July 1, 2026 adoption deadline. *[Scope of mandate]*
- **The statute is not in the folder as a document.** ORC 3301.24's text is recorded in sources (verified page) and quoted within the model policy (p.2), but the standalone codified section was not separately captured. The quoted subsections are taken from the model policy's reproduction. *[Unresolved]*
- **No leveled student-use instrument exists.** Ohio's model delegates permission to educators per assignment and offers no 0-4 or 1-5 scale and no adaptation of an external scale. This is a genuine absence.
- **The AI Toolkit lead document is orphaned.** The InnovateOhio/aiEDU AI Toolkit (Feb 2024) that data.js currently leads Ohio with returns HTTP 404 at both its landing page and PDF. The DEW model policy should become the lead document; the toolkit's "analyzes 21 guideline sets" claim could not be confirmed. *[Flag for data.js]*
- **An editable.docx of the model policy is linked but was not analyzed**; the PDF is authoritative here.

states.summary: Oklahoma pairs the dataset's clearest Perkins-lineage student-use scale with a substantive enacted statute. The OSDE guidance (v2.0, July 2025) carries the "AI Acceptable Use Rating Scale," a five-level (0-4) instrument running from Level 0 NO AI Use to Level 4 Full AI Use with Human Oversight, each level pairing a use description with explicit disclosure requirements. Its attribution line reads: "Adapted by Dr. Karen Leonard for the Oklahoma State Department of Education (OSDE) from the work of Dr. Leon Furze, Dr. Mike Perkins, Dr. Jasper Roe FHEA, & Dr. Jason Mcvaugh" (guidance p.18). This is a primary-source-confirmed lineage to the peer-reviewed AI Assessment Scale.

A strong disclosure-and-documentation habit, specifically submitting links to AI chats alongside work at Levels 1-4. This is more granular than most states' disclosure norms.
An expectation that AI cannot drive high-stakes decisions about their grades, placement, or discipline (SB 1734, sec.1.E.3).
An expectation of parental disclosure and opt-out rights around student-facing AI (SB 1734, secs.1.F-G).

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human-centered AI.** "AI augments, never replaces, human instruction" (guidance p.3). The statute echoes this: teachers "play an essential and irreplaceable role... artificial intelligence tools, when used in classrooms, should supplement educator-led instruction, not supplant it" (SB 1734, sec.1.A). *[Recommendation / Requirement-level finding of the Legislature]*
- **Clarity, accountability, and consistency with preserved local control.** SB 1734's stated purpose is to set "principles and guardrails," protect student data and integrity, preserve "local control and educator discretion," and support transparency (SB 1734, sec.1.B). *[Requirement]*
- **Workforce and national alignment.** The guidance grounds itself in Governor Stitt's Emerging Technologies Task Force and the 2025 federal executive order on AI education for youth (guidance p.3). *[Recommendation / framing]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- The guidance addresses PK-12 schools statewide (guidance p.3). *[Scope statement]*
- SB 1734 binds all public school districts and defines classroom AI tools, student-facing AI tools, educator-directed use, and human-in-the-loop (SB 1734, sec.1.C). *[Requirement scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **The AI Acceptable Use Rating Scale (guidance p.18) is the permission instrument**, offered as an adaptable classroom framework. Its five levels, verbatim in substance:
 - **Level 0 NO AI Use** — "completed entirely without AI assistance. AI MAY NOT be used at any point... students rely solely on their own knowledge." Disclosure: none required; may require an academic-honesty pledge that AI was not used.
 - **Level 1 AI-Assisted Idea Generation and Structuring** — "No AI content is allowed in the final submission. AI can be used... for brainstorming, creating structures, and generating ideas." Disclosure: statement of how AI was used, plus links to AI chats.
 - **Level 2 AI-Assisted Editing** — "No new content can be created using AI. AI can be used to make improvements to the clarity or quality of student-created work." Disclosure: statement plus AI chat links.
 - **Level 3 AI for Specified Task Completion** — "AI is used to complete certain elements of the task, as specified by the teacher... requires critical engagement." Disclosure: all AI-created content cited, plus AI chat links.
 - **Level 4 Full AI Use with Human Oversight** — "Students may use AI throughout the activity... AI should be a 'co-pilot' to enhance human creativity." Disclosure: cite AI use, plus AI chat links.
- **SB 1734 sets binding use guardrails** whenever AI is used (sec.1.E): educator-directed deployment, human-in-the-loop review of outputs before use, and a prohibition on AI as "the primary basis for student grading, discipline, placement, promotion, retention, or other high-stakes educational decisions." Student-facing tools must be age- and developmentally appropriate. *[Requirement]*
- **Prohibited misuse.** The guidance requires "strict prohibition on using AI to create or distribute deepfakes or non-consensual imagery" and to impersonate others for bullying or harassment (guidance p.19).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Data privacy is both recommended and required.** SB 1734 mandates FERPA compliance, recognized security standards, and that districts "take reasonable steps to minimize the amount of student data shared" (SB 1734, sec.1.E.5). *[Requirement]*
- **Mandatory annual parental disclosure.** Districts must disclose, at least annually, all AI tools in use, their vendors, the categories of student data collected, the extent of sharing, and each tool's educational purpose (SB 1734, sec.1.F). *[Requirement]*
- **A parental opt-out with anti-penalty protection.** Parents may opt a student out of student-facing AI tools "at any time," and opt-out students "shall not be academically penalized or denied access to core instructional content" (SB 1734, sec.1.G). *[Requirement]*
- **Academic integrity is process- and disclosure-based.** The guidance directs updating integrity policies for AI, teaching "proper attribution," and designing assessments that "value process over final product" (guidance p.18).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** cautionary. "While AI detection tools exist, they are not always reliable and may produce false positives, incorrectly flagging human-written work as AI-generated. These tools also frequently miss sophisticated AI-generated content. Instead of relying on detection software, educators should establish baseline writing samples" (guidance p.18). *[Recommendation — a caution against detectors]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Roles and responsibilities are enumerated** in the guidance (boards approve AI policies and acceptable-use guidelines, p.14) and, from 2027-28, required by statute. *[Recommendation + Requirement]*
- **SB 1734 mandates district AI policies before the 2027-2028 school year** with minimum contents: identify responsible roles, address instructional and prohibited uses, data protection and minimization, transparency to families, periodic review, and compliance with the statute's guardrails and OSDE guidance (SB 1734, sec.1.I). *[Requirement]*
- **OSDE is statutorily directed to develop guidance** (SB 1734, sec.1.H); the v2.0 guidance is that instrument. *[Requirement satisfied by guidance]*
- **Assessment guidance favors process** over product, with baseline writing samples and process conversations (guidance p.18). *[Instructional guidance]*
sections.offloading:
Oklahoma builds offloading protection into both the scale's design and its integrity guidance.

- **Level 0 preserves unaided cognition by definition.** It "ensures that students rely solely on their own knowledge, understanding, and skills" (guidance p.18).
- **The scale keeps students as active participants.** Its rationale is to ensure "students remain active participants in the learning process, not passive recipients of machine-generated content" (guidance p.17).
- **Per-level human-oversight requirements** at Levels 3-4 make the student "responsible for providing human oversight and evaluation of all AI-generated content" (guidance p.18).
- **Assessment redesign toward process** is the integrity mitigation: "Develop assessment methods that value process over final product" and "Implement project designs that make inappropriate AI use less beneficial" (guidance p.18).
- **SB 1734 legally protects high-stakes judgment from automation.** AI "shall not be used as the primary basis for student grading, discipline, placement, promotion, retention" (SB 1734, sec.1.E.3), keeping consequential decisions human. *[Requirement]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits an Oklahoma graduate *may* bring. The guidance scale is voluntary, but SB 1734 raises the statutory floor for cohorts under it (2027-28 onward).

- **Familiarity with a five-level, AIAS-derived permission scale.** A student in an adopting school will recognize levels from "NO AI Use" to "Full AI Use with Human Oversight" (guidance p.18). *Basis: guidance p.18, adaptable instrument.*
- **A strong disclosure-and-documentation habit**, specifically submitting links to AI chats alongside work at Levels 1-4 (guidance p.18). This is more granular than most states' disclosure norms. *Basis: guidance p.18.*
- **An expectation that AI cannot drive high-stakes decisions** about their grades, placement, or discipline (SB 1734, sec.1.E.3). *Basis: SB 1734, for cohorts under the statute.*
- **An expectation of parental disclosure and opt-out rights** around student-facing AI (SB 1734, secs.1.F-G). *Basis: SB 1734.*
- **An awareness that AI detectors are unreliable**, if their teachers followed the guidance (guidance p.18). *Basis: guidance p.18.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat the scale as a ceiling of possibility (voluntary) but the SB 1734 guardrails as a firmer floor for recent cohorts. The chat-link disclosure habit is distinctive enough that Oklahoma students may expect to show their AI work in a way students from other states do not.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Oklahoma's scale cites the peer-reviewed AIAS source (Furze, Perkins, Roe, McVaugh; guidance p.18). A university can adopt the same source and expect adopting-school students to recognize the 0-4 vocabulary, from "NO AI Use" to "Full AI Use with Human Oversight," rather than starting from zero.
- **Higher-education implication:** Oklahoma students may arrive habituated to *submitting links to their AI chats* as disclosure (guidance p.18). Faculty who want process transparency can build on that habit, and faculty who ban AI should know these students were taught that disclosure, not concealment, is the norm.
- **Higher-education implication:** Under SB 1734, Oklahoma students (2027-28 onward) were legally protected from AI making high-stakes decisions about them (sec.1.E.3). They may expect the same human accountability in college and may react against automated grading or placement.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students were taught that *AI detectors are unreliable and produce false positives* (guidance p.18). Institutions relying on detection software may face students trained to distrust it.
- **Higher-education implication:** The guidance recommends that districts "develop partnerships with local industry and higher education" (guidance, roles section, p.~15). Oklahoma colleges may be invited into that pipeline.
sections.response:
- **Assessment design:** Adopt an explicit per-assignment AI-permission scale, ideally the same Furze/Perkins/Roe/McVaugh AIAS source (guidance p.18), for direct continuity. Preserve Level 0 NO-AI assessments where core-skill demonstration is the goal.
- **Disclosure practice:** Consider adopting Oklahoma's chat-link disclosure convention (guidance p.18) for AI-permitted assignments, since incoming students may already practice it.
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Favor process- and disclosure-based integrity, mirroring the guidance (guidance p.18). Do not rely on AI detectors, which the students' own K-12 guidance calls unreliable.
- **Human-accountability alignment:** Recognize that Oklahoma students under SB 1734 expect human decision-makers for consequential judgments (sec.1.E.3); keep automated tooling out of high-stakes calls or disclose it clearly.
- **Onboarding and partnership:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic at entry, and where invited, join district AI workgroups and industry/higher-ed partnerships the guidance envisions.
sections.unique:
- **The AI Acceptable Use Rating Scale**, a five-level (0-4) student instrument with primary-printed AIAS attribution to Furze/Perkins/Roe/McVaugh (guidance p.18). The clearest anchor in the dataset for the Perkins-spine instruments library.
- **Per-level disclosure requirements, including submitting links to AI chats** (guidance p.18), a granular transparency mechanism few states specify.
- **An enacted, prescriptive statute (SB 1734)** with binding guardrails: educator-directed use, human-in-the-loop review, a ban on AI as the primary basis for high-stakes decisions, mandatory parental disclosure, and a no-penalty parental opt-out.
- **A statutory policy-adoption mandate** before the 2027-2028 school year with enumerated minimum contents (SB 1734, sec.1.I).
- **A cross-state attribution artifact.** The guidance's "Dr. Jason Mcvaugh" spelling matches Wyoming's, suggesting a shared intermediate source for the adapted scale, useful for the cross-state comparison. *[Cross-state note]*
- **A firm anti-detector position** with a process-based alternative (guidance p.18).
sections.gaps:
- **The scale is voluntary; the statute is binding, but recent.** The AI Acceptable Use Rating Scale is offered for adoption, so actual classroom use is district-dependent. SB 1734's requirements bind districts but take effect July 1, 2026, with policy adoption due before 2027-28, so the fullest effect postdates current graduates. *[Timing]*
- **SB 1734 explicitly does not require AI use.** "Nothing in this section shall be construed to require a public school district... to use artificial intelligence in any school" (sec.1.J). The statute governs AI *if used*; it does not guarantee any student encountered AI. *[Scope of statute]*
- **The scale's graphic was extracted as text, not image.** The level descriptions and disclosure columns are verbatim from guidance p.18, but the printable poster and its CC-licensed template link were not rendered as an image. *[Partial capture]*
- **Some page citations in the roles/higher-ed area are approximate.** The "partnerships with local industry and higher education" line is confirmed in the guidance's roles-and-responsibilities region; exact pagination for that bullet was not pinned. *[Minor]*
- **Oklahoma upgrades from tracker to primary.** Both the scale (with AIAS lineage) and the statute are now confirmed from primary documents in the folder, closing the prior tracker-only status. *[Resolved]*
