sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **A balanced, neither-ban-nor-unrestricted approach** is the stated objective (framework p.3). *[Recommendation / stated philosophy]*
- **Eight Guiding Principles** anchor the framework (framework pp.6-7): use AI to help all students achieve goals; reaffirm existing policies; educate staff and students about AI; explore opportunities and address risks; advance academic integrity; maintain student and teacher agency; audit/monitor/evaluate; and recognize AI is a tool inside and outside the classroom.
- **Deep grounding in Utah statute.** The framework lists Utah State Code provisions on internet policy, student data protection, "Utah FERPA," sensitive instructional materials, and GRAMA, alongside federal law and NIST/CIS standards (framework pp.4-5). *[Recommendation citing Requirement-level law]*
- **HB 218 sets a curriculum objective by law:** AI literacy in the grade 7-8 digital skills course (HB 218, sec.53E-4-208). *[Requirement]*

### Intended audiences and scope
- The framework applies to "all students, teachers, staff, administrators, and third parties who develop, implement, or interact with AI technologies," across instruction, administration, and operations, "where permitted by local policy" (framework p.4). *[Scope statement]*
- HB 218's scope is the grade 7 or 8 digital skills course statewide (HB 218, sec.53E-4-208). *[Requirement scope]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **There is no statewide leveled permission scale.** Utah uses a Responsible-Use / Prohibited-Use structure and delegates specifics to teachers per activity: "Teachers will clarify if, when, and how AI tools will be used, with input from students and families" (framework p.8). *[Recommendation / not a scale]*
- **Responsible uses** include aiding creativity, collaboration, translation, content creation, tutoring, assessment design, differentiation, and operations, with human review throughout (framework pp.8-10). *[Recommendation / examples]*
- **Prohibited uses are explicit** (framework pp.11-12): AI to "manipulate media to impersonate others for bullying, harassment, or any form of intimidation"; over-reliance; plagiarism and cheating; diminishing student and teacher agency; and privacy violations. *[Recommendation, phrased as prohibitions]*
- **Student access equity is required within the framework's logic:** "If an assignment permits the use of AI tools, the tools will be made available to all students" (framework p.10).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Privacy and security are heavily developed**, with a dedicated Special Consideration section, an explicit no-PII rule ("We will not share personally identifiable information with consumer-based AI systems," framework p.6), and prohibition on entering confidential/PII data (framework p.~432). *[Recommendation restating Requirement-level law]*
- **Accessibility and the digital divide** are named in Principle 1, "bridging the digital divide" and evaluating tools "for biases and ethical concerns" (framework p.6).
- **Academic integrity is a guiding principle** grounded in "honesty, trust, fairness, respect, and responsibility," with proper crediting of sources and tools (framework p.7). Documentation guidance directs citing AI in the school's preferred format (APA, MLA) (framework p.8).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** cautionary-tolerant. "Use caution when using AI plagiarism checkers, because they can sometimes produce false positives. Consider using plagiarism checkers as one of several tools in a comprehensive approach" (framework p.8). Utah permits detectors as one input, with a false-positive warning, rather than discouraging them outright.
- **A safety-monitoring use is described.** AI "could have the ability to monitor written student communications on LEA provided accounts" to flag distress and alert personnel (framework p.9). *[Recommendation / example]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **HB 218 mandates AI literacy in a required course.** The grade 7-8 digital skills course must incorporate "artificial intelligence literacy" and its capabilities/limitations, cybersecurity, and safe online practices (HB 218, sec.53E-4-208). *[Requirement]*
- **An advisory tech council may be established** by the state superintendent to recommend digital-skills standards and resources (HB 218, sec.3; note the statute uses "may," making the council discretionary). *[Requirement/discretionary]*
- **Assessment stays human-led.** "Teachers will ultimately be responsible for evaluation, feedback, and grading... AI will not be solely responsible for grading" (framework p.8).
- **Professional development** is supported through AI-recommended strategies and simulation-based training (framework p.9).
- **Library Media Standards are among the informing policies** (framework p.5).
sections.offloading:
Utah's framework treats over-reliance as a named prohibited use and speaks directly to cognitive offloading.

- **Over-reliance is listed under Prohibited Use.** "Dependence on AI tools can decrease human discretion and oversight. Important nuances and context can be overlooked and accepted," so teachers must clarify use and review outputs (framework p.11). *[Recommendation, as prohibition]*
- **The framework names cognitive offloading explicitly.** "Teachers and students need to understand how agentic AI, or any AI system, that offloads decision making and/or cognitive effort in the classroom, operate and how to use them appropriately with a human in the loop" (framework p.12).
- **Student and teacher agency is a guiding principle.** Staff and students serve as "critical consumers" and remain accountable for decisions (framework p.7); core teaching practices "will remain the teacher's responsibility" and students "remain active participants" (framework pp.11-12).
- **Plagiarism mitigation is assignment redesign.** Teachers "restructure assignments to reduce opportunities for plagiarism by requiring personal context, original arguments, or original data collection" (framework p.11).
- **Human review of AI output is required throughout** the Responsible-Use and Prohibited-Use sections (framework pp.8-12).
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a Utah graduate *may* bring. The framework is voluntary, but HB 218 raises the statutory floor for cohorts under it.

- **A mandated AI-literacy exposure in grade 7 or 8**, for students under HB 218, covering AI capabilities, limitations, and ethical/societal implications (HB 218, sec.53E-4-208). *Basis: HB 218. [Requirement, for cohorts under the statute.]*
- **A Responsible-Use / Prohibited-Use framing rather than a leveled scale**, where the district followed the framework (framework pp.8-12). *Basis: framework.*
- **A strong human-in-the-loop and anti-over-reliance orientation** (framework pp.11-12). *Basis: framework.*
- **A citation habit** using the school's preferred format for substantial AI-generated text (framework p.8). *Basis: framework.*
- **Uncertain detector expectations.** Utah permits detectors with a false-positive caution (framework p.8), so students' experience is district-dependent and not uniformly skeptical. *Basis: framework.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat the framework habits as ceilings of possibility (voluntary) but the grade 7-8 AI-literacy exposure as a firmer floor for recent cohorts under HB 218. Utah students may lack a leveled AI-use vocabulary but share a balanced, agency-centered framing.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Utah is one of the few states to *require* AI literacy in a specific course by law (HB 218). Incoming Utah students (under the statute) will have had at least one mandated exposure to AI capabilities, limitations, and ethical implications in grade 7 or 8. A university can build on that shared floor rather than assume none.
- **Higher-education implication:** Utah students may arrive framing AI use through *human agency and over-reliance avoidance* rather than a permission scale (framework pp.7, 11-12). Faculty policies that emphasize keeping the human in the loop and reviewing AI output will feel continuous.
- **Higher-education implication:** Utah's framework contains *no explicit higher-education hook*, and its enacted statutes do not reach public universities. This is the opposite of Tennessee. Utah institutions are not directed by the state on AI governance and should not expect a state framework to bind them.
- **Higher-education implication:** Utah's detector stance is *permissive-with-caveats* (framework p.8), so Utah students were not uniformly taught to distrust detection tools. Institutions should not assume a fixed prior view.
- **Higher-education implication:** Utah grounds its framework in specific state privacy statutes ("Utah FERPA," student-data-privacy code; framework pp.4-5), so Utah students may arrive with clear expectations about not entering PII into AI tools.
sections.response:
- **Onboarding:** Recognize that Utah students under HB 218 had a mandated grade 7-8 AI-literacy unit; use a short diagnostic to place them, but expect a real baseline in AI capabilities and limitations.
- **Assessment design:** State AI permission explicitly per assignment. Preserve assignments that require personal context and original work, mirroring the framework's plagiarism-mitigation approach (framework p.11).
- **Agency framing:** Build on the human-in-the-loop and anti-over-reliance orientation Utah students were taught (framework pp.11-12), extending it to disciplinary practice.
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Favor citation- and process-based integrity (framework pp.7-8). Because Utah's detector stance is permissive-with-caveats, set your own detector policy explicitly.
- **Institutional governance:** Since the state does not direct higher-education AI governance, Utah institutions should develop their own policies rather than await a state framework.
sections.unique:
- **An enacted AI-literacy curriculum requirement.** HB 218 embeds AI literacy into the required grade 7-8 digital skills course by law (sec.53E-4-208), a firmer step than voluntary guidance.
- **A Responsible-Use / Prohibited-Use structure under eight "We" principles**, rather than a leveled student-use scale (framework pp.6-12).
- **Unusually deep grounding in Utah statute**, including "Utah FERPA" and state student-data-privacy code, plus NIST/CIS cybersecurity standards (framework pp.4-5).
- **Explicit cognitive-offloading language** naming agentic AI and the offloading of "decision making and/or cognitive effort" (framework p.12).
- **A described AI safety-monitoring use** flagging student distress to school personnel (framework p.9).
- **A guiding principle for AI use outside the classroom** (personal devices), with USBE committing to support families (framework p.7).
sections.gaps:
- **Two sources flags are resolved.** The canonical USBE framework file extracted cleanly as the **March 2026 edition** (contrary to the prior "text not extractable" and edition-ambiguity notes), and SB 322 is confirmed **failed March 6, 2026**, not pending. Both should be corrected in data.js/VERIFICATION. *[Resolved / flag for data.js]*

- **The framework is voluntary.** It applies "where permitted by local policy" (framework p.4), so actual classroom practice is district-dependent. HB 218's curriculum requirement is the binding element. *[Scope]*

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Developmental appropriateness is the organizing principle** (guidance pp.8-9).
- **The Four Principles Framework** categorizes AI use (guidance pp.10-19): (1) streamline administrative and planning work, (2) support personalized learning, (3) develop students' AI literacy, and (4) use AI-infused tools for cognitively demanding tasks.
- **Balance over prohibition or free rein.** The Responsible AI Usage part opens with "Risk of Doing Nothing" (guidance p.22), rejecting inaction while insisting on careful use.
- **Learning objectives drive AI decisions.** Before assigning an AI task, teachers should ask what skills they want developed and whether AI "will perform the skill for them" (guidance p.24).

### Intended audiences and scope
- The guidance serves educators, leaders, and staff, with Quick Start Guides by role (e.g., Elementary Educators PreK-5) (guidance p.44, TOC). *[Scope statement]*
- Scope is PreK through grade 9+ (labeled AI Fluency), covering instruction, operations, and leadership (guidance pp.8-9, Part 4). *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **There is no leveled permission scale; permission is set by developmental band and by learning objective.** The developmental bands function as age-gated restrictions:
 - **PreK-2:** "Students in grades PreK-2 should not use AI chatbots." Teachers may use AI-incorporating tools (guidance p.8). *[Recommendation, as restriction]*
 - **Grades 3-5 (AI Awareness):** "Students should not use open-ended AI chatbots," only curriculum-embedded, constrained AI; teachers may demonstrate AI (guidance p.8). *[Recommendation, as restriction]*
 - **Grades 6-8 (AI Literacy):** age-appropriate, education-specific chatbots "under a teacher's direction," fully scaffolded, not generic chatbots (guidance p.9).
 - **Grades 9+ (AI Fluency):** AI as "a cognitive assistant tool" for research, learning, and co-creation, with academic-integrity systems in place (guidance p.9).
- **Prohibited uses sit under Part 3, Responsible AI Usage** (guidance p.22 onward), covering academic honesty, cognitive offloading, data privacy, and mental-health risks.
- **Teachers are empowered to prohibit AI** for specific tasks when it would harm learning (guidance p.24).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Data privacy is strict.** Schools must conform to FERPA and COPPA, and Vermont warns that "it is not enough to remove student-identifiable information" because student intellectual property still trains the system; SU/SDs should have vendor privacy agreements (guidance pp.25-26). *[Recommendation restating Requirement-level law + stronger]*
- **A dedicated Ethics, Bias and Fairness, and Equity and access set of sections** anchors fairness (guidance pp.28-30).
- **Academic honesty is "the single most cited concern"** (guidance p.22). Vermont recommends reviewing honesty policies for AI, modeling transparency, and, compassionately, "treating the academic honesty issue as a cry for help from students" (guidance pp.~864, 898).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** clearly against. "Do not rely on AI auto-detection tools. These tools are not reliable enough to be used in academic honesty disputes, sometimes show false positives" (guidance p.~903). *[Recommendation — a caution against detectors]*
- **Mental-health risks get their own section** (guidance p.26), including AI-companion toys with which "kids can form intense relationships" (guidance p.~1012), connecting to Act 156.

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **A Tool Vetting Framework** categorizes AI tools (general-purpose vs. education-specific chatbots) and guides selection (guidance pp.34-36). *[Recommendation / instrument]*
- **Role-based Quick Start Guides** support implementation (guidance p.44 onward).
- **A Needs Assessment** structures leadership implementation across policy, staff readiness, student learning, infrastructure, and community engagement (guidance pp.31-33).
- **Assessment adjustment is expected at grades 9+**, where "teachers need time to adjust assessments to respond to student usage of AI" (guidance p.9).
- **Principle #4 targets cognitively demanding tasks**, "most appropriate for grades 9-12, where" students can demonstrate genuine understanding (guidance p.~752).
sections.offloading:
This is Vermont's signature strength; it engages offloading more directly and by name than any other state in the dataset.

- **A dedicated Cognitive Offloading section** frames the central question: "The central challenge for educators is to determine when AI serves as a valuable learning tool and when it becomes a crutch that hinders skill development" (guidance p.24). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **It cites research directly**, Ethan Mollick's "Against Brain Damage," and uses the calculator/multiplication analogy to explain when offloading is harmful (guidance p.24). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **It empowers refusal.** "Teachers should feel empowered to say when AI usage is inappropriate" (guidance p.24).
- **It gives a two-question test** before assigning AI tasks: what skill should students develop, and "will AI's role in this task help them practice that skill, or will it perform the skill for them?" (guidance p.24). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **The developmental bands are themselves offloading controls.** Each band warns that premature or unstructured AI use "may bypass the essential struggle needed to develop" core competencies (guidance p.8, grades 3-5) and "may serve as a crutch, bypassing the struggle necessary for the learning process" (guidance p.9, grades 6-8). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **It names productive struggle repeatedly** (guidance pp.8-9, 24) and warns against "learners... not always the best judges of how well they are learning" (guidance p.24). *[Instructional guidance]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a Vermont graduate *may* bring. Because the guidance is voluntary and recent (Jan 2026), exposure varies and is only now taking hold.

- **A developmental trajectory from no-chatbot (PreK-5) to scaffolded use (6-8) to managed "thinking partner" fluency (9+)**, where the school followed the guidance (guidance pp.8-9). *Basis: guidance pp.8-9.*
- **An explicit understanding of cognitive offloading** and when AI is a crutch versus a tool, if teachers used the guidance's framing (guidance p.24). *Basis: guidance p.24.*
- **A metacognitive, intellectual-ownership orientation** at the upper grades, managing AI "while maintaining intellectual ownership" (guidance p.9). *Basis: guidance p.9.*
- **An expectation that AI detectors are unreliable and not used in disputes** (guidance p.~903). *Basis: guidance p.~903.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat these as ceilings of possibility. Because the guidance is new and voluntary, current graduates likely predate its full effect; its influence will grow for future cohorts. Where it took hold, Vermont students may arrive with an unusually articulate sense of when AI helps versus harms learning.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Vermont students may arrive already fluent in the *cognitive-offloading* vocabulary that motivates university AI policy, when AI is a "crutch" versus a "thinking partner" (guidance pp.9, 24). This is rare and valuable; faculty can build on a shared conceptual frame rather than introduce it.
- **Higher-education implication:** Vermont's developmental gating means younger cohorts had *deliberately limited* early AI exposure (no chatbots PreK-5). Faculty should not assume long, unstructured AI histories; structured fluency is concentrated at grades 9+.
- **Higher-education implication:** Vermont students were taught that *AI detectors are unreliable and should not decide honesty disputes* (guidance p.~903). Institutions relying on detection software may face students explicitly trained to distrust it.
- **Higher-education implication:** The Grades 9+ band is workforce- and metacognition-oriented, preparing students "for a workforce where AI usage will be expected" while "maintaining intellectual ownership" (guidance p.9). Faculty can extend that ownership framing into disciplinary practice.
- **Higher-education implication:** Vermont's framework has *no explicit higher-education hook* and its enacted statute (Act 156) is mental-health consumer protection, not education code. Vermont institutions are not directed by the state on AI and should develop their own policies.
sections.response:
- **Cognitive-offloading continuity:** Adopt Vermont's two-question test, does AI help students practice the skill or perform it for them (guidance p.24), as a shared design principle, since incoming Vermont students may already know it.
- **Assessment design:** State AI permission explicitly per assignment, reserving AI-free work where core skills are the objective, mirroring the productive-struggle logic of the developmental bands (guidance pp.8-9).
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Do not rely on AI detectors, consistent with what Vermont students were taught (guidance p.~903); favor process- and transparency-based integrity, and treat suspected misuse as a teachable/support moment (guidance p.898).
- **Onboarding:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic. The guidance is new and voluntary, so exposure varies and younger-grade experience was deliberately limited.
- **Institutional governance:** Because the state does not direct higher-education AI use, Vermont institutions should build their own policies, drawing on the AOE framework's structure.
sections.unique:
- **A dedicated Cognitive Offloading section** citing Ethan Mollick's "Against Brain Damage" and the calculator analogy (guidance p.24), the dataset's most direct treatment of the project's central concern.
- **Strict, reasoned developmental gating**, PreK-2 and grades 3-5 barred from open chatbots, with explicit developmental rationale about anthropomorphizing and bypassing "essential struggle" (guidance p.8).
- **A Four Principles Framework**, including Principle #4 on using AI for "cognitively demanding tasks" (guidance pp.10-19).
- **A clear anti-detector stance** with a compassionate "cry for help" framing of honesty violations (guidance pp.~898, 903).
- **A Tool Vetting Framework and role-based Quick Start Guides** (guidance pp.34-36, 44).
- **A strong data-privacy position** that goes beyond de-identification to student intellectual-property protection in AI training (guidance p.26).
- **A companion mental-health statute (Act 156)** adding 18 V.S.A. § 7115 prohibited AI uses, connecting to the guidance's mental-health-risk section.
sections.gaps:
- **Vermont upgrades from tracker to primary.** The guidance URL was wrong by one token in prior passes (`edu-AOE-...` not `edu-ai-...`); the correct file is confirmed 50 pages, Issue Date January 23, 2026. The grade-band gating claim is confirmed. *[Resolved]*
- **Voluntariness and recency limit every claim about students.** The guidance mandates nothing and is dated January 2026, so current graduates largely predate its full effect; exposure is school-dependent. Per-school adoption data is Not found in the provided documents.
- **No leveled student-use instrument exists.** Vermont uses developmental bands plus a Four Principles Framework, not a 0-4 or 1-5 permission scale, and adapts no external scale. This is a deliberate design choice.
- **Act 156 is not education code.** It is mental-health consumer protection, relevant to student mental-health tools but not a K-12 classroom mandate. *[Scope clarification]*
- **No explicit higher-education hook** appears in the guidance; the "Sentio University" reference in the text is an illustrative example, not a real institutional partnership. Vermont's postsecondary connection is inferential (workforce framing at grades 9+). *[Absence]*
- **The 50-page guidance was read by located region.** Verbatim passages (developmental bands, cognitive offloading, detector stance) are anchored, but the full document (Four Principles detail, Tool Vetting, Quick Start Guides) was summarized rather than transcribed in full. *[Partial capture]*

documents.title: Guidelines for AI Integration throughout Education in the Commonwealth of Virginia
documents.issuer: Office of the Governor / Secretary of Education, under Executive Order 30 (signed Jan 18, 2024)

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Education is a human endeavor AI cannot replace.** "AI should never fully replace teachers, who nurture students' critical thinking, values and character development" (guidance p.~15). *[Recommendation / stated philosophy]*
- **Six Guiding Principles** anchor the document (guidance pp.~38-65), led by "Do no harm" and "Prioritize integrity."
- **Workforce and economic framing.** AI literacy is tied to preparing "a workforce that can leverage AI to its full potential" (guidance p.~12).
- **A living, advisory-refined approach.** Roles will "continue to be refined by the Advisory Group," and principle six commits to constant revisiting ("not a one-and-done") (guidance pp.~65, 113).

### Intended audiences and scope
- Scope is all of Virginia education, K-12 and higher education. Roles are assigned to VDOE and SCHEV/VCCS, K-12 division boards, and "every public college and university" (guidance pp.~117-120). *[Scope statement]*
- Audiences include state agencies, governing boards, higher-education programs and faculty, and school/classroom leaders (guidance pp.~117-121). *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **There is no leveled permission scale and no statewide prohibition list.** Permission is governed by principle and by local condition-setting. The "Set The Right Conditions" strategy directs schools to "clearly outline the school or system's policies and protocols around data privacy, honor code, student code of conduct, acceptable use, and ethical considerations... including those related to plagiarism" (guidance p.~4, Strategies).
- **The binding constraint is the "Do no harm" principle**, requiring compliance with EO30 and state/federal policy, privacy safeguards, and bias avoidance, and allowing AI "only when its use has the potential to contribute positive good/improvement to the status quo" (guidance p.~38).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **"Do no harm" centers privacy, security, and anti-bias.** It requires "safeguarding of the privacy, security, and confidentiality of personally identifiable information" and ensuring algorithms are "not based on inherent biases that lead to discriminatory outcomes" (guidance p.~38).
- **Equity of access** is built into "Harness AI to empower student success," which insists on "ensuring access for all learners" (guidance p.~54).
- **Academic integrity is a standalone principle.** "Prioritize integrity" says education must "teach about morality, ethics, honor, cheating, and how artificial intelligence can lead to perverse and destructive outcomes" (guidance p.~44).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** the guidance does not address AI detectors. Its integrity approach is principle- and condition-based (honor code, acceptable use, plagiarism protocols), not detection-based (guidance pp.~44, 4). *[Not addressed]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Strategies for Success are implementation-oriented**: Encourage Exploration (hands-on teacher experience), Provide Professional Development (workshops, micro-credentials, micro-badges), Spotlight Success, Host Stakeholder Conversations, and Set The Right Conditions (guidance pp.~72-4).
- **VCCS is tasked with credential design.** State agencies "in partnership with the Virginia Community College System shall work in collaboration to design micro-badging and micro-credential training opportunities for the field" (guidance p.~152). *[Recommendation, a higher-ed role]*
- **It borrows another state's classroom resource.** The guidance cites Oregon's "Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in K-12 Classrooms" resource "for K-12 and Higher Education" (guidance p.~185). *[Cross-state note]*
- **Roles and Responsibilities assign implementation across the system**, from state agencies to classroom leaders and higher-education faculty (guidance pp.~117-121).
sections.offloading:
Virginia addresses over-reliance through its human-agency principles rather than a dedicated offloading section.

- **"Augment, not replace humans" is the core anti-offloading principle.** AI "should not overpower/over-ride the critical thinking, judgement, and morality of the learner" and "will never replace teachers who provide wisdom, context, feedback, empathy" (guidance p.~48).
- **Integrity instruction targets misuse.** Teaching "morality, ethics, honor, cheating" is part of AI integration (guidance p.~44).
- **Human judgment is reserved.** A faculty/staff role is to keep "human judgement" central (guidance p.~181).
- **The document does not develop a dedicated cognitive-offloading doctrine or grade-band gating** (unlike Vermont, North Carolina, or North Dakota). Its offloading protection is the augment-not-replace principle plus condition-setting. *[Absence noted]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a Virginia graduate *may* bring. Because the guidance is voluntary and division-implemented, exposure varies.

- **Governed by locally set conditions, not a state scale.** A Virginia student's AI rules came from division-level honor codes, acceptable-use, and plagiarism protocols the guidance directed (guidance p.~4). *Basis: guidance p.~4.*
- **An augment-not-replace framing of AI**, if teachers followed the principles (guidance p.~48). *Basis: guidance p.~48.*
- **An integrity orientation tied to ethics and honor**, where the "Prioritize integrity" principle shaped instruction (guidance p.~44). *Basis: guidance p.~44.*
- **A workforce-and-economy framing** of why AI literacy matters (guidance p.~12). *Basis: guidance p.~12.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat these as ceilings of possibility, not guarantees. Virginia set no state scale, so faculty should expect division-level variance and no shared leveled vocabulary, but a shared "augment not replace" and integrity framing where the guidance took hold.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Virginia is the clearest K-16 case in the dataset. Higher education is named as a governance partner from the first page (colleges and universities "lead the nation," guidance p.~20), the "Work in partnership" principle names "Virginia colleges and universities" as "key partners and guides" (guidance p.~60), and Roles and Responsibilities assign duties to SCHEV, VCCS, and "the boards of visitors/presidents/leadership teams at every public college and university" (guidance pp.~117-120). A Virginia institution is an assigned actor, not a bystander.
- **Higher-education implication:** VCCS is specifically tasked with designing micro-badging and micro-credential AI training (guidance p.~152). Virginia community colleges have a defined AI-workforce-credentialing role that four-year institutions can connect to.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because the guidance treats K-12 and higher education as one system, incoming Virginia students and their receiving institutions were addressed by the *same* document. Faculty can align entry expectations with a framework their own institution was named in.
- **Higher-education implication:** Virginia students may arrive with an *augment-not-replace* and *integrity-first* framing (guidance pp.~44, 48) but *no leveled AI-use vocabulary*, since the state set none. Faculty should teach a per-assignment permission structure explicitly.
- **Higher-education implication:** Two 2026 statutes (HB 1186 pilot, SB 394 guidance) build on this and take effect July 1, 2026, so Virginia's baseline is strengthening; entry assumptions should be revisited as those take effect.
sections.response:
- **Governance and partnership:** Virginia institutions should act on their named roles, engaging SCHEV/VCCS coordination and the "Work in partnership" mandate (guidance pp.~60, 117-120), and connect to VCCS micro-credential design (guidance p.~152).
- **Onboarding:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic at entry; division variance is high and no state scale anchors expectations.
- **Assessment design:** State AI permission explicitly per assignment. Build on the augment-not-replace and integrity framing Virginia students may share (guidance pp.~44, 48).
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Because the guidance is silent on AI detectors, set your own detector policy explicitly; favor honor-code and condition-based integrity, matching "Set The Right Conditions" (guidance p.~4).
- **Track the statutes:** Monitor HB 1186 and SB 394, which will require VDOE guidance and aligned school-board policies and may firm up the state baseline.

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human-centered AI is the organizing commitment.** The environment "always starts with human inputs and inquiry, and always concludes with human reflection and edits" (guidance p.14). *[Recommendation / stated philosophy]*
- **AI literacy, ethics, and equity** are the stated leadership priorities, developing students' AI literacy, ensuring "ethical, equitable, and safe use," and providing teacher PD (guidance p.14).
- **Student agency in AI use.** "Empower students in how and to what degree AI is utilized in their learning journey" (guidance p.14).
- **Workforce and college-career-life preparation** frames the purpose (guidance pp.14, ~986).

### Intended audiences and scope
- The guidance addresses education leaders, teachers, students, and administrators (guidance pp.14, Sections). *[Scope statement]*
- Scope is K-12 public schools, with companion instruments for students (the scale) and educators (the matrix). *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **The 5 Step Scaffolding Scale for Students is the permission instrument** (guidance p.20; standalone companion), offered as an adaptable classroom tool. Its five levels, verbatim:
 - **Level 1 No AI Assistance** — "No AI tools are used at any point. Students rely solely on their knowledge and skills."
 - **Level 2 AI-Assisted Brainstorming** — "AI tools can help generate ideas. Final content must be created by the student without direct AI input. AI assistance must be cited."
 - **Level 3 AI-Supported Drafting** — "AI can help with drafting initial versions. The final version must be significantly revised by the student. Clear distinction between AI input and student's contributions."
 - **Level 4 AI-Collaborative Creation** — "AI-generated content can be included. Student must critically evaluate and edit AI contributions. AI usage must be transparent and cited."
 - **Level 5 AI as Co-Creator** — "Extensive use of AI in content creation. Student provides a rationale for AI use and ensures original thought. Work adheres to academic integrity with proper citations."
- **The educator matrix applies the same five levels across assignment types** (reading discussion, longform drafting, reflective/creative writing, podcasts/video, research, math word problems), giving worked examples per level (educator matrix).
- **A co-created decision rubric is encouraged.** Educators should "co-create and share an AI decision-making rubric with students" (guidance p.14).

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Ethics, equity, and safety** are a leadership priority, protecting data privacy and security and "addressing potential biases and harms" (guidance p.14).
- **Accessibility and special education** are named: "Empower students receiving special education services to use AI to personalize and increase their access to learning" (guidance p.14).
- **Academic integrity is built into every scale level** through citation and transparency requirements (student scale, Levels 2-5).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** among the strongest cautions in the dataset. OSPI "highly recommended that educators do not utilize AI detection software," citing Vanderbilt and Stanford research on inaccuracy and bias "against non-native English speakers and writers," and recommends knowing "students' voice and writing style through samples of work gathered over time" plus a conversation if misuse is suspected (guidance p.40). A guiding principle also warns against "sole reliance on... 'AI detection' tools" (guidance p.14). *[Recommendation — a strong caution against detectors]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Professional development** for integrating AI into "pedagogy, curriculum, and assessment" is a leadership priority (guidance p.14).
- **Assessment integrates the scale.** The educator matrix is explicitly assignment-and-assessment oriented, and detector conversations "can form the basis" for integrity discussions when "an AI Matrix has been implemented and clearly communicated" (guidance p.40). *[Instrument / recommendation]*
- **CTE is highlighted** as "crucial in preparing students for the AI workforce" (guidance p.~986).
- **Human-centered design and policy-building** sections guide implementation (guidance Sections 1).
sections.offloading:
Washington's offloading protection is embedded in its human-centered spine and the scale's design.

- **The human-in-the-loop principle bookends every AI interaction.** Learning "always starts with human inputs and inquiry, and always concludes with human reflection and edits" (guidance p.14).
- **Level 1 preserves unaided cognition** by definition: "Students rely solely on their knowledge and skills" (student scale).
- **Escalating student responsibility across levels.** By Level 5, the student "provides a rationale for AI use and ensures original thought" (student scale).
- **Critical evaluation is required at higher levels.** At Level 4, the "student must critically evaluate and edit AI contributions" (student scale).
- **Aligning AI with learning principles.** OSPI directs "supporting student agency, fostering collaboration, enhancing feedback, and promoting critical thinking" (guidance p.14).
- Washington does not include a standalone cognitive-offloading section by that name (unlike Vermont), but the scale's leveled design is itself an offloading-management instrument. *[Structural note]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a Washington graduate *may* bring. Because the guidance is voluntary and district-implemented, exposure varies.

- **Familiarity with a five-level per-assignment AI scale**, from "No AI Assistance" to "AI as Co-Creator," where the district adopted it (guidance p.20; student scale). *Basis: guidance p.20, adaptable instrument.*
- **A per-level citation-and-transparency habit** (student scale, Levels 2-5). *Basis: student scale.*
- **A human-centered framing** that AI use begins and ends with human inquiry and reflection (guidance p.14). *Basis: guidance p.14.*
- **An expectation that AI detectors are unreliable and biased**, and that suspected misuse is handled by conversation, not software (guidance p.40). *Basis: guidance p.40.*
- **College-career-life readiness framing** of AI literacy (guidance p.14). *Basis: guidance p.14.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat these as ceilings of possibility, not guarantees. Where the scale was adopted, Washington students may arrive with genuinely transferable per-assignment vocabulary, but adoption is voluntary and district-dependent.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Washington's five-level scale is a directly adoptable per-assignment instrument, and its educator matrix supplies ready exemplars. A university can adopt the same level structure and expect adopting-district students to recognize "No AI Assistance" through "AI as Co-Creator." Note that Puerto Rico translated this exact scale, so it has cross-jurisdiction reach.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students were taught that *AI detectors are unreliable and biased against non-native English writers*, with research citations (guidance p.40). Institutions relying on detection software may face students explicitly and confidently trained to distrust it, a research-backed position.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students from adopting districts may expect AI permission to be *specified per assignment*, *cited*, and *transparent*, and may expect suspected misuse to be handled through a conversation rather than a detector verdict (guidance p.40). A silent or blanket syllabus will read as less clear than what they experienced.
- **Higher-education implication:** Washington's higher-education connection is college-career-life readiness, not institutional governance. Unlike Tennessee or Virginia, the guidance assigns no roles to universities, so faculty should not assume a state-level K-16 pipeline, only a college-readiness framing.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students receiving special-education services may arrive having been empowered to use AI for access and personalization (guidance p.14); institutions should align disability-services practice accordingly.
sections.response:
- **Assessment design:** Adopt an explicit per-assignment AI-permission scale; Washington's five-level scale and educator matrix are ready to lift and give continuity for adopting-district students (guidance p.20; educator matrix). Preserve Level 1 No-AI assessments where core skills are the objective.
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Do not rely on AI detectors, consistent with what Washington students were taught and the research OSPI cites (guidance p.40). Favor process-based integrity and voice-familiarity, and use conversations to resolve suspected misuse.
- **Onboarding:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic at entry; the scale's five levels are a ready rubric for placement.
- **Human-centered framing:** Build on the "starts with human inquiry, ends with human reflection" principle (guidance p.14), which maps cleanly onto university expectations of original thought.
- **Special education:** Continue the access-and-personalization framing Washington students may have experienced (guidance p.14).
sections.unique:
- **A five-level student AI-permission scale plus a companion educator matrix** (student scale; educator matrix), one of the most complete and liftable instrument pairs in the dataset.
- **Cross-jurisdiction reach.** Puerto Rico's five-level scale is a verbatim Spanish translation of Washington's, corroborating the structure and extending its influence beyond the state (see Puerto Rico analysis).
- **A strong, research-cited anti-detector position** naming Vanderbilt and Stanford studies and English-language-learner bias (guidance p.40).
- **A crisp human-centered principle** that bookends AI use with human inquiry and reflection (guidance p.14).
- **Explicit special-education empowerment** to use AI for access (guidance p.14).
- **An educator matrix organized by real assignment types** with worked, discipline-specific examples at each of the five levels (educator matrix).
sections.gaps:
- **This reverses a prior project error.** The July 28 "correction" claiming Washington used a four-step teacher-support matrix (Modeling/Guided/Collaborative/Independent Practice) was **wrong**. OSPI's instrument is the five-level student AI-permission scale, confirmed verbatim in the main guidance (p.20) and the standalone companion. The word "Independent" appears only inside a table cell ("Independently conduct..."), never as a level. VERIFICATION and data.js should restore Washington to the scaffolded-scale pattern group. *[Resolved / flag for VERIFICATION]*
- **Voluntariness limits every claim about students.** The guidance mandates nothing and is district-implemented, so actual exposure is unknown and district-dependent. Per-district adoption data is Not found in the provided documents.
- **The scale is OSPI-original, not Perkins-attributed.** Washington's five-level scale carries no AIAS attribution; it is structurally a cousin of the Perkins-lineage scales but is its own instrument. Puerto Rico's translation traces to Washington, not directly to Perkins. *[Lineage note]*
- **ESHB 2225 is not education code.** It regulates AI companion chatbots under Title 19 RCW (consumer protection), with minor-safety and suicidal-ideation-protocol provisions. The current data.js framing of it as school legislation ("reporting requirements related to harmful behaviors") mis-scopes it and should be re-scoped or dropped. *[Flag for data.js]*
- **The non-accessible full guidance variant exceeds fetch limits**; the accessible-format v3.0 (2014-line extract) was used, and the scale and detector passages are verbatim-anchored. Some page citations are approximate. *[Minor]*
- **Higher-education hook is framing, not governance.** Washington names college-career-life readiness but assigns no institutional roles; the K-16 connection is weaker than Tennessee's or Virginia's. *[Scope of hook]*

documents.title: Guidance, Considerations, and Intentions for the Use of Artificial Intelligence in West Virginia Schools, Version 1.2
documents.issuer: West Virginia Department of Education (WVDE), West Virginia Board of Education
documents.type: State education-agency guidance (voluntary), adapted from TeachAI

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Human agency and existing-policy alignment.** The educator principles commit to using AI "in alignment with existing policies and regulations" and not sharing PII with consumer-based AI (guidance p.14).
- **AI literacy for students and self.** "I will educate myself about AI. Promoting AI literacy among students is central to addressing the risks of AI use" (guidance p.14).
- **Academic integrity as a culture.** "I will use AI in my classroom to advance a culture of academic integrity," preserving honesty, trust, fairness, respect, and responsibility (guidance p.14).
- **Workforce awareness.** Students "should be informed of the possible ways in which AI will impact the job market they will eventually enter" (guidance p.~200).

### Intended audiences and scope
- The guidance addresses educators (the "I will" principles) and schools/districts (the "We will" principles) (guidance pp.14, 23). *[Scope statement]*
- Scope is West Virginia public schools, grounded in WVBE governance and existing board policies. *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **There is no leveled permission scale.** West Virginia uses a principles-plus-prohibited-use structure. Educators "may decide to permit the use of generative AI tools for certain parts or types of assignments, providing clear explanations for its restricted use" (guidance p.21).
- **A Prohibited Use section sets explicit boundaries** (guidance p.24), each tied to a binding WVBE policy:
 - **Bullying/harassment** via AI-manipulated media is "strictly prohibited" (WVBE Policy 4373). *[Recommendation citing Requirement-level policy]*
 - **Overreliance** on AI is a named prohibited use (below).
 - **Plagiarism and cheating**, tied to WVBE Policy 2460, which prohibits plagiarism and requires teaching its consequences. *[Recommendation citing Requirement-level policy]*
 - **Equal access:** "If an assignment permits the use of AI tools, the tools will be made available to all students."
 - **Inappropriate material**, tied to WVBE Policy 2460's prohibitions. *[Recommendation citing Requirement-level policy]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Privacy is a principle.** Educators "will not share personally identifiable information with consumer-based AI" (guidance p.14).
- **Equity of access** is a prohibited-use safeguard, ensuring AI tools reach all students when permitted (guidance p.24).
- **Academic integrity has a dedicated section and recommendations** (guidance p.21): permit AI selectively with clear explanations; refrain from unreliable detectors; and require citation of AI use, with MLA, APA, and Chicago resources provided.
- **Position on AI detection tools:** advises against. Educators should "refrain from using programs that claim to detect the use of generative AI for cheating or plagiarism purposes due to concerns about their reliability" (guidance p.21). *[Recommendation — a caution against detectors]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **Curriculum integration is grounded in existing standards.** WVBE Policy 2520.14 (College- and Career-Readiness Standards for Technology and Computer Science) is repeatedly referenced as the standards backbone (guidance pp.~687, 781, 926). *[Recommendation citing Requirement-level policy]*
- **A companion Canvas hub** supports educator development.
- **Assessment guidance favors redesign.** Teachers "restructure assignments to reduce opportunities for plagiarism by requiring personal context, original arguments, or original data collection" (guidance p.24). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **A living-document practice** with a version-history table tracks updates (guidance Version History).
sections.offloading:
West Virginia names over-reliance as a predictable risk and a prohibited use.

- **Over-reliance is flagged as a predictable risk** early in the document, "predictable risks include over-reliance on AI" (guidance p.~186). *[Instructional guidance]*
- **Overreliance is a named Prohibited Use.** "Dependence on AI tools can decrease human discretion and oversight. Important nuances and context can be overlooked and accepted. Teachers will clarify if, when, and how AI tools should be used... through discussions and modeling, and teachers and students are expected to review outputs generated by AI before use" (guidance p.24). *[Recommendation, as prohibition]*
- **Human agency is a school/district principle.** Staff and students serve as "critical consumers" of AI, and "humans, and not the AI, will be responsible and accountable for pedagogical or decision-making processes" (guidance p.23).
- **Assignment redesign protects original work**, requiring "personal context, original arguments, or original data collection" (guidance p.24). *[Instructional guidance]*
- West Virginia does not include a dedicated cognitive-offloading section or grade-band gating; its offloading control is the overreliance prohibition plus the human-agency principle. *[Structural note]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a West Virginia graduate *may* bring. Because the guidance is voluntary and district-implemented, exposure varies.

- **Governed by district policy grounded in existing WVBE policies**, not a state scale (guidance pp.14, 24). *Basis: guidance.*
- **A citation-and-transparency habit** around AI use, with MLA/APA/Chicago guidance (guidance p.21). *Basis: guidance p.21.*
- **An overreliance-aware, human-agency framing** where teachers followed the principles (guidance pp.23-24). *Basis: guidance.*
- **An expectation that AI detectors are unreliable and discouraged** (guidance p.21). *Basis: guidance p.21.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat these as ceilings of possibility, not guarantees. West Virginia set no state scale, so faculty should expect district variance and no shared leveled vocabulary, but a shared TeachAI-style integrity and human-agency framing where the guidance took hold.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** West Virginia has a built-in K-16 governance link. The WVBE that issued this K-12 guidance seats, ex officio, the Chancellor of the WV Higher Education Policy Commission and the WV Council for Community and Technical College Education (guidance pp.28-29). Higher education is structurally present in the body that governs K-12 AI policy, even though the guidance does not assign universities operational roles.
- **Higher-education implication:** West Virginia students were taught that *AI detectors are unreliable and should be avoided* (guidance p.21). Institutions relying on detection software may face students trained to distrust it.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students from adopting districts may arrive expecting *selective, per-assignment AI permission with required citation* (guidance p.21) and an overreliance-aware, human-in-the-loop framing (guidance pp.23-24). A syllabus that specifies AI use per assignment and requires citation will feel continuous.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because West Virginia grounds AI in existing College- and Career-Readiness standards (WVBE Policy 2520.14), incoming students may connect AI literacy to career readiness rather than to a standalone AI regime.
- **Higher-education implication:** West Virginia shares TeachAI DNA with several other states (e.g., Utah). A university drawing students from multiple TeachAI-derived states may find a common principle vocabulary (help students, reaffirm policy, educate about AI, explore/address risks, advance integrity) worth building on.
sections.response:
- **Assessment design:** State AI permission explicitly per assignment with required citation, mirroring the guidance (guidance p.21). Preserve assignments requiring personal context and original work to protect against overreliance (guidance p.24).
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Do not rely on AI detectors, consistent with what West Virginia students were taught (guidance p.21); favor citation-, disclosure-, and process-based integrity.
- **Onboarding:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic at entry; district variance is high and no state scale anchors expectations.
- **Governance:** West Virginia institutions, particularly those under the Higher Education Policy Commission and the community/technical college council, can leverage their ex officio presence on the WVBE to align entry expectations with K-12 policy (guidance pp.28-29).
- **Human-agency framing:** Build on the "critical consumers" and human-accountability language West Virginia students may share (guidance p.23).
sections.unique:
- **A built-in K-16 governance link.** The WVBE roster seats the higher-education Chancellor ex officio (guidance pp.28-29), so the body governing K-12 AI policy includes higher education by design, an unusual structural feature.
- **A TeachAI-adapted, first-person principle structure**, five "I will" educator principles and parallel "We will" school/district principles (guidance pp.14, 23), shared with other TeachAI-derived states.
- **A Prohibited Use section anchored to existing WVBE policies** (2460, 4373, 2520.14), tying voluntary guidance to binding board policy (guidance p.24).
- **A clear anti-detector advisory** with a citation-first alternative (guidance p.21).
- **Grounding in College- and Career-Readiness standards** (WVBE Policy 2520.14), connecting AI to career readiness.
- **A version-controlled living document** with a change-history table (guidance Version History).
sections.gaps:
- **Voluntariness limits every claim about students.** The guidance mandates nothing itself and is district-implemented, so actual exposure is unknown and district-dependent. Per-district adoption data is Not found in the provided documents.
- **No leveled student-use instrument exists.** West Virginia uses a principles-plus-prohibited-use structure, not a 0-4 or 1-5 scale, and adapts TeachAI rather than the Perkins AIAS. This is a deliberate design choice.
- **The higher-education link is structural, not operational.** The Chancellor's ex officio WVBE seat (guidance pp.28-29) shows K-16 governance overlap, but the guidance does not assign universities AI roles or tasks. The hook is weaker than Tennessee's mandate or Virginia's assigned roles. *[Scope of hook]*
- **HB 5205 (WV Balance Act) is introduced, not enacted.** Per sources it would add screen-time limits by grade band, parental access to tools/credentials/browsing history, an AI sandbox course, and AI in CS standards, with State Board model-policy templates by Dec 1, 2026 and county adoption by July 1, 2027. All pending; no current requirement can be asserted. *[Unresolved]*
- **The underlying WVBE policies (2460, 4373, 2520.14) are cited but not provided as documents.** Their summaries are taken from the guidance's cross-references; the policy texts were not read for this analysis. *[Unresolved]*
- **PDF extraction produced font/ligature warnings**, but the principles, detector, and prohibited-use passages extracted cleanly and are verbatim-anchored; some page citations are approximate. *[Minor]*

documents.title: Empowering Lifelong Learning: AI Guidance for Enhancing K-12 and Library Education
documents.issuer: Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction (DPI), Division of Academic Excellence; State Superintendent Jill K. Underly

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **AI supports but cannot replace educators or librarians.** "AI supports human teaching and learning but cannot replace educators. The human component... teachers' and librarians' ability to inspire, motivate, and respond to individual needs, is irreplaceable" (guidance p.~136). *[Recommendation / stated philosophy]*
- **Lifelong learning through schools and public libraries.** The document frames AI integration "across Wisconsin's schools, libraries, and communities" (guidance p.~110). *[Recommendation / framing]*
- **Responsible, ethical, safe use** with attention to plagiarism, false resources, and bias (guidance p.~140).
- **Information and media literacy** as the critical-thinking backbone, guiding "staff and students in critically examining AI-generated results" (guidance p.~162).

### Intended audiences and scope
- Audiences are "K-12 educators, librarians, students, and administrators," plus "Library Staff and Patrons" (guidance pp.~118, 158). *[Scope statement]*
- Scope spans K-12 schools and public libraries, explicitly extending to lifelong and community learning (guidance p.~129). *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **There is no statewide permission scale and no statewide prohibition list.** Wisconsin delegates specifics to districts and libraries and offers a policy-consideration checklist rather than a permission instrument (guidance p.~165). *[Recommendation / not a scale]*
- The guidance's operative structure is a set of policy considerations (below) plus professional-development pillars, not a graduated student-use ladder. *[Structural note]*

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **A policy-considerations checklist anchors governance** (guidance p.~165): Code of Conduct and Academic Integrity Policies, Digital Citizenship Standards, Transparency and Consent, Data Encryption and Storage, Copyright Policies and Citation Guidelines, Digital Equity and Student Access, FERPA and COPPA compliance, Vendor Compliance, and Continuous Monitoring.
- **Data privacy and security have detailed key takeaways**: restrict student-data access, remove PII from datasets, define retention periods, maintain a breach-response plan, and comply with accessibility standards (guidance p.~178).
- **Digital equity and student access** are named policy areas (guidance p.~165).
- **Academic integrity is a listed policy area** tied to code-of-conduct and citation guidelines (guidance p.~165).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** the document does not center AI detectors. Its integrity approach is policy-, citation-, and media-literacy-based rather than detection-based (guidance pp.~162, 165). *[Not emphasized]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **The 5 Training Pillars structure professional development** for both K-12 and public-library faculty (guidance pp.204-207). Each pillar names concrete tools, e.g., Teachable Machine and Machine Learning for Kids under Hands-On Experiences (guidance p.~225). *[Recommendation / instrument]*
- **Curriculum integration is cross-disciplinary.** AI should be integrated "into various subject areas, not just computer science," from math to social studies to science (guidance p.~218).
- **Implementation favors starting small.** "Start small: Begin by implementing AI in a controlled setting before a full-scale integration" (guidance p.~278).
- **Wisconsin-specific professional networks** support ongoing learning: SLATE, the CESA Instructional Technology Services Committee, WEMTA (supporting "librarians and educators"), and the Wisconsin Digital Learning Collaborative (guidance pp.~233-239).
sections.offloading:
Wisconsin's offloading protection runs through its human-irreplaceability principle and its media-literacy emphasis rather than a dedicated section.

- **The human component is irreplaceable.** Teachers' and librarians' ability "to inspire, motivate, and respond to individual needs" cannot be replaced by AI (guidance p.~136).
- **Critical examination of AI output is the core habit.** The guidance promotes "information and media literacy efforts to guide staff and students in critically examining AI-generated results" (guidance p.~162). This librarian-led framing is Wisconsin's distinctive cognitive safeguard.
- **Foundational AI understanding precedes use.** Pillar 1 gives educators "foundational knowledge about AI and machine learning, including how these technologies work, their capabilities, and their limitations" (guidance p.~213).
- **Ethical reflection is built in.** AI use "presents opportunities to reflect on ethical concerns, such as plagiarism, false resources, and biases" (guidance p.~140). *[Instructional guidance]*
- Wisconsin does not include an explicit over-reliance/"productive struggle" section or grade-band gating; its cognitive protection is media literacy plus the human-irreplaceability principle. *[Structural note]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a Wisconsin graduate *may* bring. Because the guidance is voluntary and district/library-implemented, exposure varies.

- **Governed by district policy, not a state scale**, shaped by the state's policy-considerations checklist (guidance p.~165). *Basis: guidance p.~165.*
- **A media- and information-literacy orientation** toward critically examining AI output, if their teachers or librarians followed the guidance (guidance p.~162). *Basis: guidance p.~162.*
- **Possible exposure to hands-on AI tools** (Teachable Machine, Machine Learning for Kids, TensorFlow Playground) where educators used the pillars (guidance p.~225). *Basis: guidance p.~225.*
- **Familiarity with AI as a cross-disciplinary topic**, not only in computer science (guidance p.~218). *Basis: guidance p.~218.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat these as ceilings of possibility, not guarantees. Wisconsin set no state scale, so faculty should expect district variance and no shared leveled vocabulary, but possibly a stronger-than-average media-literacy habit given the librarian lens.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Wisconsin's distinctive contribution is reframing AI literacy as *lifelong and community-wide*, delivered partly through public libraries (guidance pp.~110, 129). This is not a university-governance hook, but it means incoming Wisconsin students grew up in a state that treated AI literacy as an adult and community capability, and academic and public libraries are positioned as continuing partners.
- **Higher-education implication:** The guidance's *media- and information-literacy* emphasis (guidance p.~162), driven by librarian authors, may leave Wisconsin students better prepared than average to critically evaluate AI output. University librarians can build directly on that foundation.
- **Higher-education implication:** Because Wisconsin set no state scale, incoming students are unlikely to share a leveled AI-use vocabulary. Faculty should specify per-assignment AI expectations explicitly.
- **Higher-education implication:** Wisconsin taught AI as a *cross-disciplinary* topic (guidance p.~218), so students may expect AI to appear across subjects rather than confined to computing courses.
- **Higher-education implication:** Wisconsin's guidance is silent on AI detectors, so students' prior experience with detection tools is unknown and district-dependent. Institutions should not assume a fixed prior stance.
sections.response:
- **Leverage libraries:** Because Wisconsin frames AI literacy through libraries (guidance p.~136), university and academic libraries are natural partners for AI-literacy onboarding, continuing the model incoming students experienced.
- **Media-literacy continuity:** Build on the critical-examination-of-AI-output habit Wisconsin students may share (guidance p.~162), extending it to disciplinary source evaluation and citation.
- **Onboarding:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic at entry; district/library variance is high and no state scale anchors expectations.
- **Assessment design:** State AI permission explicitly per assignment; Wisconsin students share no statewide scale or vocabulary.
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Favor policy-, citation-, and media-literacy-based integrity, matching the state's approach (guidance pp.~162, 165); set your own detector policy explicitly, since Wisconsin took no position.
sections.unique:
- **An explicit K-12-and-library, lifelong-learning scope**, including public libraries and community learning, with a School Library Consultant and a Public Library Consultant among the named authors (guidance pp.~30, 129). This library/lifelong-learning framing is unique in the dataset.

states.summary: Wyoming's guidance is a compact (9-page), recommendation-level policy-development guide built on two borrowed structures. Its principles come from the TeachAI toolkit, seven named principles: Purpose, Compliance, Knowledge, Balance, Integrity, Agency, and Evaluation (guidance p.~149). Its student-use instrument, the "Student AI Usage Continuum for Empowered Learning" (p.7), is adapted from the Perkins et al. AI Assessment Scale, with the attribution line "As adapted from: Dr. Leon Furze, Dr. Mike Perkins, Dr. Jasper Roe FHEA, & Dr. Jason Mcvaugh" (guidance p.7). Definitions are adapted from Washington OSPI's Human-Centered AI Guidance v1.0.

documents.title: Guidance for Wyoming School Districts on Developing Artificial Intelligence Use Policy
documents.issuer: Wyoming Department of Education (WDE); State Superintendent Megan Degenfelder; Digital Learning Plan Advisory Panel

sections.policy:
### Primary themes and policy objectives
- **Seven TeachAI-derived guiding principles** anchor the guidance (guidance p.~149): Purpose (use AI ethically to help all students), Compliance (reaffirm existing policies and federal law), Knowledge (promote AI literacy), Balance (realize benefits, address risks), Integrity (advance academic integrity), Agency (maintain human decision-making), and Evaluation (regularly assess AI's impact).
- **Human decision-making is preserved.** The Agency principle keeps "human decision-making when using AI" and asks how guidance "ensures that students retain appropriate agency" (guidance pp.~156, 261).
- **College and workforce preparation** frames AI literacy under the Knowledge principle (guidance p.~214).

### Intended audiences and scope
- The guidance is written for Wyoming school districts developing AI use policy, with a recommended advisory committee that includes a "Local College Representative" (guidance p.~141). *[Scope statement]*
- Scope is K-12 policy development, using guiding questions rather than mandates. *[Scope statement]*

### Permitted, restricted, and prohibited AI uses
- **The Student AI Usage Continuum (p.7) is the permission instrument**, an adaptable four-level example:
 - **AI FREE** — "Work must be completed entirely without any AI assistance. Students must rely entirely on their own knowledge, understanding, and skills. Any AI use is a violation of student academic integrity. An academic honesty pledge that AI was not used may be required."
 - **AI ASSISTED** — "AI is used for tasks as specified such as brainstorming, planning, or feedback. No AI content is allowed in the final submission. Usage beyond specified tasks is a violation of academic integrity. Disclosure statement & links to AI Chats should be submitted with final product."
 - **AI ENHANCED** — "AI is used interactively throughout... Student must provide human oversight and evaluation of all AI generated content... Student is responsible for the accuracy and [fairness] of all AI-generated content. Detailed disclosure statement and links to AI Chats."
 - **AI EMPOWERED** — full integration "enabling previously impossible creations," student responsible for accuracy, fairness, and originality, with detailed disclosure and chat links (guidance p.7).
- The continuum is offered as a model for districts to adopt or adapt, not a state rule.

### Privacy, security, equity, accessibility, ethics, and academic integrity
- **Compliance is a full principle.** Key policy areas are "privacy," compliance with federal law, and existing procedures (guidance p.~176).
- **Academic integrity is a principle and a continuum feature.** The Integrity principle addresses "plagiarism, and proper attribution issues," and every continuum level defines its integrity boundary (guidance pp.~228, 238, 7).
- **Equity and ethics** appear under Knowledge, "safe, equitable, and ethical use of AI" (guidance p.~214).
- **Position on AI detection tools:** the 9-page guidance does not center AI detectors; its integrity approach is continuum- and disclosure-based (chat links, honesty pledges) rather than detection-based (guidance p.7). *[Not emphasized]*

### Teacher training, curriculum integration, assessment, and implementation
- **A recommended district AI-policy committee** structures implementation and includes a Local College Representative (guidance p.~141).
- **Guiding questions drive policy development** under each principle (e.g., "How does our guidance highlight the purposeful use of AI to achieve our shared education vision?", guidance p.~168).
- **The continuum doubles as an assessment tool**, letting teachers set the permitted AI level per assignment with matching disclosure (guidance p.7).
- **Evaluation is a standing principle**, "regularly assess the impacts of AI" (guidance p.~157).
sections.offloading:
Wyoming's offloading protection is built into the continuum's design and the Agency principle.

- **AI FREE preserves unaided cognition** by definition: students "must rely entirely on their own knowledge, understanding, and skills," and any AI use is an integrity violation (guidance p.7).
- **Escalating human oversight across levels.** From AI ENHANCED up, students "must provide human oversight and evaluation of all AI generated content" and are "responsible for the accuracy and [fairness]" of it (guidance p.7).
- **The Agency principle keeps humans deciding.** It maintains "human decision-making when using AI" and asks how students "retain appropriate agency" (guidance pp.~156, 261).
- **Disclosure and chat-link submission** make AI use visible and accountable at every level above AI FREE (guidance p.7).
- Wyoming does not include a dedicated cognitive-offloading section or grade-band gating; its offloading control is the leveled continuum plus the Agency principle. *[Structural note]*
sections.graduate:
These describe habits a Wyoming graduate *may* bring. Because the guidance is voluntary and district-implemented, exposure varies.

- **Familiarity with a four-level AI-use continuum**, from AI FREE to AI EMPOWERED, where the district adopted it (guidance p.7). *Basis: guidance p.7, adaptable instrument.*
- **A strong disclosure-and-documentation habit**, specifically submitting links to AI chats with work above AI FREE (guidance p.7). Wyoming shares this with Oklahoma. *Basis: guidance p.7.*
- **A human-oversight-and-accountability orientation** at higher levels (guidance p.7). *Basis: guidance p.7.*
- **A college-and-career framing** of AI literacy under the Knowledge principle (guidance p.~214). *Basis: guidance p.~214.*
- **Higher-education implication:** Treat these as ceilings of possibility, not guarantees. Where the continuum was adopted, Wyoming students may arrive with transferable per-assignment AIAS-style vocabulary and a chat-link disclosure habit, but adoption is voluntary and district-dependent.
sections.implications:
- **Higher-education implication:** Wyoming's continuum shares its lineage with the peer-reviewed AIAS (Furze, Perkins, Roe, MacVaugh; guidance p.7). A university adopting the AIAS can expect adopting-district Wyoming students to recognize the leveled structure, and can cite the same peer-reviewed source for continuity.
- **Higher-education implication:** Wyoming builds higher education into district AI governance by recommending a "Local College Representative" on the policy committee (guidance p.~141). A Wyoming college may already be a named partner in the districts feeding it.
- **Higher-education implication:** Wyoming students may arrive habituated to *submitting links to their AI chats* as disclosure (guidance p.7), the same distinctive practice Oklahoma teaches. Faculty who want process transparency can build on it.
- **Higher-education implication:** Students from adopting districts may expect AI permission to be *specified per assignment* along a four-level continuum with matching disclosure and honesty pledges (guidance p.7). A silent or blanket syllabus will read as less clear than what they experienced.
- **Higher-education implication:** The Knowledge principle's college-preparation framing (guidance p.~214) suggests Wyoming students may connect AI literacy to postsecondary readiness.
sections.response:
- **Assessment design:** Adopt an explicit per-assignment AI-permission scale; the AIAS gives direct continuity with Wyoming's continuum (guidance p.7). Preserve AI FREE assessments where core-skill demonstration is the goal.
- **Disclosure practice:** Consider adopting the chat-link disclosure convention Wyoming (and Oklahoma) teach (guidance p.7), since incoming students may already practice it.
- **Governance and partnership:** Wyoming colleges can leverage the "Local College Representative" role (guidance p.~141) to align entry expectations with feeder districts.
- **Onboarding:** Give a short AI-literacy diagnostic at entry; the continuum's four levels are a ready placement rubric.
- **Academic-integrity processes:** Favor disclosure- and continuum-based integrity, matching the state's approach (guidance p.7); set your own detector policy explicitly, since the guidance takes no position.
sections.unique:
- **A four-level Student AI Usage Continuum** (AI FREE, AI ASSISTED, AI ENHANCED, AI EMPOWERED) with primary-printed AIAS attribution (guidance p.7), the third clearly confirmed AIAS-lineage instrument in the dataset.
- **A shared-source signal with Oklahoma.** Both states misspell "MacVaugh" as "Mcvaugh" in their AIAS attribution and both require submitting links to AI chats, suggesting a common intermediate adaptation source, useful for the cross-state comparison. *[Cross-state note]*

- **Definitions borrowed from Washington OSPI**, showing multi-source adaptation (guidance p.~55).
- **A compact, guiding-question policy-development format** (9 pages) aimed squarely at helping districts write their own policy.

frameworks.title: Course-Level Permission Scales
frameworks.body:
The single most transferable K-12 invention. Each scale makes AI permission a property of the assignment, not the course, and pairs every level with a disclosure expectation.

**The peer-reviewed spine.** Perkins, Furze, Roe & MacVaugh (2024), *The Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS)*. Four states print this citation in their official guidance. A university adopting the AIAS can cite scholarship rather than a state PDF, and gains vocabulary continuity with students from the adapting states.

**Oklahoma — AI Acceptable Use Rating Scale** (OSDE Guidance v2.0, July 2025, p.18). Five levels, 0 through 4, each with a use description and a disclosure requirement. Level 0 NO AI Use. Level 1 AI-Assisted Idea Generation and Structuring. Level 2 AI-Assisted Editing. Level 3 AI for Specified Task Completion. Level 4 Full AI Use with Human Oversight. Its distinctive feature is the disclosure column, which escalates from an optional honesty pledge at Level 0 to citation plus **links to AI chat transcripts** at Levels 1 through 4. *University adaptation: the most directly liftable version for a syllabus. The chat-link convention gives faculty process evidence without surveillance.*

**Washington — 5 Step Scaffolding Scale plus the Educator Matrix** (OSPI Human-Centered AI Guidance v3.0, p.20, with standalone companions). Levels run No AI Assistance, AI-Assisted Brainstorming, AI-Supported Drafting, AI-Collaborative Creation, AI as Co-Creator. The companion **Example AI Assignment Scaffolding Matrix** crosses real assignment types (longform essays, reflective writing, podcasts and video, research, problem sets) against the five levels, with a worked example in every cell. *University adaptation: the matrix is a course-design template. Fill one row per assessment type in your course and the AI policy writes itself. Puerto Rico teaches a verbatim Spanish translation of this scale, useful for bilingual campuses.*

**New Mexico — the AIAS with verbatim level names** (NMPED AI Guidance, signed April 2025, p.19, printed Perkins attribution with CC BY-NC-SA mark). NO AI, AI PLANNING, AI COLLABORATION, FULL AI, AI EXPLORATION. *University adaptation: the cleanest one-to-one bridge to the peer-reviewed source.*

**North Carolina — the "0 to Infinity" AI Use Continuum v2.0** (NCDPI living document, Appendix B). Five levels, 0 through 4, published in **two versions**: a teacher edition with assessment-design guidance and a student edition with plain-language dos and disclosure requirements. NCDPI's implementation tips include annotating unit plans with the intended level and starting the term at Level 0 or 1 before progressing to 3 and 4. *University adaptation: the two-audience design is the insight. Publish a faculty version and a student version of the same scale, and sequence levels across the semester.*

**A numbering caution.** Oklahoma and North Carolina number from 0. New Mexico, Washington, and Puerto Rico number from 1. Pick one numbering institution-wide and say so, because incoming students may know either.

---
