frameworks.title: Assignment Design and Decision Tools
frameworks.body:
**Vermont — the two-question test** (Vermont AOE AI Guidance v1.0, Jan 2026, Cognitive Offloading section). Before permitting AI on any task, ask what skill students should develop in the activity, and whether AI will help them practice that skill or perform it for them. The same document empowers instructors to say no. "Teachers should feel empowered to say when AI usage is inappropriate." *University adaptation: this is a complete assignment-design heuristic in two sentences. Put it in every course-design workshop.*

**Arizona — microtask and productive-friction design** (NAU Institute guidance, pp.26-27). The most sophisticated offloading treatment in the corpus argues that not all cognitive offloading is harmful, and that the real question is which thinking students offload and why. Instructors decide "which cognitive muscles to focus on and which ones rest," and design AI-infused tasks where students must explain their reasoning. *University adaptation: the framework for AI-permitted assignments. Let AI carry the mechanical load while the assessed object becomes the student's reasoning about it.*

**Kentucky — the three paradigms** (KDE brief, p.12, citing Ouyang & Jiao 2021). AI-directed (learner as recipient), AI-supported (learner as collaborator), AI-empowered (learner as leader). *University adaptation: a lens for classifying any AI-integrated activity by how much cognitive agency stays with the student. Maps cleanly onto course design and onto rubric language.*

**Colorado — the "If and How Checklist"** (Colorado Roadmap, Aug 2024, p.13). A structured decision aid for whether and how a given AI use enters instruction. *University adaptation: an adoption gate for new AI uses in a course or program.*

**Georgia — the redlight system** (GaDOE guidance, p.12, adapted from Phil Hintz). A three-signal per-assignment convention for showing students how much AI is permitted. *University adaptation: the lightest-weight option in the catalog. Where a five-level scale is too much machinery, three colors on the assignment sheet still beat silence.*

---
frameworks.summary: Vermont — the two-question test (Vermont AOE AI Guidance v1.0, Jan 2026, Cognitive Offloading section). Before permitting AI on any task, ask what skill students should develop in the activity, and whether AI will help them practice that skill or perform it for them. The same document empowers instructors to say no. "Teachers should feel empowered to say when AI usage is inappropriate." University adaptation: this is a complete assignment-design heuristic in two sentences. Put it in every course-design workshop.

frameworks.title: Lines AI Must Not Cross
frameworks.body:
**Georgia — the high-stakes versus non-high-stakes table** (GaDOE guidance, p.4). Enumerates uses where AI should not be the basis of decisions, including subjective grading, educator evaluations, and individualized-plan decisions. *University adaptation: the model for a faculty-facing "never delegate" list covering grading, admissions review, advising holds, and accommodation decisions.*

**Oklahoma — the statutory guardrail** (SB 1734, 2026, sec.1.E). AI tools "shall not be used as the primary basis for student grading, discipline, placement, promotion, retention, or other high-stakes educational decisions," with educator-directed deployment and human-in-the-loop review of outputs. *University adaptation: ready statutory language for an institutional policy on consequential decisions. Utah's framework states the compact version, "AI will not be solely responsible for grading."*

**Illinois and Maryland — the support-versus-judgment line.** AI may assist the machinery around evaluation (rubric drafting, feedback organization) while the consequential judgment remains human. Maryland adds the mirror-image warning for staff, citing the documented tendency to over-trust automated recommendations. *University adaptation: pair the student-facing rule with the faculty-facing automation-bias caution. Offloading is not only a student risk.*

---
frameworks.summary: Georgia — the high-stakes versus non-high-stakes table (GaDOE guidance, p.4). Enumerates uses where AI should not be the basis of decisions, including subjective grading, educator evaluations, and individualized-plan decisions. University adaptation: the model for a faculty-facing "never delegate" list covering grading, admissions review, advising holds, and accommodation decisions.

frameworks.title: Academic Integrity Without Detectors
frameworks.body:
**The fourteen-state caution.** Six jurisdictions tell educators to refrain from or eliminate reliance on AI-detection software (Washington, Massachusetts, West Virginia, Vermont, Colorado, Maryland). Eight more bar it as sole evidence (Illinois, Indiana, California, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico, Mississippi). Eight of the fourteen cite research or the tools' bias against multilingual writers. Louisiana stands alone in recommending detectors. *University adaptation: whatever position an institution takes, publish it. Fourteen state agencies wrote theirs down.*

**Washington — conversation anchored to the published scale** (OSPI v3.0, p.40). Instead of detector verdicts, know the student's voice through work gathered over time, and when misuse is suspected, hold a conversation anchored to the posted AI level for the assignment. *University adaptation: the procedural replacement for detection. The published scale converts an accusation into a shared reference point.*

**North Carolina — the teachable moment** (NCDPI living document, p.32). Suspected over-reliance "should be viewed as a teachable moment to reinforce the appropriate partnership with AI tools rather than a 'gotcha' moment." Vermont adds the welfare framing, treating integrity violations as potentially "a cry for help." *University adaptation: tone guidance for integrity offices. The first response is pedagogical, the process is preserved for genuine cases.*

**Disclosure and citation conventions.** Utah, West Virginia, Ohio, and North Carolina direct students to cite AI use in standard formats (APA, MLA, Chicago), with West Virginia linking the style guides directly. Oklahoma and Wyoming add disclosure statements plus chat links. Tennessee's model policy teaches "the difference between cheating and seeking support." *University adaptation: a one-page campus standard for AI attribution ends per-course reinvention.*

**Alabama and Colorado — the appeal right.** Alabama's template requires a process for students to contest AI-generated grades. Colorado recommends an appeal process covering both AI grading and accusations of AI use. *University adaptation: due process is the piece most campus AI policies forget. Two states already drafted it.*

---

frameworks.title: Protecting Learning from Cognitive Offloading
frameworks.body:
**Vermont — the dedicated treatment** (AOE Guidance v1.0, Cognitive Offloading section). Cites Mollick's "Against Brain Damage," uses the calculator analogy (you would not hand a calculator to a student first learning multiplication), and frames the educator's task as distinguishing the valuable learning tool from the crutch. *University adaptation: the rationale text for why some coursework stays AI-free. Quotable in any syllabus.*

**Minnesota — the repetition rationale** (MDE guidance, p.3). "Without clear boundaries, students may rely on AI to complete tasks they should be practicing themselves, bypassing the repetition necessary to build foundational skills and cognitive capacity." *University adaptation: the plainest-language justification in the corpus for AI-free foundational courses.*

**The AI-free floor.** Every leveled scale in the corpus reserves a bottom level where students rely solely on their own knowledge and skills. *University adaptation: a design principle, not just a rule. Any course using AI should also contain assessed work that certifiably does not.*

**North Carolina — semester sequencing** (NCDPI, Appendix B). Start the term at Level 0 or 1, progress to Levels 3 and 4 as students demonstrate disclosure, verification, and ethical use. Mississippi adds the mirror principle for supports, "gradually reducing students' reliance on these tools." *University adaptation: a semester arc. Early weeks certify unaided skill, later weeks grant earned AI collaboration.*

**Rhode Island — in-person performance checkpoints** (RIDE guidance, grade 9-12 band). Students "should demonstrate knowledge and skills with performance-based and in-person assessments to ensure they can perform without AI assistance." *University adaptation: periodic unaided demonstrations calibrate everything the process artifacts claim.*

**Pennsylvania — offloading as an assessed competency** (PDE AI Endorsement Framework, Domain 6). Teacher candidates must analyze "how cognitive offloading to AI systems influences attention, memory, and problem-solving," plus effects on socialization and belonging. *University adaptation: a ready module specification for faculty development and TA training.*

---
frameworks.summary: Vermont — the dedicated treatment (AOE Guidance v1.0, Cognitive Offloading section). Cites Mollick's "Against Brain Damage," uses the calculator analogy (you would not hand a calculator to a student first learning multiplication), and frames the educator's task as distinguishing the valuable learning tool from the crutch. University adaptation: the rationale text for why some coursework stays AI-free. Quotable in any syllabus.

frameworks.title: AI Literacy and Skill Frameworks
frameworks.body:
**New Mexico — the three-part literacy definition** (NMPED guidance, p.6, after Digital Promise). Users should "understand how AI systems function, evaluate its potential and risks, and apply it thoughtfully in real-world contexts." *University adaptation: a ready rubric for an entry diagnostic. Three axes, scorable in one short instrument.*

**Nevada — Understand, Apply, Integrate, Grow** (STELLAR Pathway, p.24). A four-stage learning arc for all stakeholders. *University adaptation: doubles as a within-course sequence for introducing any AI-permitted workflow.*

**The EVERY framework — Alaska and North Carolina.** Evaluate, Verify, Engage, Revise, and remember that **You** are responsible for the final product. *University adaptation: the verification habit in a mnemonic. The closing step, personal responsibility for AI-assisted output, is the norm universities most need to preserve.*

**Prompting frameworks, three options.** Missouri's Five S (Set the scene, be Specific, Simplify, Structure the output, Share feedback). North Carolina's CRAFT 2.0 with Power-Ups. Nevada's four elements (task, format, voice, context). *University adaptation: pick one and extend it toward disciplinary verification and sourcing, which is the college-level addition no state built.*

**Wisconsin — the five training pillars** (DPI guidance, June 2024). Understanding AI and Machine Learning Basics, Integrating AI into Subject Areas, Hands-On AI Experiences, Collaboration and Networking, Continuous Learning and Adaptability, each with named tools. *University adaptation: a complete faculty-development curriculum outline. Wisconsin's inclusion of librarians suggests the natural campus partner.*

---
frameworks.summary: New Mexico — the three-part literacy definition (NMPED guidance, p.6, after Digital Promise). Users should "understand how AI systems function, evaluate its potential and risks, and apply it thoughtfully in real-world contexts." University adaptation: a ready rubric for an entry diagnostic. Three axes, scorable in one short instrument.

frameworks.title: Faculty Development Models
frameworks.body:
**Massachusetts — the Design Divide** (DESE guidance, after the National Educational Technology Plan). Access to AI and use of AI get attention, while the capacity to *design* meaningful AI-integrated learning experiences does not. *University adaptation: the diagnosis that should set the faculty-development budget. Most campus AI training teaches acceptable use. The gap is assessment design.*

**Virginia — exploration first** (EO 30 Guidelines, Strategies). Educators need "hands-on experience to understand these technologies' capabilities and limitations" through structured, guided experimentation before policy debates. Montana and Nevada add low-stakes practice settings and communities of practice. *University adaptation: run faculty AI workshops as labs, not lectures, before asking departments to write policy.*

**Maryland — the automation-bias module** (MSDE framework). Professional learning must counter "the documented tendency to over-trust automated recommendations." *University adaptation: the faculty-side offloading training almost no institution runs.*

frameworks.title: Tool Vetting, Procurement, and Equity of Access
frameworks.body:
**Georgia — the seven-criterion Evaluation Process Rubric** (GaDOE guidance, p.10). A structured instrument for vetting AI tools before adoption. Vermont's Tool Vetting Framework adds the useful category split between general-purpose AI and education-specific chatbots. Colorado contributes an ISTE-derived evaluation tool, and Rhode Island a procurement checklist. *University adaptation: any of these converts ad hoc tool adoption into a reviewable process.*

**New Mexico — M.A.Z.E.** (NMPED guidance, p.10). Monitor data privacy, Assess for accuracy, Zero-in on bias, Evaluate value. *University adaptation: the pocket version, teachable to students as well as staff.*

**The tool-parity rule — Utah, West Virginia, North Dakota, Ohio.** If an assignment permits AI tools, the tools are made available to all students. North Dakota and Mississippi explicitly flag free-versus-paid tier gaps. *University adaptation: the equity floor. An institution that permits AI on assessed work either provides the tool or accepts that grades partially price a subscription.*

**Vermont — the training-data standard** (AOE guidance, Data Privacy). Removing student names is not enough, because student work itself is intellectual property that trains the vendor's model. Contract against secondary use. Alabama grounds its whole template in the NIST AI Risk Management Framework for institutions that want a formal risk scaffold. *University adaptation: two clauses for every AI procurement contract, no training on student work and no secondary use of student data.*

---
frameworks.summary: Georgia — the seven-criterion Evaluation Process Rubric (GaDOE guidance, p.10). A structured instrument for vetting AI tools before adoption. Vermont's Tool Vetting Framework adds the useful category split between general-purpose AI and education-specific chatbots. Colorado contributes an ISTE-derived evaluation tool, and Rhode Island a procurement checklist. University adaptation: any of these converts ad hoc tool adoption into a reviewable process.

frameworks.title: Institutional Governance and Self-Assessment
frameworks.body:
**Michigan — the maturity rubric** (Michigan Virtual AI Integration Framework). Three stages (Investigating, Implementing, Innovating) crossed with eight domains (Leadership and Vision, Policy and Legal, Instructional Framework, Learning Assessments, Professional Learning, Student Use, Operations, Outreach). The project's own analysis notes it works for a university by substituting "institution" for "district." Arkansas's adoption of it proves the rubric travels. *University adaptation: the annual self-assessment. Locate your institution in each row, then fund the lowest-stage domain.*

**Ohio — the fill-in-the-blank model policy** (DEW Model Policy, Dec 2025). A complete board-policy template with bracketed placeholders, covering purpose, definitions, literacy, stakeholders, privacy, procurement, ethics, acceptable use, integrity, and review. Its stakeholder section seats postsecondary partners by name. *University adaptation: the fastest honest starting draft for an institutional policy, and a reminder to put student and faculty representatives in the drafting room.*

**Maryland — the named owner** (SB 720). Every system designates a central-office AI coordinator. Missouri and Ohio recommend the same role. *University adaptation: accountability has a job title. Without one, AI policy is everyone's committee and no one's job.*

**North Carolina — the living document with a public update log** (NCDPI). Version history table, dated changes, continuous revision. Montana commits to a biannual review cycle. *University adaptation: publish the policy with its changelog. The log is what makes revision routine instead of controversial.*

**North Dakota — role-based checklists.** Five implementation checklists (School Leadership, Educators, Business and IT, Policy and Legal, Public Outreach). *University adaptation: the format insight. One institutional policy, five one-page role translations, so the registrar and the department chair each get their own to-do list.*

---
frameworks.summary: Michigan — the maturity rubric (Michigan Virtual AI Integration Framework). Three stages (Investigating, Implementing, Innovating) crossed with eight domains (Leadership and Vision, Policy and Legal, Instructional Framework, Learning Assessments, Professional Learning, Student Use, Operations, Outreach). The project's own analysis notes it works for a university by substituting "institution" for "district." Arkansas's adoption of it proves the rubric travels. University adaptation: the annual self-assessment. Locate your institution in each row, then fund the lowest-stage domain.

frameworks.title: Student Rights and Support
frameworks.body:
**The appeal path — Alabama and Colorado**. Contest rights for AI-assisted grades and AI-use accusations.

**Rhode Island — accommodations protection** (RIDE guidance). Grading approaches must not penalize students for accommodations or modifications supported by AI, with explicit instruction for differently-abled students. Washington empowers special-education students to use AI for access and personalization. *University adaptation: an explicit carve-out in every course AI policy so a ban never makes assistive technology contraband. Coordinate with disability services before publishing any restriction.*

**Oklahoma — transparency and opt-out architecture** (SB 1734, secs.1.F-G). Annual disclosure of every AI tool in use, its vendor, the data collected, and its purpose, plus an opt-out that cannot academically penalize the student. *University adaptation: an annual student-facing AI tool disclosure would exceed nearly every university's current transparency, and the no-penalty principle matters wherever campus tools quietly embed AI.*

**Ohio — conduct provisions for AI-enabled harm** (DEW Model Policy, Other Considerations). Names non-consensual intimate imagery and AI-enabled impersonation for bullying and harassment, tied to state law. Six states carry deepfake or NCII prohibitions. *University adaptation: student-conduct codes written before generative AI rarely cover synthetic media harms. The K-12 language is a ready patch.*

---

instruments.name: AI Acceptable Use Rating Scale
instruments.source: Guidance and Considerations for Using Artificial Intelligence in Oklahoma K-12 Schools, Version 2.0, July 2025, page 17
instruments.attribution: Adapted by Dr. Karen Leonard for the Oklahoma State Department of Education (OSDE) from the work of Dr. Leon Furze, Dr. Mike Perkins, Dr. Jasper Roe FHEA, & Dr. Jason Mcvaugh.

levels.label: NO AI Use
levels.permits: This activity is to be completed entirely without AI assistance. AI MAY NOT be used at any point during the activity. This level ensures that students rely solely on their own knowledge, understanding, and skills.
levels.disclose: No AI disclosure required. May require an academic honesty pledge that AI was not used.

levels.label: AI-Assisted Idea Generation and Structuring
levels.permits: No AI content is allowed in the final submission. AI can be used in the activity for brainstorming, creating structures, and generating ideas for improving work.
levels.disclose: AI disclosure statement. Link(s) to AI chat(s) must be submitted.

levels.label: AI-Assisted Editing
levels.permits: No new content can be created using AI. AI can be used to make improvements to the clarity or quality of student-created work to improve the final output.
levels.disclose: AI disclosure statement. Link(s) to AI chat(s) must be submitted.

levels.label: AI for Specified Task Completion
levels.permits: AI is used to complete certain elements of the task, as specified by the teacher. This level requires critical engagement with AI-generated content and evaluating its output.
levels.disclose: All AI-created content cited. Link(s) to AI chat(s) must be submitted.

levels.label: Full AI Use with Human Oversight
levels.permits: Students may use AI throughout the activity to support their own work in any way the educator allows. AI should be a co-pilot to enhance human creativity.
levels.disclose: Cite the use of AI. Link(s) to AI chat(s) must be submitted.

exposure.headline: Your students arrive with
preshow: This is a diagnosis, not a checklist. Each point below names one thing your incoming students were taught to expect, one thing your syllabus or handbook probably does not say, and who the mismatch fails.

Nothing here assumes every student arrived trained. Adoption varies by district and most K-12 guidance is voluntary, so you cannot tell which students were taught a rule and which were not. A syllabus that says nothing about AI fails both of them, in opposite directions. The trained student concludes your course expects less than her high school did. The untrained student concludes anything is allowed.
exposure.noHook: No state requirement reaches your institution. The case rests entirely on merits, and your students were taught these rules anyway.

points.title: Permission is a property of the assignment, not the course.
points.taught: Each task carries a posted level, from an AI-free floor up to full disclosed collaboration. The level was taught, not inferred.
points.says: One rule for the whole course, or nothing at all.
points.fails: The trained student, who reads a blanket rule as less rigorous than their high school.
points.position: Post a level on every assignment rather than one rule for the term. Where your institution has not chosen a vocabulary, use the AI Assessment Scale, since it is the peer-reviewed source four states already print.
points.evidence: Seven jurisdictions publish a leveled permission scale. Four attribute it to Perkins, Furze, Roe and MacVaugh (2024). Oklahoma runs Level 0 through Level 4 and requires disclosure that escalates with the level.

objection.q: This is micromanagement, and it intrudes on academic freedom.
a: Academic freedom covers what you decide, not whether students can find out what you decided. A posted level does not tell you which level to pick. It makes the choice you already made legible to the person being graded on it.

The current alternative is not freedom. Each student privately guesses what you allow, and is then graded against the guess. Publishing the level costs one line per assignment and removes the guessing.

points.title: Disclosure has a named format.
points.taught: A citation format, a disclosure statement, and in two states a retained link to the AI chat itself.
points.fails: The honest student, who wants to disclose and cannot find out how.
points.position: Name the disclosure format in the syllabus. State where the disclosure goes, what it must say, and whether you want the chat transcript.
points.evidence: Oklahoma requires a disclosure statement plus links to the AI chats at every level from 1 upward, meaning any AI contact at all obliges the student to hand over the conversation. Wyoming carries the same chat-link convention.
chips: UT, WV, OH, NC citation formats

objection.q: Students will simply lie about it.
a: Some will. Disclosure is not detection and does not pretend to be. What it changes is the default for the students who were going to be honest and currently have nowhere to put it.
A chat link is also a verifiable artifact rather than an assertion, which is a stronger evidentiary position than the one you hold now.

points.title: If a tool is required, it is provided.
points.taught: Tool parity. A school that requires a tool supplies it, so the paying student holds no advantage.
points.says: Nothing about who pays for the tool it assumes you have.
points.fails: The student on the free tier, graded against classmates on the paid one.
points.position: Adopt a parity rule. Either the institution supplies the tool an assignment requires, or the assignment cannot require it. Audit what free-tier access actually produces before assuming it is equivalent.
points.evidence: Utah, West Virginia, North Dakota and Ohio publish tool-parity expectations, and several states pair them with a vetting rubric covering privacy and vendor accountability.

objection.q: We cannot afford site licenses for every tool a faculty member wants.
a: Then the rule bites in the other direction. Parity is a design constraint on assignments, not a budget line. An assignment that requires a paid tool the institution will not buy is an assignment that grades household income.
K-12 systems with far smaller budgets reached this conclusion first, which makes it difficult to argue the principle is unaffordable rather than unexamined.

points.title: Some work is AI-free, and the reason is taught.
points.taught: An explicit rationale for protecting unaided work, including the calculator analogy and the argument from repetition.
points.says: AI is prohibited on this assignment, with no reason given.
points.fails: Every student, who reads an unexplained ban as distrust rather than as pedagogy.
points.position: Keep an AI-free floor and say why it exists. Tie it to the specific skill the assessment is meant to demonstrate rather than to integrity in general.
points.evidence: Every leveled scale in the corpus preserves an AI-free floor. Oklahoma states that Level 0 "ensures that students rely solely on their own knowledge, understanding, and skills." Vermont borrows the calculator analogy and Minnesota argues from repetition.

objection.q: Explaining the reason just invites students to negotiate it.
a: They negotiate now, and they do it from a worse starting position, because an unexplained prohibition looks arbitrary and arbitrary rules attract challenge.
A stated reason converts the conversation from whether the rule is fair into whether the skill matters, which is a conversation you are equipped to win and they were taught to have.

points.title: A detector result is not proof, and they were told so.
points.taught: Seven jurisdictions publish detector skepticism in writing. Maryland calls detectors unreliable and inequitable. Illinois calls a result one data point.
points.says: Nothing, while the detector runs inside your LMS by default.
points.fails: The multilingual student, who carries the highest false-positive exposure and was never taught to expect it here.
points.position: Publish your detector stance before a case arises. State that detector output never stands alone as evidence, that concerns begin with a conversation anchored to the posted level of that assignment, and that a student may contest any AI-related finding.
points.evidence: Seven jurisdictions publish caution about detectors and 22 are silent, which this project records as a gap rather than as endorsement. No state guidance in the corpus instructs a teacher to treat a detector result as sufficient evidence of misconduct. Washington and North Carolina describe the response as a conversation, and North Carolina names it a teachable moment.
chips: IL one data point, not proof

objection.q: We already have an academic integrity office and the detector is built into the LMS. This is solved.
a: The detector being available is not a position on what it proves. Your integrity office has a process for adjudicating a charge. It does not have a published standard of evidence for this particular charge, and the difference surfaces the first time a multilingual student is flagged and asks what the threshold was.

Seven state education agencies wrote that standard down for teenagers. A faculty member enforcing an unpublished one is exposed personally, and so is the institution on appeal. Publishing the stance costs a paragraph and removes the improvisation.

points.title: There is a way to contest the finding.
points.taught: An appeal path, including for a grade that AI helped produce.
points.says: Appeals exist for grades, and no one has said whether this counts.
points.fails: The wrongly accused student, who cannot tell which office to go to.
points.position: Name the appeal route for AI-related findings explicitly, and cover AI-assisted grading as well as AI-use allegations. If the existing grade appeal covers it, say so in those words.
points.evidence: Alabama and Colorado publish appeal paths. Several states bar AI from serving as the sole basis for consequential judgments about students, including Oklahoma by statute and Utah, which rules that AI "will not be solely responsible for grading."
chips: OK statutory bar on high-stakes AI
UT not solely responsible for grading

objection.q: Our existing grade appeal process already covers this.
a: Then the fix is a sentence, not a process. The problem is not that the route is missing. It is that no student can tell whether an AI allegation is a grade dispute, a conduct charge, or both, and the two run on different clocks with different standards.
Students arriving from states that published the route will look for yours, and not finding it reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

featuredFrameworks:
1. **A per-assignment permission scale** with a genuine AI-free level (start from Oklahoma's, below, or the peer-reviewed AIAS it adapts).
2. **Vermont's two-question test** as the faculty habit for deciding when AI belongs in an assignment.
3. **A published institutional position on AI detectors and appeals**, informed by the fourteen-state caution documented below.

Everything else in this catalog strengthens those three.

---

overview.scene:
Two first-year students sit in the same section of the same course. One came through Oklahoma. Her high school taught a five-level AI Acceptable Use Rating Scale adapted from a peer-reviewed academic source. Every assignment carried a posted level. At Level 0 she signed an honesty pledge that no AI touched the work. Above Level 0 she submitted links to her AI chat transcripts with the final product. Her state guidance told her AI detectors produce false positives and should not decide integrity cases. The other student came through Texas. His state issued no classroom AI guidance at all. Whatever rules he met were his district's invention.

The syllabus in front of them says nothing about AI. Their other four syllabi say four different things, or nothing. The Oklahoma student reads the silence as a step down in rigor from her high school. The Texas student guesses. Both are one misreading away from an integrity case.

*Provenance: a composite built from the project's per-state analyses (Oklahoma, Texas) and the cross-state comparison, Implications #2. It is illustrative. State guidance is mostly voluntary and adoption varies by district, so not every Oklahoma graduate had this training. Some did. You cannot tell which by looking.*
overview.thesis:
Two independent claims. Neither borrows strength from the other.

- **The merits claim.** K-12 built instruments higher education should adopt because they are good: a peer-reviewed permission scale, disclosure-based integrity, and a defensible rationale for keeping some work AI-free. This is true no matter how many students arrive trained.
- **The tail claim.** A growing minority of entrants carry taught priors: per-assignment permission expectations, distrust of detectors, disclosure habits down to chat links. Those priors will collide with improvised course policies. Because no one can tell which students carry them, the only rational response is entry diagnosis plus one published institutional floor.
overview.moves:
1. **Adopt one institutional permission scale with a genuine AI-free floor** and require every syllabus to use it. Owner: provost.
2. **Publish three positions now**: the detector stance, the data rule, and the appeal path. Owner: provost and general counsel.
3. **Answer six questions on every syllabus**: which scale, what default level, how to disclose, which tools are provided to all, what happens on suspicion, how to appeal.
4. **Run an entry diagnostic** instead of assuming a baseline, and screen both tails: CTE-trained students with real technical skill, and no-baseline students who need the full floor. Owner: first-year experience.
5. **Audit your own syllabi** for one week. Count how many state any AI rule at all. That number is your local readiness evidence. Owner: teaching center.

readiness.verdict:
**The short answer is no, in three provable senses, with one legal exception and one timing grace period.** This section states the verdict the rest of the document acts on, and it splits the thesis into two independent claims so that neither has to borrow strength from the other.

**The two-claim thesis.**
- **The merits claim.** Higher education should adopt K-12's instruments because they are good on their own terms: a peer-reviewed permission scale, a disclosure-based integrity model, and a defensible rationale for AI-free work. This claim is true regardless of how many students arrive trained. **[K-12 Evidence + Recommendation]**
- **The tail claim.** A growing minority of entrants carry taught priors — per-assignment permission expectations, disclosure and chat-link habits, detector skepticism — that will collide with silent or improvised course policies. Because no institution can tell which students those are, the only rational response is an entry diagnostic plus one published institutional floor.

Stated separately, the two claims resolve the corpus's own tension: the finding that within-cohort variance exceeds between-state variance weakens "students arrive trained" as a universal, but leaves it intact as a tail claim — and the tail is what collides first.

**The three provable deficits.**
1. **No shared course-level vocabulary.** Seven K-12 jurisdictions taught a leveled permission scale, four citing a peer-reviewed source universities could adopt tomorrow; higher education, per the author's premise, offers none. **[K-12 Evidence + Author framing]**
2. **No published positions on the documented collision points.** K-12 wrote down its detector stances, disclosure conventions, and appeal paths; an institution without published positions on those three points meets the first dispute unprepared. **[K-12 Evidence + Inference]**
3. **No diagnostic capacity.** No one measures what entrants actually know about AI — and K-12 does not either; only Idaho even directs an assessment, still pending. An institution that cannot see its incoming variance cannot manage it. This deficit is universal and fully evidence-based.

**The Tennessee nuance.** The corpus's only direct evidence about higher education's own obligations cuts against a simple "higher ed lagged" story: Tennessee law required every public university to adopt an AI policy by July 1, 2025 — *before* most K-12 district deadlines (Ohio's July 1, 2026; Oklahoma's 2027-28), with a legislative-hearing backstop for noncompliance. A skeptical dean will raise this, so raise it first — and note what it converts into: compliance is unrecorded anywhere in the corpus, so a Tennessee public institution without an adopted policy today is not merely unready but past-due noncompliant. That is the single most concrete readiness finding available. **[K-12 Evidence + Inference]**

**The timing window.** Every scale instrument in the corpus dates from 2024-2025 (North Carolina January 2024, Washington March 2024, Wyoming June 2024, Puerto Rico August 2024, New Mexico April 2025, Oklahoma v2.0 July 2025). A student entering college in fall 2026 spent at most about two years under the earliest instrument, and only if their district adopted voluntary guidance. Scale-socialized cohorts therefore arrive in force roughly 2027-2029. The accurate urgency claim is not "they are already here" but "institutions have a two-to-four-year preparation window" — with one exception that collapses the window to zero: dual-enrollment students are living the collision now, governed by a K-12 scale and a college syllabus in the same week. **[Inference from instrument dates in the Comparison

---
readiness.faculty:
### Course-level AI expectations
1. **Declare an AI level for every assignment**, not one global course rule. Scale-state students experienced permission as a property of the task, posted and explicitly taught. A silent or blanket syllabus reads as *less* clear than their high school.
2. **Use the AIAS as the level vocabulary** where the institution has not chosen one: it is the peer-reviewed source four states print, and structurally compatible with Washington's and Puerto Rico's scales.
3. **Reserve a genuine AI-free floor** for assessments whose goal is core-skill demonstration, the one control every scale state implemented.
4. **Keep AI out of consequential judgment about students.** Follow Georgia's high-stakes table, Oklahoma's statutory bar, Illinois's and Maryland's support-versus-high-stakes lines, and Utah's rule that AI "will not be solely responsible for grading".

### Syllabus language
Every syllabus should answer six questions, each grounded in a taught K-12 practice:
- **Which scale governs, and what is the default level?**
- **How is AI use disclosed?** Named citation format, disclosure statement, and, where process transparency matters, links to AI chats.
- **Which tools are permitted, and are they provided?** Tool-parity rule.
- **Why are some tasks AI-free?** Borrow the taught rationales: the calculator analogy and the repetition argument.
- **What happens on suspicion?** A conversation anchored to the published level, not a detector verdict.
- **How does a student contest a finding or an AI-assisted grade?**

*Model clause, synthesized from the cited practices*: "Each assignment in this course carries a posted AI level, from an AI-free floor (no AI at any point; you rely on your own knowledge and skills) to full, disclosed AI collaboration. Where AI is permitted, you must disclose how you used it, cite it in [format], and retain your chat links. I will never treat detector output as proof; concerns begin with a conversation, and you may appeal any AI-related finding." *(Numbering note: state adaptations differ — Oklahoma and North Carolina number the floor Level 0; New Mexico and Puerto Rico number it Level 1. Pick one numbering, publish it, and keep it; see the Instruments Annex.)*

### Assessment and assignment design
- Design **AI-resilient tasks**: personal context, original arguments, original data collection; reasoning, analysis, reflection, and process over recall, with visible evidence of student thinking; real-world and collaborative work.
- **Collect process artifacts** — outlines, drafts, chat links — as the assessed object at AI-permitted levels.
- **Anchor unaided competence** with performance-based, in-person checkpoints, the practice Rhode Island sets for grades 9-12.
- **Sequence levels across the term**: begin at Level 0-1 and progress toward 3-4 as students demonstrate disclosure, verification, and ethical use.

### Teaching practices that reduce cognitive offloading
See; the two course-level essentials:
- Apply Vermont's two-question test before permitting AI on any task: what skill should students develop, and will AI help them practice it or perform it for them.
- Use Arizona's microtask/productive-friction design: decide "which cognitive muscles to focus on and which ones rest," and require students to explain their reasoning inside AI-infused tasks.

### AI literacy instruction
- Teach evaluation before generation: the verification duty and output critique for accuracy and bias, extending the middle-school habit the gating states built.
- Use New Mexico's **teaching-with versus teaching-about** distinction and its interrogation prompts as ready-made classroom moves.
- Extend, do not restart, prompting instruction: students may arrive with Five S, CRAFT, or task/format/voice/context; the college-level addition is disciplinary verification and sourcing.

### Feedback, attribution, and academic-integrity processes
- **Accept and normalize attribution**: APA/MLA/Chicago AI citation plus disclosure statements; invite chat links where they help.
- **Handle suspicion by conversation, not verdict**: anchored to the posted level, framed as a teachable moment, alert to distress.
- **Never use a detector as sole or decisive evidence.** Fourteen states' guidance cautioned against relying on the tools, and eight of those files cite unreliability or bias against multilingual writers; expect some students to cite that guidance. If the institution permits detectors at all, publish that position explicitly.
- **Do not penalize AI-supported accommodations**.
- **Keep grading human.** AI may support instructor workflow, but consequential evaluation stays with the instructor.

---
readiness.administrators:
### Institution-wide AI policy
1. **Check your statutory position first.** Tennessee public institutions were required to adopt AI policies by July 1, 2025, with a noncompliance hearing; Maryland names a four-year institution to certify K-12 tools; Virginia assigns roles to every public college; Texas exempts higher education; New Jersey's program-offering mandate is pending.
2. **Adopt one institutional permission scale with an AI-free floor**, and require every syllabus to use it. Learn from the mandate states' gap: requiring that a policy exist without minimum content reproduces K-12's variance problem.
3. **Integrate rather than proliferate.** Fold AI into existing integrity, conduct, and procurement policy with cross-references, the Kentucky normalization and Indiana fold-in approach, rather than a standalone parallel regime.
4. **Publish the institution's detector position explicitly** — the corpus guarantees students arrive with contradictory taught priors.
5. **Operate a review cycle, not a document**: scheduled review plus a public update log.
6. **Build the appeal path** covering AI-assisted grading and AI-use allegations, and keep AI out of high-stakes decisions institutionally, mirroring Oklahoma's statutory bar.

### Approved tool availability
- **Guarantee tool parity**: any tool an assignment permits, the institution provides to every enrolled student. Audit free-versus-paid tiers annually.
- **Adopt a vetting rubric**: Georgia's seven-criterion evaluation rubric, Vermont's Tool Vetting Framework, Colorado's ISTE-derived evaluation tool, and Rhode Island's procurement checklist are ready templates.
- **Contract against training on student work.** Vermont's position — de-identification is insufficient because student intellectual property still trains the model — is the strongest taught privacy standard; procurement should meet it.
- **Meet accessibility standards in procurement**.

### Student onboarding
Fund and mandate the program described in, a common-floor module, and targeted bridges. Onboarding is where the corpus's variance problem is either absorbed or passed through to every classroom.

### Faculty development
- **Target the Design Divide** — faculty capacity to *design* AI-integrated learning, the gap Massachusetts names and Oregon echoes — not merely acceptable-use awareness.
- **Run exploration-first, low-stakes PD**: hands-on structured experimentation before policy debate, safe practice settings and communities of practice.
- **Import ready pedagogy** rather than commissioning it: Arizona's microtask design, Vermont's two-question test, New Mexico's distinctions and prompts, Wisconsin's five training pillars.
- **Train against automation bias**, the educator-side offloading risk Maryland names.
- **Align teacher-preparation programs** with the state instruments that now govern them: Pennsylvania's six-domain, 12-credit endorsement with a PK-12 capstone; Georgia's educator-preparation involvement; Montana's university-system mandate; Iowa's pending invitation to CS teacher-prep institutions.

### Privacy, accessibility, equity, and procurement
- Hold the FERPA/COPPA floor plus applicable state overlays; enforce the PII prohibition in every sanctioned workflow.
- **Govern surveillance-adjacent tools with care.** The same tool category is described approvingly in Utah (distress monitoring) and litigated on First and Fourth Amendment grounds in Kansas (the Gaggle case). Proctoring, wellness-flagging, and communications monitoring sit in unresolved legal space.
- Protect AI-supported accommodations from integrity penalties.

### Academic support and advising
- Equip advisors with the state-variance picture (the Comparison's matrix) so they can read an incoming student's likely priors from jurisdiction and district.
- Position writing centers and libraries to teach disclosure, citation, and verification — extending the librarian-led media-literacy model Wisconsin demonstrates.
- Provide a bilingual bridge for Puerto Rico students, whose AI vocabulary (SENSE, the five niveles) is Spanish and whose experience was single-platform and supervised.
- Train integrity officers in conversation-first process.

### Governance, assessment, and continuous improvement
- **Name an accountable owner**, mirroring Maryland's required AI coordinator and the coordinator roles Missouri and Ohio recommend.
- **Take the offered seats**: Ohio and Wyoming invite postsecondary representatives onto district AI workgroups — a direct channel to feeder-district expectations.
- **Self-assess annually** with an adapted maturity rubric: Michigan's three-stage, eight-domain instrument transfers to institutions by substitution, per its own state file; Rhode Island and North Dakota supply getting-started and procurement checklists.
- **Track the moving parts**: pending statutes (NJ, IA, SC, NY, WV; Virginia's unverified enacted text) and living documents (NC, WI) can change entry assumptions between admission cycles.

---
readiness.roadmap:
Phased, with owners and evidence anchors.

**Phase 0 — Orient (first 30 days).** *Owner: provost + general counsel.*
- Determine the institution's statutory position (bound, tasked, invited, exempt, or pending: TN / MD / VA-MT-WV / OH-WY / TX / NJ).
- Inventory existing integrity, conduct, privacy, and procurement policies; choose integration over a standalone AI regime.
- Publish three interim positions immediately: detector stance, PII rule, tool-parity commitment.

**Phase 1 — Establish the floor (first term).** *Owner: named AI coordinator.*
- Adopt the institutional per-assignment scale with an AI-free floor; prefer AIAS vocabulary for K-16 continuity.
- Issue the syllabus template answering the six questions.
- Pilot the entry diagnostic and two-tail screen.
- Stand up the tool-vetting rubric and run the first parity and free-tier audit.

**Phase 2 — Build capacity (first year).** *Owner: teaching-and-learning center + student affairs.*
- Launch Design-Divide faculty development: exploration-first, low-stakes, community-of-practice format, with the imported pedagogy set and an automation-bias module (MA/OR; VA; MT/NV; AZ/VT/NM/WI; MD).
- Roll the onboarding module to all entrants; open the bridges (PR bilingual; multi-tool orientation).
- Establish the appeal path and conversation-first integrity procedure; train integrity officers (AL/CO; WA/NC/VT).
- Where applicable, align teacher-preparation programs to the state endorsement/preparation instruments (PA; GA; MT; IA).
- Request seats on feeder-district AI workgroups (OH, WY).

**Phase 3 — Operate and improve (ongoing annual cycle).** *Owner: AI coordinator, reporting to governance.*
- Run the annual review with a public update log (MT/MO/OH/NC practice).
- Self-assess with the adapted Michigan maturity rubric; act on the lowest-stage domain.
- Track pending and maturing statutes (NJ, IA, SC, NY, WV; VA text verification) and living state documents (NC, WI); refresh onboarding assumptions per cohort.
- Measure and report: diagnostic score distributions over time, integrity-case outcomes under the conversation-first process, accommodation non-penalization audits, and tool-parity compliance. *Measurement design is institutional invention; the corpus contains no outcome-measurement models to borrow*.

---
readiness.limitations:
**Inherited from the Comparison (apply to every claim above):**
1. **Voluntariness bounds all student-level claims.** Most K-12 guidance is non-binding and district-implemented; no per-district adoption data exists anywhere in the corpus.
2. **Coverage holes:** five jurisdictions' guidance substance was uncaptured (DE, FL, HI, ME, NY's district guidance); two rest on ledger records rather than read text (NY, TX); four third-party substitute documents are non-retrievable (NH coalition, SD ASBSD, KS KU framework, MT MTSBA); Virginia's two enacted statutes are text-unverified. Students from these jurisdictions cannot be profiled beyond the structural facts.
3. **Absence claims are search-bounded**, not certified; **living documents** (NC, WI, MT, WV) may have changed since capture; **detector silence is systematically ambiguous**.
4. DC and Puerto Rico are **not states**, and their governance differs in ways that change how "guidance" binds.

**Specific to this translation document:**
5. **Policy ≠ practice ≠ learning.** This document reasons from what policies *say* to what students *may know*. The corpus contains no measured student outcomes; only Idaho even directs the creation of AI-literacy assessment, still pending. Every profile claim is therefore an inference from policy exposure, which is why the diagnostic, not the profile, should drive placement.
6. **The cohort-variance thesis is itself an inference** — well-grounded in the corpus's structure, but not an empirical finding.
7. **Recommendations are synthesis, not validated interventions.** The faculty and administrator guidelines extend documented K-12 practices into a higher-education setting; none has been evaluated in that setting within this evidence base.
8. **Discipline-specific guidance is absent from the corpus**, so all discipline-level advice here is inference from general-purpose instruments.
9. Corrections identified during the state pass (Washington's scale reversal, Puerto Rico's level names, Louisiana's single SAMR model, Utah SB 322's failure, and the consumer-protection statutes mis-scoped as school law) are folded into the Comparison but still pending in the project's `VERIFICATION` and `data.js`.

---
